i declare resumed the session of the european parliament adjourned on friday 18 december 2020. first of all, i would like to wish all my colleagues a happy new year and hope that everyone had a good holiday.
ladies and gentlemen, 30 years ago, on 13 january 1991, 14 civilians were killed and hundreds were injured when soviet tanks attacked the television tower in vilnius. lithuanians were defending their independence and freedom, they were defending democracy and the rule of law. these are our european values and today we pay tribute to those citizens who defended these values with their lives. and speaking of fundamental values, we are deeply concerned by the arrest of alexei navalny, which took place on his return to moscow yesterday. europe saved his life and we thank the german authorities for their care and assistance. we call on the russian authorities to release mr navalny. his detention constitutes a violation of human rights; we support him and we would like him to come and visit us here in the european parliament soon.
the agenda includes the report by javier zarzalejos, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the implementation of the european arrest warrant and surrender procedures between member states (2019/2207 ((ini)) (a9-0248/2020). i would remind the honourable members that there is no catch-the-eye procedure for all the debates this part-session, as there is unfortunately at this stage, nor will there be any blue-card questions. in addition, there are plans for remote intervention by the parliament's liaison offices in the member states, as we are now used to doing.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i present to the house the report on the application of the european arrest warrant drawn up by the libe committee. we are talking about an essential instrument of judicial cooperation and, consequently, one of the foundations of the area of freedom, security and justice. the order, which was introduced by the framework decision of 13 july 2002, is without doubt the most outstanding achievement in the field of judicial cooperation that we have achieved in the union and has paved the way for other instruments that have subsequently allowed this path of progress to continue. replacing the traditional extradition procedure, based on distrust between legal systems, with a surrender procedure based on trust and mutual recognition of judicial decisions, was a real leap forward for the rule of law and for the reparation of victims by eliminating the areas of impunity. throughout the discussion of this report - for which i have had the honour of being rapporteur - i have insisted that the european arrest warrant's track record is, on the whole, a remarkable success. but at the same time, we believe there is room for improvement. the debate on these improvements has been a complex one from a legal point of view, but it is a good and timely one. the order has raised important issues throughout its lifetime which have been largely clarified by valuable case law of the court of justice of the european union. the court has strengthened this instrument of cooperation in two ways. on the one hand, it has clearly situated the surrender procedure within the framework of the fundamental rights and procedural guarantees it must respect. it also reaffirmed the states' obligations to cooperate, avoiding any departure from the spirit and letter of the framework decision in its application and transposition into national law. i think the commission is aware of this situation, as is clear from the report it has recently presented, and we encourage it to correct these deviations, also, if necessary, through the relevant infringement procedures. the report i am presenting is based on this balance between effective cooperation and guarantees. the text is clear in proposing that the use of the order should meet criteria of proportionality and consistency with other instruments of judicial cooperation already in force and less intrusive, so that, where those instruments can achieve the same result, they are used. i would like to make it clear and conclusively clear that the concern to incorporate a framework of stringent guarantees with respect for fundamental rights is very clearly present in the text and has been the central subject of our discussions. we have not ignored the objective factors which are affecting confidence between states today, but, in the line of interpretation laid down by the court of justice, we want to maintain an attitude of extreme caution so as not to damage this crucial instrument of cooperation. delivery is the general principle, and refusal to execute an order should be the exception, interpreted narrowly and duly substantiated. the report proposes to extend the current list of 32 crimes or categories of crime that do not require double criminality control to include 10 new categories ranging from certain types of tax evasion, violence against women, web-specific crimes, hate crimes, acts of mass pollution, crimes against public order involving the grave threat or use of violence or against the constitutional integrity of states involving the use of violence, as well as crimes of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. we believe that the logic of cooperation must lead to new spaces in which cooperation can take place more smoothly between states which protect essential legal assets, between states which are parties to and which are recognised as members of a community of law. it is precisely in order to make this cooperation more fluid that we do not overlook the practical aspects of strengthening the role and means of eurojust, as well as improving the training of legal operators, specialising the national bodies that have to deal with the delivery procedures and also improving the information available on the application of the order. i would like to thank all the groups for their contributions. we have been able to discuss this matter in the best possible spirit, and i have personally tried to make a special effort to facilitate a broad agreement which was reflected in the vote of the libe committee at the beginning of last december. i would like to stress in this connection that the commitments agreed broadly cover the vast majority of the 235 amendments which were tabled. i hope that consensus will be maintained and i hope that those who did not join that initial agreement will be able to join today. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, no one will deny that security and freedom - the binomial that is wrapped up in what we call the rule of law - are facing new challenges, new forms of crime, powerful technological means used against them, new threats of violent destabilisation, new forms of victimisation. the only alternative to impunity is cooperation. the best guarantee for the defence of fundamental rights is effective judicial cooperation against crime. this report seeks to contribute to that reflection, to contribute to strengthening this cooperation with all the guarantees that are part of the legal acquis of the european union, and to that end i ask parliament to support the text proposed today.
madam president, commissioner reynders, the euro-order is a mechanism which operates on the principles of mutual trust between states and respect for fundamental rights. but mutual trust cannot be confused with blind trust, since there are still european countries with clear deficiencies in the field of justice. that is why the debate today should be about how to strengthen procedural guarantees, not about how to get an express arrest. ladies and gentlemen, this house cannot open debates or propose reforms of mechanisms just to satisfy the repressive impulses of some. we are playing with the credibility of this parliament. adding the crime of constitutional integrity to the list of direct extradition crimes will not facilitate the arrest of catalan leaders, but will open the door to unjust or arbitrary extraditions for those states with little affection for the european values of justice and freedom.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the need to reform and improve the council framework decision governing the euro order is of vital importance, a fact which is also indisputable for this group. membership of the european union implies respect for the rights and guarantees enshrined in article 2 of the treaty and, therefore, the removal of border controls in the schengen area cannot serve as an excuse for criminals with economic means to seek convenient fora to evade justice in the member states and avoid what happened in 2018, when only 7 000 of the 17 000 euro-warrants issued were executed. this is the case, for example, of the terrorist natividad jáuregui, who was tried by the spanish judges for the murder of lieutenant colonel ramon romeo, who spent seventeen years in belgium without the belgian courts accepting a decision of the spanish courts. despite the urgency and the scale of the problem, this own-initiative report is lukewarm and ideological in content, because, while it recognizes the fundamental principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions, it opens up numerous loopholes and avenues to avoid their application. it is an abusive instrument of the rule of law mechanism, which has nothing to do with it. we are here. we either respect the laws passed by the member states in the national parliaments or we respect the position of criminals who seek refuge in forums of convenience. it is therefore necessary for us in the european parliament to say that crimes against the integrity and constitutional order of the member states are crimes in any case, without any need to call for violence. nor do we think it is appropriate for ideological issues such as opinion crimes to be included in this reform of the euro order under the guise of hate crime or even the controversial guise of gender-based violence. for all these reasons, and out of respect for the victims in all cases, we are going to decide to abstain from voting on this decision and to ask the commission to improve this document technically, in order to guarantee the judicial sovereignty of the member states.

the next item on the agenda is the debate on the statement by the vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy on the arrest of aleksei navalny (2021/2513 ((rsp)). i would like to inform the honourable members that, for all the debates of this part-session, there will be no 'catch-the-eye' procedure and no blue papers will be accepted. in addition, remote interventions by parliament's liaison offices in the member states are foreseen.
vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, the arrest on live tv of the russian opposition leader, alexei navalny, upon his return to moscow last sunday, is unacceptable both to europe and to the international community, who believe in the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. yesterday, i issued, on behalf of the european union, a declaration with a clear message that we condemn the arrest of mr navalny, and that we stand in strong solidarity with him. the president of the european council and the president of the commission also issued a statement in this sense. mr navalny’s rights must be fully and unconditionally respected and enforced, and the politicisation of justice is unacceptable. we call upon the russian authorities to release mr navalny and all the journalists and activists who have been detained in connection with his return. let me also share how glad i am that mr navalny has recovered from the severe poisoning he suffered in august 2020. my biggest recognition goes to all those, especially the medical staff and the team around mr navalny, who have been treating and supporting him over the last months. as i said, in our plenary discussion on the case of mr navalny that we had here in september, the eu condemns in the strongest possible terms the assassination attempt, through poisoning, using a military chemical nerve agent from the novichok group. as a reaction, the european union, in october 2020, responded by imposing in a strict manner restrictive measures on six individuals and one entity involved in the assassination attempt. these are highly ranked officials in russia, including the director of the federal security service of the russian federation (fsb). as you know, any further decision on sanctions is for the council to take. i am looking forward to this very timely discussion about such an important issue.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, dear members of the european parliament, at the foreign affairs council meeting in october, the european union ministers and i agreed that our relations with latin america and the caribbean have not been high enough in our political agenda and that we should change this, not just by saying but through concrete action. the first act of this action was the ministerial conference that the german presidency hosted in berlin on 14 december, which i had the honour to chair, and i think it was a great success. 49 foreign ministers from the european union, latin america and the caribbean participated in berlin together with leading partners like the european investment bank, the eu-lac foundation and the eu-american general secretariat. the european parliament also play an important role. the chairs of the committees on foreign affairs (afet), international trade (inta) and development (deve) as well as the chair of the eurolat and the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly were also invited to participate as observers. dear members, as we wait for the incoming president, joe biden (president of the united states, evidently), there is a strong interest about the new transatlantic relationship with washington. however, on the other side of the atlantic there is not only the us; sometimes when you talk about transatlantic relations it looks like on the other side there is only the united states. there are other transatlantic relations. we must not forget these other transatlantic relations – the one that unites europe with latin american and caribbean countries. we, in many respects, are the closest people in the world. we share a history, dramatic history but our history, languages and cultural values. we have a dense network of institutional ties with the region. we have political and trade cooperation agreements with 27 out of the 33 countries in this region. it’s one of the most dense networks of institutional relations that we have with any other region in the world. we are the third largest trading partner, the third – we were the second, now the second is china, every day more present in latin america, and china has recently moved ahead of us. but we are still the leading investor in latin america, with a direct investment stock worth almost eur 800 billion at the end of 2018. and i want to tell you something that people are surprised at, because it’s not very well known. the investment of the european union economy’s firms in latin america is bigger that what we have been investing in china, in india, in japan and russia all together. all together, not one by one. more than in china, plus india, plus japan, plus russia – surprising, but it’s real. our investment focuses on a strategic sector – telecommunications and energy – and these are priority areas for our green deal and the digital transformation. so, as demonstrated during the ministerial conference in berlin, our regions fully agree on the need to defend multilateralism and will join forces to advance towards a greener, more sustainable development model. together we represent almost one third of the votes in the united nations. it’s a big political potential. our aggregated influence, as a standard-setter, will become even stronger. together we can better tackle the existing health crisis and its socio-economic consequences. latin american and caribbean countries have been very active, particularly in the covid-19 pandemic. unhappily they have been heavily hit. with 8% of the world population, the region represents one third of global deaths and now is facing the biggest economic recession in its history. the pandemic is exacerbating structural gaps, inequalities and social exclusion. the increase in social unrest does not help, particularly where governments are making a strong effort to tackle the structural violence. these are, i think, good and enough reasons why we must show real solidarity and engagement with latin america. we are already doing something – more than something; not enough, but quite a lot. we are already the region’s leading development cooperation partner and the leading provider of humanitarian assistance. we have mobilised eur 2.4 billion in emergency aid to help latin america to fight against the pandemic. it looks a lot, but it’s a drop of water in the ocean of the need they have. this is, however, not enough, given the scale of the problem. dear members of the european parliament, working together with our transatlantic partners on environmental issues is especially important, given that latin america is home to 50% of the world’s biodiversity – and don’t forget the amazon rainforest is the major lung for our planet. as part of the green partnership with the region, we are preparing a key european initiative that can address the drivers of deforestation of the amazon. that will be aligned with the 2019 leticia pact. we also look ahead to the cop26 in 2021. we all need to step up our ambitions on climate issues, as we agreed also in berlin. there we also agreed on the need to promote digital alliances to make the most of the opportunities offered by people focused on digital technologies. you know that we are going to have a new underwater optic cable stretching across the atlantic. it’s called bella. it’s a digital highway for knowledge and exchange of information between our countries: a powerful example of the benefits of working together. in a nutshell, the berlin ministerial conference has confirmed that we are on the right track, but we have to go quicker – we have to speed up our relationship. the track is good, but we are too slow. we have important work in front of us. this year we need to move forward with the signature and ratification of our modernisation agreement with mexico and chile, as well as an eu agreement with mercosur, which has been in negotiation for 20 years. i know these are sensitive issues, but we cannot say that we want to engage and to be best partners and to work together with latin america and not ratify in the way that you consider appropriate, because this parliament has to ratify this agreement, these long deal agreements with mercosur and the modernisation of the agreements with mexico and chile, who have a long story behind them. they were the first and the best agreements that we signed with a third country. they have provided extraordinarily good results and they have to be modernised. mexico is this year the chair of the latin american countries association. this is a good year to sign this agreement. this is a good year to have a high-level meeting with latin america. in the last five years we haven’t celebrated any summit with latin american countries. here in brussels we have a summit almost every day with someone. in the last five years, we haven’t had any one with latin america. do you think it is a sensible thing? no, it’s not. so i would like the parliament to put on all the pressure in order to reinvigorate our relations with latin america and to take seriously the ratification of the agreements with mexico and chile and to look for a solution for the mercosur. i know that this parliament has already said that under the current circumstances and the way it is, it will not be ratified by the honourable members. let’s look for a solution. let’s look for a complementary statement, declaration, whatever you can imagine, but don’t throw through the window 20 years of effort and work, go back to the initial point and tell the latin american countries that in this difficult moment of their history we are not going to agree with them in order to increase our economic and trade and investment relationship. i really urge you to take this very much into consideration. these ambitious treaties include political, cooperation, trade, and sustainable development aspects which will reinforce our ties and our shared defence of an international rules-based order, and from any point of view we will be better off with these association agreements than without them. you can rest assured that the position of this parliament is well noted, and please help me, help us, help the commission, help the council, on working to set the right conditions for the entry into force of these agreements.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, i would like to thank all the honourable members. i am very much aware that it’s very late. we have been accumulating delays and i have also contributed to that because i was too long in my first intervention. i am not going to try to answer all the questions that you have put in your interventions. i have to summarise by saying that, overall, all in all, i think we can be relatively satisfied by what we have achieved in 2020. i will not make hyperbolic declarations about how well we have been doing on everything, because i am very much aware that we have to do more. i prefer to say that we have to do more and better. but, at the same time, let’s value what we have done on the cfsp, csdp and human rights. covid has accelerated changes in the international landscape and this means that we have to continue working on our strategic autonomy. this only means a capacity to act, nothing more and nothing less, working with partners – and tomorrow we will have a new and important partner – reinforcing multilateralism, and remaining multilateral and autonomous – autonomous when it’s needed, and together with others when we can. in these efforts the european parliament has played, and will continue to play, an important role. i thank all of you for your contributions, and i continue to count on you to push forward the agenda of building a security and foreign policy for the european union and to protect human rights worldwide.
in writing. – the european union continues to encounter multi-faced threats to its regional security and the annual csdp report of 2020 provides a comprehensive summary of the current global issues. the report reflects on and sets main goals for the csdp accentuating the need to increase the eu`s resilience and preparedness. i want to highlight that international society must keep a unified standing and continue to condemn russia`s military intervention and illegal annexation of the crimean peninsula and the keeping of the frozen conflict in moldova. we strongly disapprove of russian violations of international law, attempts to destabilise the region and oppression of opposition. i support the need to introduce more robust strategy and endorse the necessity to proactively counter aggressive and malicious disinformation campaigns coming from third countries and non-state actors. attention must be paid to the fact that eu is witnessing an unprecedented scale of state-sponsored disinformation campaigns in the eastern neighbourhood countries and other regions. this calls for a need to also strengthen the mandate of the eeas strategic communication team to address foreign interference. i will express strong support to the annual csdp report with my vote.
in writing. today i would like to highlight the important report by ms santos, as the issue of human rights and democracy in the world is an important part of the european union's policy. it affects international relations and is also a reference point for internal community relations. the crisis caused by the global covid-19 pandemic and the way countries have responded to it have reduced the sense of economic and legal security, especially for the most vulnerable and marginalised groups. this has caused a crisis in international relations. in addition, human rights activities have been severely affected. the crisis caused by the pandemic has led many countries to adopt measures that restrict civil liberties. there were reasonable doubts as to their necessity, proportionality and non-discriminatory nature. the violation of religious and religious freedoms is of particular concern. let us not forget that an important part of human rights is also the rights of national minorities, especially indigenous ones, which cannot be restricted or violated in any way, and this is unfortunately the case in many countries of the world and in the european union. the latest european initiative minority safepack, supported by over a million citizens and actively participated by poles in the vilnius region, should therefore become a model for legal solutions in the field of protection of the rights of national minorities in europe and the world, since the right to preserve one's ethnic, linguistic and cultural identity is an inalienable human right.

esfuerzos, no ha mejorado. hemos tenido ocasión en anteriores encuentros de discutir, informarles a ustedes y recibir sus críticas y opiniones sobre los esfuerzos diplomáticos que la unión europea ha consecuencia, la asamblea nacional que resulta de esas elecciones no puede considerarse legítimamente elegida. la falta de pluralismo político y la descalificación de los dirigentes de la oposición, que finalmente decidió no presentarse a los comicios —también, sobre eso, en el pasado mes de agosto tuve la ocasión de intervenir tratando de mediar entre la oposición y el gobierno, sin éxito—, sumadas a la falta de participación del electorado no nos permiten considerar que la asamblea nacional constituida el 5 de enero pasado sea representativa de la voluntad democrática, libremente expresada, del pueblo de venezuela. las elecciones no cumplieron con los parámetros internacionalmente aceptados para dar credibilidad al proceso y, mediante dos declaraciones en nombre de la unión europea, hemos dicho claramente que no podemos reconocer ni las elecciones ni la legitimidad de la asamblea resultante de ella. mantendremos la necesaria presión —calibrada y selectiva— y dialogaremos con todos los actores que estén dispuestos a trabajar por la restauración democrática del país, empezando, por supuesto, por juan guaidó y los representantes de la asamblea nacional saliente y legítimamente elegida en el 2015. es evidente que las dificultades son grandes. queda mucho camino por recorrer. y con este proceso electoral fallido se acaba de desaprovechar una oportunidad que hubiera sido muy valiosa para alcanzar el objetivo de una salida política democráticamente establecida a la crisis del país. ahora, más que nunca, debemos ayudar a nuestros amigos venezolanos —a todos los venezolanos— a superar la división política, que cada vez demuestra ser más improductiva y que ha alejado a la ciudadanía de sus líderes —como quedó demostrado también con una enorme abstención—, y la unidad de acción de la oposición venezolana es fundamental. tuvimos que reclamar esa unidad de acción en los meses previos a las elecciones y seguiremos exigiendo el fin de las amenazas contra la oposición, las persistentes violaciones de derechos humanos y que se dé protección a los actores de la sociedad civil, que cada día trabajan para proveer a decenas de miles de personas de servicios esenciales para su supervivencia. según las cifras que estiman la organización internacional para las migraciones y la oficina del alto comisionado de las naciones unidas para los refugiados, son cinco millones de venezolanos los que han salido del país. pero, si continúa la tendencia, a finales de este año pueden ser más de seis millones. el gobierno de venezuela del señor maduro niega esas cifras —las disminuye mucho—, pero yo creo que las cifras que nos dan los organismos de las naciones unidas merecen credibilidad y, si son lo que dicen ser, estamos a los niveles de siria. a finales de este año puede haber tantos emigrantes venezolanos como los ha habido en siria por una atroz guerra civil. por lo tanto, señoras y señores miembros del parlamento europeo, tenemos que afrontar la situación con honestidad y con la voluntad de encontrar soluciones. las soluciones no serán exógenas. no se alcanzarán con declaraciones y mucho menos con intervenciones militares. tampoco se forjarán de la noche a la mañana internamente en venezuela. pero si algo podemos hacer desde europa —desde luego, podemos y debemos hacerlo— es apoyar a los protagonistas verdaderos de esta tragedia —que son los venezolanos— promoviendo el acercamiento de posiciones para la convocatoria de nuevas elecciones sobre bases que ambas partes puedan aceptar. y repito, la única salida duradera a los graves problemas de venezuela será una que sea políticamente dialogada, integradora, pacífica, con la participación de todos los actores políticos de la sociedad civil. sé que eso es difícil; la experiencia nos lo ha demostrado —y a mí personal y directamente de una manera evidente en este año pasado—. requerirá una voluntad de diálogo y concesiones por parte de todos los actores. la nueva administración americana puede también contribuir a este proceso. este parlamento sabe mejor que ninguno la importancia del consenso, y también sabemos que, en todas las transiciones políticas que ha habido en el mundo, la solución ha sido pactada. es fundamental que se acerquen posiciones para que venezuela no siga cayendo en el vacío de su crisis. vamos a convocar al grupo internacional de contacto. no lo hemos hecho hasta ahora por las dificultades logísticas que implicaban las circunstancias de la covid en muchos países. ha habido una toma de posición por parte de la unión europea; otra, por parte del grupo de lima. y, para terminar, y a escasas veinticuatro horas de la inauguración de un nuevo gobierno en estados unidos, permítanme —aparte de reiterar la felicitación al nuevo presidente— esperar que podamos compartir con la nueva administración americana —un socio imprescindible— esfuerzos para promover esta solución pacífica, dialogada e integradora que necesita venezuela. estaremos en contacto con la nueva administración —como lo estamos con la delegación noruega y con otros agentes políticos— para seguir trabajando políticamente con este fin. y también espero el apoyo del parlamento europeo a través de sus deliberaciones, debates y tomas de posición para contribuir a conseguirlo.

madam president, mr prime minister, you have made climate the heart of your speech and the european agenda and, not surprisingly, you have not mentioned mercosur, because the free trade agreement on mercosur, because of soybeans, beef, bioethanol, is more than 25% deforestation and therefore contributes massively to climate change. however, mr prime minister, since 2000, the year in which negotiations with mercosur were opened, portugal has deforested 5.5 times its area in the amazon. 5.5 times the size of your country and you know, you were prime minister at the time of the terrible fires that ravaged your country. so, mr prime minister, since you want the agreement to be ratified, how will you justify to your portuguese compatriots the forthcoming forest fires caused by climate change? madam president, when there is a new pandemic caused by deforestation, industrial livestock farming, what will you say to the citizens of europe? when there is a health scandal about pesticides or animal abuse in brazil, when there is a corruption scandal, how will you justify to the europeans that you have signed? so reopen this agreement, you cannot say that today we cannot reopen the agreement with mercosur, at a time when everything is changing.
madam president, prime minister, the cloud of key words that will identify the portuguese semester will be very similar to that which identified the german presidency: next generation eu, digital transition, climate emergency, but also pandemic, confinement, vaccines, economic crisis and unemployment. it is true that the portuguese presidency will open a new stage in the relationship with the united states and will have the opportunity to restore, with president biden, everything that president trump has broken. in this sense, we have full confidence in the ability and the atlantic vision of portugal. but what worries me most is everything that is clouded by the pandemic cloud. i am referring above all to rights and freedoms, certainly in eu countries like spain that have political prisoners and use repression against political dissidents. please mr prime minister, fight to ensure that the pandemic does not make human rights and fundamental rights invisible. can we beat the virus without freedom? covid—19 maybe yes, but the crypto-fascism virus, no.

madam president, i say to the prime minister: thank you for your clear commitment on the conference on the future of the european union. i know that there are still some problems in the council, but i know your strengths. i think you are maybe the only one who can overcome that in the council, and there is also good reason to do so, that conference, because it’s not because now that trump is out and biden is in that we can do business as usual. we have reacted better to the covid-19 crisis in comparison to the financial crisis – which was a disaster, because it took us 10 years to have the banking union and it’s still not there. there are still weaknesses in the european union. migration is not solved. the problem of our geopolitical weakness in our relationship, for example, to russia: not solved. the rule of law: a number of countries not biding by the rules. i think we need this conference urgently and i count on you, prime minister, to achieve that in the council in the coming weeks if possible.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. you were right to defend the european vaccination strategy. but for the current phase of the pandemic, we need much more than a common vaccination strategy. acute is a highly contagious mutation that spreads across borders. many more people could die if the safeguards and shutdowns continue to be decided at different times and at national level. we now need a binding synchronisation of the corona policy in europe, that is, a common staged plan with as uniform measures as possible at the same incidence levels. top scientists have already made similar suggestions in the contain covid initiative. mrs von der leyen, prime minister costa, please be brave at the eu summit tomorrow. the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal to make it more flexible. anything else, with border closures, would cause massive damage. a strong eu plan against corona is the order of the day in the face of the new threat! that is the task of the eu summit tomorrow!
madam president, the german presidency of the council has been a forgettable one. under his mandate a multiannual financial framework has been negotiated for the next seven years, which consists of an unacceptable reduction in the cap to satisfy the green lobby and which is not designed at all to help european companies and workers, who, after our elders, are the worst affected by this pandemic. a financial framework that will blindly allocate billions to the green agenda without paying attention to the reality of our economies, while unemployment and the desperation of the self-employed and small and medium-sized enterprises rise. a german presidency that has ended with the announcement of a regrettable investment agreement with communist china, a country responsible for this crisis of death and desolation by action or omission. we spaniards have high hopes that the presidency of a sister nation, portugal, will bring some common sense to this drift, strengthen the protection of the mediterranean axis and help to explain that the great diversity of our agricultural and livestock sector does not constitute a threat to the environment, but remains its greatest and best ally. all the luck in the world, president costa.
in writing. the portuguese presidency presented its three main priorities: promoting europe's recovery; implementing the union's social pillar; and strengthening europe's strategic autonomy by keeping it open to the world. the presidency will support the creation of a health eu, which strengthens the capacity to respond to public health crises, to produce and distribute safe vaccines, to ensure a universal, simultaneous, public and free vaccination process. the spanish delegation shares these priorities and calls on the presidency to accelerate the transition to a more sustainable model, taking advantage of new technologies and promoting a fair recovery: investment must contribute to reducing inequalities, the wage gap, unemployment and ensuring decent housing for all. we need to reform economic governance so that the social pillar is as important as economic growth, and suspend tax rules until 2023, taking this time to reform them, introducing, for example, the golden rule for social investment. we must put forward an action plan at the social summit in porto, with measures such as child benefit, unemployment insurance, and the creation of a european health response mechanism to move forward with the european health union.
in writing. the current pandemic has triggered a social and employment crisis, already generating an upward trend in rising unemployment, worsening working conditions, as well as an increase in inequalities and poverty in europe. the recovery plan and the new mff are primarily aimed at mitigating the negative effects of this crisis in all its forms. however, from a social point of view, we need more. we need to emphasise more the social dimension within these recovery mechanisms, if we are to really achieve a socially sustainable europe that leaves no one behind. we also need the new financial framework to increase the budget for the esf+, the only instrument designed to alleviate the adverse social effects of this crisis, to implement the pillar of social rights, and to put in place measures which are a priority for socialists, such as the child guarantee. in short, a large budget, which ensures that the social objectives are compulsorily met, and the establishment of concrete and tangible indicators of social investment to be included in the european semester and in the national recovery plans.

that the housing cost overburden indicator reflects the reality of what families are living and is set at no more than 25% of their disposable income; that the provision of adequate and affordable housing is guaranteed for the bottom three quintiles of society; and that 30% of new housing is affordable for people on medium and low incomes. evictions and homelessness are a violation of human rights. we must firmly support the housing first programme. regulation of the rental market and the real estate sector is also needed, by tackling housing speculation, increasing taxes on large housing holders and the supply of rented housing - especially publicly owned housing - and regulating holiday platforms. finally, the energy renewal wave has to start by rehabilitating the homes of the most disadvantaged groups, and it is up to us as regulators to ensure that electricity suppliers adopt protection schemes to ensure the supply of energy to the most... on behalf of the green group, madam president, i would like to emphasize the constructive attitude that has been shown during the preparation of this report. the result is an ambitious text that demonstrates how covid-19 has only widened gender inequalities that were already unacceptable before the pandemic. this report provides a good analysis of the consequences of covid from a gender perspective and, in addition, makes concrete proposals to reverse, or at least curb, these inequalities. however, we have two things to regret. first, that the report is late. this text was to be used to influence the recovery funds, but its vote comes when the packages and measures are already agreed. the second is that we have lost an opportunity to call for a care pact, a care pact that not only invests in the care sector, but also fosters a transition to a care economy that puts people's well-being and lives at the center of all policies. i am sure we will have occasion to discuss the assistance pact, because it must be the central issue for the union from now on.

the authorities conducted mass arrests under the national security law. the 53 arrested stand accused of subversion for participating in the pro—democracy primary elections held in july 2020. the criminalisation of legitimate political activity is aimed at stifling pluralism, pro—democracy voices and the exercise of political and fundamental freedoms in hong kong. the arrests on 14 january of 11 individuals implicated in the attempted escape to taiwan of 12 hong kongers further compounds the impression that the criminal justice system is being deployed to punish dissent. since the imposition of the national security legislation by beijing over hong kong, the eu has conveyed with the great unity its strong concerns publicly in a serious of declarations and directly to the chinese leadership at the summit in june and the leaders’ meeting in september. the leaders’ meeting of december was not only the occasion to conclude negotiations in principle on a comprehensive agreement on investment with china but also to raise concern on hong kong. the eu will continue to stand firm on its values and principles, while pursuing its interests. and the same effort in july, the council adopted an eu response package comprising a mix of measures at eu and national level, such as further scrutinising exports of sensitive equipment, suspending extradition agreements, stepping up scholarships and academic exchanges, further engaging with civil society and observing trials of pro—democracy activists. there is consensus on continuing to apply the measures and to consider additional steps in case of further deterioration. unity and solidarity continue to prevail. we cannot let any member state, any citizen, any member of parliament be singled out with respect to hong kong, xinjiang or more broadly, china. by calling for the release of swedish citizen, gui minhai, the eu will continue to stand firm on protecting its citizens. coordination with like—minded democracies on hong kong and addressing other challenges brought along by china will continue to be a cornerstone of our approach. hong kong remains high on our political agenda and will be discussed at the upcoming foreign affairs council on 25 january.

in writing. – the current covid-19 crisis has highlighted our external dependency and lack of open strategic autonomy in relation to resources and value-chains. this has caused our industry and smes to suffer an unprecedented impact. transitioning towards a circular economy will bring new economic opportunities. for this to happen, we need a functioning market for high-quality recycling with a level playing field for recycled materials, better waste management systems and a science-based binding 2030 eu-level target for reducing the materials and consumption footprints, based on agreed indicators. consequently, the eu must diversify its supply, and reduce its dependency, including by researching and developing alternative materials and efficient recycling processes, such as chemical recycling. sustainable products need to become the norm on the eu market. improving our circular economy will stimulate economic growth, create job opportunities, will help to achieve climate neutrality by 2050 by reducing co2 emissions, whilst at the same time not overusing the planet’s resources.

on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, commissioner nicolas schmit, all of us and all institutions agree on the importance of improving our skills and competences for our economies to move forward in competitiveness, resilience and social justice, and for a successful transition to a green and digital economy. but the skills, are they what we need? who defines it? how and who accesses them? are we all equally willing to access them? normally, when we approach the debate on competences, we think that they are neutral and accessible to everyone and that achieving them or not depends only on our merits and efforts. but is it really just an individual's responsibility? i think not, that we do not have to individualise responsibility for these processes, nor do we need them to be neutral. for example, skills are not independent of gender or ethnic stereotypes and therefore neither are opportunities to acquire them throughout our lives. and to individually hold each person accountable for the skills they are able to acquire is unfair, because we don't all have the same opportunities, especially given the educational inequalities that we've come to the labor market with and that have increased, in addition, with the pandemic. we must therefore, from the public institutions and from the european parliament, try to ensure that the processes of qualification and retraining are accessible to all people, with particular attention to people from the most vulnerable groups, areas with higher levels of unemployment or rural and isolated areas. these processes should be free of stereotypes because we need all the talents to make europe move forward in a more innovative and fair way. the learning process should be remunerated so that people from disadvantaged backgrounds do not play at a disadvantage. the commission is also proposing that the european parliament and the council should be given the opportunity to discuss the issue of the right of asylum with the european parliament.
on behalf of the left group. mr president, the european skills agenda cannot simply facilitate the transition to expanding sectors and jobs. it is not a question of responding to the needs of a changing labour market which swallows up workers at will, makes training paths more precarious and reinforces the instability of labour markets. we have to think seriously about the kind of professionals we want, not just the markets we have. the agenda has to empower those who need it most, thinking about them and eliminating the class, race and gender biases that perpetuate inequality, and not just to do justice, but because to be competitive you have to have all the talents and capabilities possible. we know that diversity is cost effective, and this proposal therefore involves not only the public authorities but also companies: employers must improve the skills of their workers, avoiding the preference for the usual ones, providing training opportunities and contributing to their training. it is clear that we must continue to strive for the good of all.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we must decide which model of society we want: one that privileges efficiency and competitiveness over social justice or one that puts people first. what has made us move towards the welfare state is not the exploitation of workers and the privatization of public services. our european union is the superlative example of a social market economy, where competitiveness is achieved while improving the living conditions of citizens. and this is done with models that are committed to public intervention and investment, protection of labour rights, decent wages, collective bargaining, progressive tax policy and the fight against tax fraud. the european union is the melting pot of fundamental rights. some will say: 'yes, but they also hinder economic competitiveness'. i say to them: "is it possible to live a life without dignity, without social justice?" let us choose the right model, because if we do not, then as inequalities and poverty continue to grow, it will be politics that will have become inefficient.

member of the commission. – madam president, thank you for the very warm welcome, and i am glad to be back in this house debating a really important topic about our companies and our recovery. i want to begin by thanking our rapporteurs and shadow rapporteurs for their efforts, and to look first at the prospective regulation. it’s been said already by the previous two speakers that the covid-19 pandemic has hit eu firms harder, and over a longer time period, than we had initially anticipated, especially small and medium—sized companies. many of our companies find themselves in a very difficult situation and really do need new investment to keep afloat. the proposed eu recovery prospectus is one way to enable eu companies to raise new equity capital on public markets quickly and without excessive bureaucracy. this short prospectus will be easy to produce for companies, easy to understand for investors and easy to scrutinise for national regulators. that means that it will help companies to raise capital more easily, helping them to stay solvent, recapitalise their business and strengthen their resilience in the recovery. thanks to your efforts, we’ve achieved a format for the new recovery prospectus that eases the administrative burden on companies while giving investors enough information to allow them to make an informed decision. now turning to the reform of the markets in financial instruments directive ii (mifid ii). let me explain why this reform is just as important in my view. the new rules on small cap research will enhance the visibility of small and medium—sized companies for investors, so it will help these companies to raise capital on public markets. on the derivatives reform, the amendments are essentially about green energy, and how to make it easier to finance a new generation of renewable energy projects. providers of renewable energy rely on a secure income stream and this is what the derivatives markets for energy achieve. to be effective, derivatives markets need to be liquid. if we maintain the current low position limit at 25% per market participant, the nascent energy exchanges will never take off. in smaller member states, exchanges have only two or three active market participants. there is also a clear link between these amendments on the derivatives market and the pandemic. during this covid-19 crisis, energy prices have been volatile because of a more erratic pattern of energy demand. it is essential to protect income for renewable energy suppliers, particularly when demand is so volatile. as highlighted the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr president, climate change is the most complex challenge facing humanity. to defeat it, we need more than good intentions, we need truly innovative solutions. one of the most important is the border adjustment mechanism which we are presenting today, with a lot of work by our colleagues in the committee on the environment and the other committees. the logic of the mechanism is simple. think of a car: a car is made up of hundreds of materials, including aluminum, steel and glass. if these materials are produced within the european union, they have to pay about 40 euros for every ton of co2 they generate. however, if these materials are produced outside the european union, they pay no cost for that carbon. cars made in the european union are therefore less competitive. we lose competitiveness if the materials come from within the european union. this puts our industries in a very difficult position, but above all it does our planet a disservice, because it only gets factories to close in europe and move elsewhere, with the same carbon cost, with the same effect on the planet, but with fewer jobs for europeans. thanks to the border adjustment mechanism, any material will pay for emissions whatever it has to pay, whether it is produced inside or outside the european union. for example, car importers will have to pay for the weight of the basic components of the co2 they produce, whether steel, glass or aluminium. commissioner gentiloni, the great majority of the european parliament is saying loud and clear that we want the carbon border adjustment mechanism. the commission should take note of the strong preference in the parliament for a system based on emissions trading (ets), our willingness to cover all ets sectors, as well as final products, and the proposal of the committee on economic and monetary affairs for fiscal design to assess the carbon content of imports. if the commission delivers, it will find strong support and a really strong ally in the european parliament. i think that we have today presented a really feasible proposal to solve one of the biggest problems that we face, and i hope the commission will really take this forward from here and build a really strong proposal very soon.

in writing. the eu's response to the current economic crisis has been radically different from that of a decade ago. the european central bank has launched an ambitious debt purchase plan from the outset, and the european investment bank has launched a major programme to support smes. the political consensus needed to launch a european investment plan, the next generation eu programme, financed with community debt, has also been reached. however, the current economic crisis is dragging on longer than we could have predicted a year ago. it is therefore essential that the relaxation of tax rules be continued in order to allow member states to continue to stimulate their economies. in this context, we socialists welcome the maintenance of the general safeguard clause at least until 2022 'recently announced by the commission', while stressing the need for both the ecb and the commission to be prepared to give a new impetus to expansionary fiscal policy if necessary.

the rapporteur. madam president, first of all i would like to thank the members, the political groups and the technical teams for their contribution to the agreement and consensus in the final outcome of this report. thank you, because we have made an effort to put aside our differences and put the common good and the interests of the people who voted for us first. this dossier should help to lay the foundations for the post-covid-19 europe, for that new economic and social framework that we urgently need to build in order to be able to offer solutions that mitigate the suffering and discouragement of a large part of the european population. we need to be able to design a roadmap in which social rights and goals and equity are as central to our governance and economic policy as environmental goals are beginning to be. if this was necessary before covid-19, it is even more so now. we have no excuse: covid-19 has put us in front of the mirror, and we must confront the profound socioeconomic consequences that the pandemic is showing us, by offering policy solutions that leave no one behind, live where they live. we know that millions of jobs and hours of work have been lost; that 10% of european workers were already in poverty before the pandemic; that the youth unemployment rate is at 17% and is likely to go higher; that we are also in the midst of a technological revolution that will bring about profound changes and a complicated situation. we know that women are suffering especially from the consequences of this pandemic, because we continue to be assigned the social mandate of care, and our integration into labour markets has been segregated and, in many cases, precarious. we know that on any given night 700 000 people in the european union sleep on the streets or in shelters - 70% more than in the last ten years - and that the crisis has worsened the physical and mental health, especially of the most vulnerable groups. and, ladies and gentlemen, this is not a story, these are not empty words from a speech. this is a reality that we would all see if it were not for some blinders, for a political and economic discourse that has shown us that it is not worth, that it is no longer worth. the panorama that the pandemic is leaving us with is in many places reminiscent of the consequences of other wars that we have fought in europe. we cannot and must not return to austerity policies. we cannot repeat the mistakes of the last crisis. we are risking our future, our well-being and the consolidation of the european project, including the very essence of the values which led us to draw up our charter of fundamental rights and which have created an area of freedom, security and justice. that is why - and this is a priority for my group of the progressive alliance of socialists and democrats - as we will be defending at the social summit in porto, we must not accept a governance that limits the quantity and quality of the jobs we generate or the redistribution of wealth in a context of growing inequality, all of which are also negative for the functioning of our companies and the resilience of our economies. the oecd improved its growth estimates yesterday, but that is not enough if growth is not well distributed. that is why we insist in this report that equity and social rights must be given the same importance as macroeconomic or environmental objectives. we need economic indicators that are able to perceive the social problems that the economy poses. this requires an ex ante assessment of the social consequences of measures and policies. the european semester should allow all member states to make the most of the potential offered by the escape clause, firstly, to support companies in difficulty and lacking liquidity, safeguarding the jobs, wages and working conditions of european workers; and secondly, to invest in people and in basic social welfare, health, care or education systems. this flexibility must be carried over into the near future, so that the negative social consequences of the deactivation of the general safeguard clause are foreseen. for the same reason, we propose that the emergency measures put in place be maintained for as long as necessary. the foreseeable national reforms must be based on solidarity, integration and social justice, with the aim of creating quality employment in all territories, to ensure sustainable growth as far as possible, moving towards a new social organisation of care so that it does not primarily rely on unpaid and unrecognised work by women. i firmly believe that upholding the centrality of social in economic policy and governance is perfectly compatible with the competitiveness of the european economy, which will thus be more sustainable and resilient. the european parliament must review the transparency of the whole process, from the definition of these indicators to the monitoring of the recommendations made to the member states. ladies and gentlemen, if we are to be that prosperous and social europe which involves citizens in its political project, we must not and cannot leave anyone behind. and we must act swiftly, but also clearly and firmly. the european union is a reality built on a pacifist, social and economic proposal that has endured to this day, a magnificent human creation built on the understanding of states and economic agreements. but let us never lose sight of the fact that this equation must result in the social well-being of the people and the unwavering commitment to democracy. i am convinced that this parliament wants to be up to date in its response to the historical needs of an era. and this report is just one more contribution to moving towards those institutions and policies that we need, without a doubt, in the europe of the future and in this post-covid-19 europe.
madam president, mr executive vice-president, you announced this week that you were extending the escape clause of the stability and growth pact for another year: that is good news. it would have been nonsense to have started the year with excessive deficit procedures in full in the european recovery fund, and i certainly think that the news - and the announcement they made - is to be welcomed. however, it is clear that the current rules we have cannot be reintroduced as they are; everyone knows this and that is why i dare to suggest to you today, mr executive vice-president, five lines of action in that debate on the reforms we are going to have. first, we need to continue to deepen europe's budgetary capacity, as we have done with the recovery and resilience facility. secondly, we need a golden rule for certain investments: there will be no ecological transition and no fight against climate change without certain investments, and we need that golden rule. thirdly, we should replace deficit limits with a spending rule which would somehow establish how nominal expenditure grows in the member states: it would be an observable variable, much more objective than the ones we use now, such as the output gap or the structural balance, which are somehow totally ineffective. fourthly, we need a different approach to debt: the levels of debt we have cannot be dealt with by the standards we have, and the monetary conditions are very different today from when we set these standards; we need to change that. and fifthly, we must strengthen the macroeconomic dialogue between countries, including their trade balances. i think that these five lines of action would allow us to have much more serious and reasonable budgetary rules; of course, the flexibility we have is not going to help us for the period we are about to start after 2023.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the employment problem, and particularly the young people's employment problem, which has been neglected, must be given priority. we must restore lost jobs, maintain jobs, but at the same time create new jobs. to do that, we need public and private investment, to modernize our economy, to eliminate red tape. that's what the recovery and resilience mechanism is for. and member states should use national recovery and resilience plans for these objectives, to also promote territorial, economic and social cohesion. unfortunately, poverty is not confined to the large metropolitan areas, and many member states preach solidarity here and then forget to practice it at home. member states cannot use national recovery plans to finance the state, to do more of the same, to finance current expenditure. you can't miss this opportunity. we have a precedent here that we must use for the future. the recovery and resilience mechanism, the european semester, must be an asset if necessary.
madam president, mr dombrovskis, when we look at the economic situation we are facing, we see two problems. on the one hand, we have the pandemic, which is getting longer and creating a much longer economic crisis than we imagined when we passed the recovery plan and parliament's proposals this spring. on the other hand, we have a very significant increase in debt that makes many people worry about how we will pay it. the answers to these two problems differ between the left and right sides of the camera. on the left side they say, "well, the important thing is the pandemic; let's spend and spend and spend now, and then, if we can, we'll ask the european central bank to forgive us the debt". on the right side of the camera you start to hear already "tax consolidation", you start to hear already about the concern about the debt and that the brake must be put. i don't think either of those answers is right. when you look at european economies, what is needed are two things: today, spending; today we have to spend much more. let us look at what the united states is spending; the fiscal stimulus they are talking about, compared with ours, is indeed much, much greater: we are talking about four trillion with twelve zeros, compared with what we have approved here. but at the same time we must ensure the sustainability of finance in the medium term and we must make it sustainable. it seems obvious, but it's not. my government, the government of our country, is doing the opposite: it is spending for the long term, introducing structural programmes, and it is skimping on the help that the self-employed need right now. let's do what we have to do to get out of this crisis.
madam president, first of all, i would like to thank and compliment the commission. we don’t do that that often, i do realise, but i see that the commission is learning from the previous crisis and seeing that the semester needs an improvement and that we need to change the rules. i have to compliment the commission because on the right side of this parliament, they don’t seem to have learned that yet, so i really wish the commission to put that forward. i also hope that in the council we will see a bit of a learning curve. let’s see what porto will bring. we are talking about economic governance here and economic governance is there to achieve targets. economic governance is not a target in itself. we do that to deliver on the targets of social and environmental development within europe. that’s why we have economic governance. that’s why we need to discuss how to change the rules to have more space for investments, how to be more countercyclical. these are the questions that need to be addressed, and that’s why we need a reform of the semester. i’m happy that the commission is going down that path, hopefully the council too, and then in the end, who knows, maybe the epp?

madam president, i think we should now ask ourselves whether we should withdraw from the budgetary stability pact. these rules were absurd yesterday, but they have become dangerous today with the crisis that is going to continue, the divergences between the economies growing, cohesion receding and before us the risk of the euro zone exploding. in reality, this fiscal stability pact, which will limit the capacity of the states to stimulate long-term growth, is becoming a pact of social disorder and growing inequalities, and only ideological blindness could lead to its continuation. it is therefore time to get out of this and invent a new form of economic governance based on cohesion criteria, social and climate criteria and it is a new time, an unexpected opportunity that may open up for a reform of the european semester.
madam president, the european parliament has not taken a decision on the union's annual strategy for sustainable growth for two years, and has not reached agreement on the important instrument for coordinating economic and budgetary policies, the european semester, for two years. for those citizens who are following us today, the european semester is giving recommendations to member states to adopt economic policies that will help to bring about financial stability and make us more competitive. in this sense, we have just approved a huge package, with a huge outlay, to deal with the terrible social and financial crisis that follows the pandemic, and european citizens have to understand that these recommendations cannot be diluted, because today they are more important than ever: we need to have control over spending so that that spending is done in the most efficient way. as a spaniard, i know very well what i am talking about: we have to avoid having more plans e on the table in this crisis, which are used to spend and spend, but they are not investments that make us come out stronger and more competitive and, if you like, resilient, that is what it is about. that is why it is so important that the european semester sticks to its objectives, to those recommendations, and that we do not intend to make, as other colleagues of mine in the european people's party have said, a christmas tree in which too many subjects are included that dilute that objective. it is essential to establish a control on spending and it is essential to establish the recommendations for reforms - labour reforms, structural reforms - that will allow europeans, the generations to come, to have more opportunities.

madam president, commissioner, if the european project is a construction, we have built the foundations, we have built the commercial plants, the offices... but we lack the spaces where people live. and the european social pillar is the key element in building that area of protection for citizens. however, almost a year and a half after this commission took office, we are now being given the blueprints for the construction of this key social pillar. i think we are a little late, and we are late because it is essential and necessary. well, in the plans which have been presented to us, in this action plan, for the implementation of the european social pillar, there is one aspect which i would like to stress. the pandemic has shown that teleworking is a key element in the transformations we are experiencing. and you propose, in this plan, to give the hot potato to the trade unions to update the european framework agreement on telework of 2002, when the commission would have to take up the issue and define a european legislative framework agreement to determine telework, because there are implications for productive, labour, economic relations; there are also policies, inclusion, mobility, environment, equality, depopulation, cross-border... i therefore ask you, commissioner, to join the european presidency and use the opportunity of porto to propose a european legislative framework on teleworking which provides a comprehensive european framework, a key element for the present and future of not only industrial relations but also economic, social, environmental, depopulation, crossborder and inclusion relations.
madam president, commissioner, it is true that the action plan presented paves the way for a social europe, but with far less ambition than that which was requested from parliament. more decisive progress is needed and can be made, because while it is the member states that are responsible for implementing the policies needed to meet the social objectives, the european union has a role to play in supporting, coordinating and harmonizing social systems for upward convergence. there is therefore still room to develop instruments to ensure a real social europe. we need a reform of the european union's governance model that makes social objectives binding and includes a protocol on social progress in the treaties, protecting social rights on an equal footing with economic freedoms, and this can only be done from an interinstitutional commitment between the commission, parliament and the council. we hope that the commission and the council will be prepared to take on this responsibility at the social summit in porto, because this house is clear on this.
in writing. the debate focused on the action plan presented by the commission. this action plan is the commission's contribution to the implementation of the principles of the social pillar, and is presented as a new social regulation. it sets out three objectives for 2030 to help guide national policies and reforms, and presents a long list of proposals, some of them legislative in nature. in addition, the plan includes as a novelty the updating of the social indicators table. thanks to the work of the socialist family, the portuguese presidency and commissioner schmidt, social rights have returned to where they belong: at the top of the eu agenda. the action plan has been welcomed by the s&d group, as it includes many of our proposals. however, we call on the commission and the member states to be ambitious and to commit themselves to linking the objectives in a joint declaration with the european parliament at the social summit in porto. the proposed social indicators are a start, but social rights must be integrated into the same governance structure as economic and ecological objectives to ensure their proper applicability.
