rapporteur. – mr president, the 2008 financial crisis is still with us today in the form of high debts and imbalances in the euro zone. that crisis had many causes, including the search for yields in an era of low interest rates, but what ignited it were the same financial products we are discussing today, securitisation. and these products are much better explained in popularised movies like the big short, by people much more engaging and much more attractive than i am, but in essence, they allow banks to package and sell loans and in this way they reduce their exposure to financial risks and free up capital for new loans. and these are useful products, remind us of that, because you don’t want to put all your eggs in one basket and they otherwise help to increase the financing of the real economy, and in our current covid crisis this is exactly what we want. and this is why parliament was happy to engage when the commission proposed an impetus to europe’s securitisation market. the market itself is currently not big, it’s rather small, and small not because of the restrictions of the current legislation but also mainly because of the abundance of cheap alternatives for financing loans as a result also of the ecb’s monetary policy. so it remains to be seen what the proposed changes in the legislation will deliver, but in a crisis every bit counts. and the commission proposed to make it easier to sell off non-performing loans, something of increased importance in the years to come, and it also proposed to expand the sts label for simple, transparent and standardised securitisation to a new class of synthetic securitisation. this would give capital benefits to certain types of products that were not the loans themselves but only their revenue streams that are sold off. parliament, like i said, was happy to engage in this but is always aware of the dangers. selling of loans can be a way to hide internal weaknesses or exposing others to unexpected risks. and we saw exactly this in the recently bankrupted greensill bank. they issued risky loans but sold them off in packages, largely risk free. this went well until credit suisse noticed that in fact most of these loans were made to a single materials company close to bankruptcy. credit suisse pulled out, everyone pulled out, and greensill went under. it’s a classic example. and the main worry should be not these individual cases, but that these individual cases do not become a systemic risk. spreading risk is the aim of securitisation, but as history shows us, it may also lead to a concentration of risk if not well regulated and if not well supervised, and that remains crucial. we don’t want the financial market to turn into one big domino day, when suddenly abstract complex products cause very real harm to our citizens. this is what parliament wants and wanted to avoid, so we pushed for changes to the commission proposal. we’ve always mandated supervisors to closely monitor risks, including systemic risks, and give warning signs when things get out of hand. we are also very much focused on the structure of securitisation to avoid problems arising in the first place. first, the issuing bank should always maintain a material exposure to the loans to avoid wrong incentives. second, we minimised counterparty risk, this way investors don’t need to suffer if an issuing bank goes down like greensill did. and third, we further simplified the structure of the financial products to avoid them being used to trick the supervisor. these changes make for a safer european securitisation market, but financial markets shouldn’t just be safe: they should also help us to move forward towards a sustainable and fair economy and to promote sustainability we mandated the european banking authority to develop rules for sustainable securitisation, which should be put in place when the larger review of the regulation comes into question at the end of the year. to promote a fair economy we included strong safeguards against tax avoidance – safeguards that turned out to be so strong that australia has already – even before the law was voted upon – committed to putting an end to its harmful tax regime of offshore banking units. the risk of reduced access to european financing set off alarm bells on the other side of the world in a clear sign of the strength of the european market. to conclude, with this text we can achieve the best of three worlds: a stronger economic recovery; good checks on potential risks; and a contribution to a fair and sustainable economy. finally i would like to thank my co-negotiators othmar karas and luis garicano, and their teams of course, for what was not always an easy process given the time pressure. and i would like to thank the commission’s departments and the council presidency very much for a constructive approach up until the very end. it is now up to our financial markets to make the most of the tools given to them and support our economy through these difficult times.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. you're actually expecting othmar karas to be here and see me. i would like to thank the president-in-office for his kind words, but he was unable to arrange to be here and he regrets it very much. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the eu's biggest investment package ever, the nextgenerationeu building plan, with the new eu long-term budget, the green deal and monetary policy measures, must be followed by our financial market. unlike the experience of the last financial crisis, the financial market is not part of the problem this time, but part of the solution. and that is why we must put it more fully at the service of our common future. we successfully tightened the first screw in the banking sector. at record speed, we have overhauled banking rules to mobilise a whopping €450 billion in additional credit, which will benefit small and medium-sized enterprises in particular. the second screw was the amendments to the prospectus regulation and the mifid ii financial markets directive which we adopted here in the european parliament a few weeks ago and which help to strengthen the financing possibilities of companies in crisis. and we are now turning the third screw by completing the comprehensive package of measures for the recovery of the financial markets with new rules for the financial instrument of securitisation. i mean, i know how badly securitization is known. after all, they are considered to be one of the causes of the banking and financial crisis of 2008/2009. as with so many things, it's not the instrument itself that's bad, it's what you make of it. unfortunately, the experience of the financial crisis has led to a certain general suspicion of securitisations. securitisations are not good or bad in themselves, however. if used properly, they can help to spread risk in the financial system, avoid risk of clumping and thus improve the financing conditions of the real economy. and that's a very important factor in these times, because if there's one thing we can't afford, it's that the economic recovery from the pandemic will ultimately fail because businesses can't finance themselves and banks can't extend loans. when banks resell open loans or other assets in packages as tradable securities, this relieves the burden on bank balance sheets and thus further stimulates lending. this in turn contributes to the fact that risks in the financial markets are borne by those who are best able to do so. financial markets are not only a risk factor, but they can also help manage risks, spread them over more people, and in the end, benefit us all. the new securitisation rules thus strengthen an important building block of the capital markets union. what was once poison is becoming medicine for the economic collapse after corona. when properly dosed, securitisations can help to speed up recovery. firstly, because new investment opportunities are emerging, and secondly because banks are given more scope for new loans to households, but also to small and mediumsized enterprises. i am glad that the european parliament, in tough negotiations with the council and the member states, has been able to achieve many improvements. we have further strengthened and improved the strict regulatory framework we introduced more than three years ago with targeted adjustments to enable securitisations to take on an even more meaningful economic role. we have introduced risk-intensive capital requirements for non-performing securitisation loans and so-called sts and balance sheet securitisations. we've increased transparency requirements. we have laid the foundation for the establishment of a sustainable securitization label in response to the climate challenges. and we have significantly improved the handling of potential tax avoidance by securitization vehicles in global tax havens. this momentum must now be taken into account in the further strengthening of the banking and capital markets union. this is due to a number of major regulatory projects later this year, with further revisions to the equity directive basel iii finalisation , the financial markets directive the great review of mifid ii and the insurance directive the great review of solvency ii . i very much hope that we can then continue working together on the successful package to strengthen capital markets. this is also urgently needed in the context of brexit and the economic challenges posed by the pandemic. i would like to thank paul tang, personally and, of course, on behalf of othmar karas, the whole negotiating team and, of course, the european commission, which always has an important role in bringing the parties to the conflict together and finding solutions. i would have thanked the council too if it had been present.
member of the commission. – mr president, i’m very happy to join you before you vote tomorrow on the second half of the capital markets recovery package. today’s debate and indeed tomorrow’s vote will soundness of the current framework. i believe that securitisation within a sound and well-calibrated regulatory framework can play a crucial role in funding the post-crisis recovery. banks need to be mr president, it’s really great to have ms mcguinness here, and it’s been a pleasure to work with her team to make these two sets of regulations concerning securitisation. many people who are watching us, many colleagues, will wonder what these synthetic securitisations are, and what the point is of what we are passing tomorrow as a result of these negotiations. basically, wrong securitisations were at the root of the financial crisis: securitisations that weren’t transparent were the weapons of mass financial destruction that led to the troubles that we suffered in 2008, partly. but on the other hand, securitisations are useful tools. the reason they’re useful tools is because they allow banks to shed risk, to get rid of the non-performing loans and continue making loans into the future. so the trick is to make sure that the risk that is transferred is fully transferred. what happened with those american institutions that had trillions and trillions of dollars of risk return to their balance sheets was that they had made securitisations that made it look as if they were really transferring risk when in fact the moment there were troubles, the risks came back to their balance sheets. so what we are looking for in these two regulations is to facilitate the use of securitisation to make sure that banks can shed these risks, but in a way that actually eliminates the possibility to fake the risk transfer, and encourages the transfer of real risk; when that risk is transferred, it really is transferred. that’s why we have put in place this set of rules that we believe is going to ensure that securitisations work, but they work in a transparent, simple way that actually allows the real economy to have larger access to credit without creating these opaque structures that were so complex, and that caused the last financial crisis.

member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank you for this morning's debate on both the european data strategy and the commission's report published last and i would like to thank the members of the itre committee and the rapporteur, mrs kumpula-natri, for her very comprehensive report on this subject, and the associated committees for enriching this report with their opinions. when the commission published its european data strategy in february last year, we could not have imagined what an extraordinarily turbulent year it would be. a year marked, of course, by the covid-19 pandemic. the crisis has further highlighted the importance of data and digital technologies in meeting unprecedented challenges. the commission fully shares the rapporteur's view that the potential of data is not yet fully exploited in europe, mainly due to the lack of trust in the sharing of such data and the lack of interoperability and standards to allow it to circulate between sectors and between member states. the commission also shares the view that we must chart our own european path towards a data economy and society; i would like to emphasize this point, our common values. europe needs to take greater control of its strategic interests, while maintaining an open economy and, as the gdpr already allows for personal data, ensuring that european businesses and citizens have control over their data. with the european data strategy, our aim is to create a true single market for data, where data flows across sectors and member states, and where high quality data is available for innovation and value creation, while minimising the environmental footprint and ensuring the protection of personal data. as you know, last november the commission adopted a proposal for a regulation on european data governance - the first part of the strategy - with the aim of unlocking the value of data voluntarily made available by its holders for re-use. this framework aims to promote data availability by increasing trust in intermediaries and strengthening data sharing mechanisms within the union in a pro-competitive manner. we are aiming here, perhaps as early as this summer, to adopt an implementing act on high value datasets so that more high quality public sector data will be available for re-use, free of charge, in machine readable formats across the union via application programming interfaces. to improve access to and use of data, the commission will also propose, by the end of the year, a data act, a legislative initiative to improve fairness in the data economy by clarifying rights of use, notably in business to government and business to business configurations. it is important to emphasise that all these initiatives are or will be fully compliant with existing data protection and fundamental rights legislation, as well as with the union's international trade obligations. finally, the data strategy also provides for the deployment of common european data spaces in strategic sectors and areas of public interest. the commission plans to support these data spaces. the digital europe programme and the second connecting europe programme will play a key role in achieving our objective of strengthening a european data infrastructure and its use in full respect of european values. we also expect industry to invest in data infrastructures, as we expect member states to do, including through the recovery and resilience facility, the rrf, and through multi-country projects. ladies and gentlemen, allow me to now move on to the second item of our debate. i am pleased that your parliament has decided to debate today the commission's report on the first two years of implementation of the general data protection regulation, published in june last year, and to express its position in a resolution. in the light of the libe draft resolution, i can only welcome the fact that it highlights the importance of the gdpr as the global standard for data protection and the need to focus our efforts on the effective implementation of this instrument. we also agree on the assessment of the main challenges that will need to be addressed in the months and years ahead. first, it is clear that it is important to continue to support small and medium-sized enterprises to facilitate compliance with the gdpr. this is why the commission financially supports national data protection authorities in their efforts to reach out to the general public and businesses, in particular smes. a new call for proposals covering in particular the development of practical tools to help smes will be launched before the summer. national data protection authorities are the cornerstone of the effective application of the gdpr, as it is up to them and to national courts to enforce its rules. we need to continue to closely monitor the resources allocated to them, while noting that many have benefited from increases in recent years. we also need to facilitate their cooperation in crossborder cases. we welcome the european data protection board's new procedures to ensure that the one-stop shop mechanisms function effectively. we recognise that more must be done towards a european data protection culture, also among data protection authorities, and notably within the edpb. the commission is working towards this objective. with regard to some national divergences in the application of the gdpr, we will continue our discussions with the member states and consider how these issues can best be addressed. let me say generally that if gdpr provisions are violated, the commission does not shy away from having recourse to all the tools at its disposal, including infringement proceedings. we also use harmonisation tools, such as the standard contractual clauses for intra-eu transfers, to help controllers and processors across the eu to comply with the gdpr and to use the same set of clauses. as the recent proposal on the digital green certificate shows, the commission strives to ensure the highest level of personal data protection, in line with the gdpr, in its initiatives. we systematically ask for the opinion of the european data protection supervisor as well as, for major proposals, like the certificate, that of the edpb. in this context, i would like to address more generally the relationship between the gdpr and technological development. as already demonstrated during the covid pandemic, the gdpr allows for developing innovative tools in compliance with fundamental rights. being technologically neutral, the gdpr frames innovation, but does not preclude it. a precondition for this is that the gdpr is also interpreted and enforced in a technologically neutral way. ladies and gentlemen, with the current pandemic, we are once again realizing how fundamental the issue of protecting fundamental rights, including the right to privacy, is. the gdpr provides the flexibility to address the challenges of our time. for example, in the context of the current covid-19 pandemic, the union's response is not to erect barriers, but to remain open to data exchange, while ensuring the continuity of their protection. the objectives of privacy and data flow liberalisation, and therefore trade, must be complementary. in this context, it is encouraging to see that a growing number of countries around the world are converging towards the establishment of modern data protection regimes, which share many similarities with the gdpr. this is a global trend, with countries such as brazil, japan, south korea, india and kenya taking part. on a bilateral basis we have set up with japan the world's largest area of safe data flows. we will soon finalise a similar arrangement with south korea and we have drafted two adequacy decisions in relation to the uk. following the recent case law of the european court of justice on the privacy shield, we are engaging with the united states to reach a solid and legally sound arrangement. moreover, we are working with like-minded partners to define standards at multilateral level. i am thinking for example of the promising work taking place at the level of the oecd on developing common principles on access to data by public authorities. we are also pursuing debates in the wto as concerns data protection in an ecommerce context. i look forward to our debate today and to your final resolution, of course. as always, your resolutions will inspire our work and offer us thierry breton, myself and the entire commission a roadmap for the key objectives to achieve.

on behalf of the left group. mr president, first of all i would like to thank my colleagues for their cooperation in this very important resolution. unlike air or water, soil is not regulated by the european union. and it's not a trivial matter: soil is a fundamental element for climate action and for life in our territories. your protection today cannot wait. i start with a reminder of the tireless work of civil society. in 2016, the citizen initiative people4soil brought together the efforts of hundreds of organizations. they pointed to the critical state of the soil and called for determined action to protect it. five years later, the situation is even more alarming. the depletion of our soils globally is one of the most worrying and least understood crises of the current climate emergency. thirty-three percent of the earth's soils are already damaged and more than 90 percent could be degraded by 2050. the deterioration is progressing at a rapid pace, with 60% to 70% of europe's soils now in a state of unhealthiness. so far, measures to protect soil have been woefully inadequate, and we urgently need a binding legal framework to protect soil and ensure its sustainable use. soil - the earth - is much more than a natural resource: it is a complex, living ecosystem that plays a key role in regulating climate. it is one of the best tools for tackling climate change, for adaptation and mitigation. but it is also on the soil that our agriculture, our livestock, depend: a commodity essential to our livelihood and the basis of our food sovereignty. the production and exploitation patterns of the sea have a direct impact on its conservation. it is not the same for large farms - the macropark - to opt, as many farmers and livestock farmers do, for sustainable farming in terms of health, the environment and society. in this sense, it is also an essential factor for regional cohesion and regional integration. just as the soil is diverse, so are the activities that feed on it and the environments that host and inhabit it. the link between soil - the land - and the rural world is close, and we must be able to ensure that it is cared for. the roots, the heritage that flows from it, are diverse, and this stock is what makes the soil a common public good. it is the link between the climate fight and sustainable territorial and economic development. today, parliament is sending a strong message to the commission and the council. we are waiting for a proposal for a legal framework that protects the soil, that defines it as what it is: a common good, the source of life for our peoples, our agriculture and livestock, and an essential tool in the fight against climate change. i take this opportunity to remind this house of what the citizens are telling us in the streets: the climate law, today, is not up to the story. we cannot wait 30 years to achieve climate neutrality. why are they so intent on protecting the great economic interests of a few against the land of all? to paraphrase antonio machado: the earth, "the evening is dying like a humble hearth that goes out".

in writing. the european globalisation adjustment fund for migrant workers (egf) is the solidarity fund set up in 2007 to finance labour market activation measures (such as training, job search and business creation) in the context of unexpected redundancies caused by globalisation or by global economic and financial crises, which have a significant impact on the economy at regional or local level. the new egf 2021-2027 will not only ensure the continuation of the fund beyond 2020, but will also allow for increased support for people who lose their jobs due to restructuring processes in europe, by having an increased annual budget, and by including additional reasons for considering a case of redundancy as eligible for funding. we have succeeded in reducing the number of redundancies that can be mobilised from 500 to 200. we have secured childcare allowance for workers made redundant with children and we have increased financial support for selfemployed people who want to start their own business to eur 22 000.

good news for the entire world. the colombian peace agreement is cited internationally as a model because of its determination to address the root causes of the conflict and its central focus on the demonstrated by both the government and farc, who have now disarmed and transitioned to politics with the names of communes. however, important challenges and setbacks persist in this process. the trust fund, which today stands at eur 130 million, with contributions from 21 member states, the united kingdom and chile, as well as loans pledged by the european investment bank, short-term actions and ongoing programmes. there are 30 projects running on eu contributions to support victims, the development of rural communities and the reintegration of ex-combatants. the continued work of the eu envoy to continue in his role. the eu is not alone in its support for colombia. the international community has been united in supporting the peace process, including the un security council. this member of the commission. – madam president, this is an extremely important debate. this regulation will make it harder for terrorists to exploit the internet to spread fear, violence and terror. this regulation will make it more difficult for terrorists to abuse the internet, to recruit online, to incite attacks online, to glorify their atrocities online. with this regulation, we take european action against terrorist activities online: action that is quick, cross—border and compulsory. quick: member states will be able to order internet providers to take down terrorist content within the hour. cross-border: member states will be able to issue orders to take down terrorist content hosted by any service provider anywhere in the european union. compulsory: providers must carry out these demands and pay fines if they don’t. proportionate fines: small companies must not fall victim to terrorists abusing their systems. i’m sure you all remember the christchurch attacks: 60 minutes and 55 seconds of mass murder broadcast live to the world. some platforms still have copies of that attack online. what’s worse, animated versions aimed at children keep appearing on videogaming platforms. that too can soon be taken down in the whole of europe within the hour. as we speak, jihadi groups are calling for attacks online: calling on followers to exploit political unrest during the pandemic, to kill people and damage property. that too, soon, can be taken down in the whole of europe within the hour. with this regulation, we will strike a blow against terrorists. without online manuals to tell you how, it’s harder to make bombs. without flashy propaganda videos, it’s harder to poison the minds of young people. without streaming attacks online, it’s harder to inspire copycat attacks. it’s difficult to measure: people are not radicalised, bombs not made, attacks not carried out. we may never be able to count how many, but this regulation will save lives, and we can be proud of this result. this regulation strikes a major blow against terrorists, but it’s only one of many steps in the fight against terrorism, offline and online. in december 2020, i launched our counterterrorism agenda. besides fighting terrorists online, we will, among other things, boost european police cooperation and information exchange, make it more difficult for foreign fighters to enter the european union undetected, protect people in public spaces like churches, mosques, synagogues, stadiums and public transport. this regulation upholds our values and fundamental rights by fighting terrorists who attack our freedoms and our democracies, by putting safeguards in place, and by limiting removal of content to what is clearly illegal. we will take down terrorist content and uphold freedom of expression. i would like to warmly thank the rapporteur, patryk jaki, and also all the shadow rapporteurs for these results. a lot of work has gone into this. i would like to thank the parliament for your support. thank you for making this regulation a reality, and thank you for the very good cooperation. as a society, we are facing the enormous challenge of digital change, which fundamentally affects the way we live and the way we work. it affects our security and our privacy. we must face this challenge as law—makers and as a union. in december, the commission launched the digital services act to foster online markets and to protect fundamental rights online. we must also give law enforcement the right rules and tools to fight crime and terrorism in the digital age. it’s up to us now to find agreements on child sexual abuse online, our short—term and future long-term proposals on detecting and reporting child sexual exploitation online, and to find agreements on e—evidence – 85% of evidence is electronic. to fight crime and terrorism, law enforcement needs timely access to cross—border evidence. to find agreement on data retention, we need to look at possibilities in line with eu law so that digital evidence of crimes or leads to investigations do not accidentally disappear. to find agreement on encryption, police must be able to gain effective access to encrypted electronic evidence when they are granted the legal authorisation to do so. to make agreements on artificial intelligence, law enforcement should use the full potential of ai to find missing children and very dangerous criminals, to prevent terrorist attacks and to respond to the malicious use of technology by criminals. all of these policies are as sensitive as they are important. the successful negotiating result achieved on this file – the terrorist content online – gives me the confidence that we will also find agreement on the commission’s other proposals on digital law enforcement. so let this result inspire us together to make europe safe for everyone.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, madam commissioner, samuel paty, falsely accused of islamophobia, was lynched on the net before being beheaded at the door of his school. last friday a french police officer, mother of two, was murdered in rambouillet by a terrorist who had consumed large amounts of jihadist propaganda on the web before his crime. as the commissioner recalled, two years ago, a white supremacist in christchurch broadcast on facebook the massacre of muslim worshippers at the al noor mosque. these and many other cases bring us to the huge problem of the dissemination of terrorist content on the net. sometimes it is a matter of exposing and spreading the crime itself while it is being committed; other times it is a matter of fuelling the processes of radicalization, from which new terrorists will emerge, or, in paty's case, the networks were used to spread the threat and incite murder. that is why the regulation we are about to adopt must make a clear difference in terms of improving efficiency, cooperation and the continued effort to fight terrorism on this front, the online world, which we know is essential in the strategy of terrorists. it has taken time and a lot of effort, and i would like to emphasize the role of our rapporteur in this regulation. but the use of the net for terrorist purposes, which is a phenomenon without frontiers, must be met by cooperation also without frontiers. we have struck a good balance between new cooperation instruments and procedures and the necessary safeguards of fundamental rights. withdrawal orders - explained here - are a crucial innovation in crossborder counter-terrorism cooperation. it is clear that nothing can replace the action on the ground of the military forces, the security forces, the intelligence services, the judges... but it is also essential to prevent terrorism from spreading its shadow, from polluting minds and from glorifying criminals.

i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr kanev, for his work on this report. when groups cooperate and work - despite their differences - in the same direction, it is much easier to achieve a good text. and this report is good evidence of that. with the own-initiative report we are debating today, we are taking a step forward and we are moving towards a freer, fairer and safer labour mobility. in this europe where almost 4% of its citizens live in another eu country and where there are more and more mobile and displaced workers, we cannot allow the single market to be used as a pretext to undermine rights and perpetuate precarious working conditions. the european union must redouble its efforts and fully address such important issues as safety and health at work, strengthening social dialogue, and business investment in formal and informal training and lifelong learning. and of course it must put an end to the intolerable, abusive practices of subcontracting, employment through temporary employment agencies and front companies. we must also create a legal framework to regulate teleworking, to ensure decent working conditions. and as for the european labour authority, we must ensure that it has real inspection powers in crossborder cases to put an end to fraud, exploitation and abuse in the european union. in short, only by reforming these key elements can we truly guarantee equal treatment in the internal market, while safeguarding respect for fundamental rights and national labour market models.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner lenarčič, first of all, i would like to convey the excitement i have in presenting my first own-initiative report to this parliament today and my thanks to all those who have been involved in this work and who have helped me to put this topical issue on the agenda. the terrible pandemic we're living through has paralyzed almost everything, but not climate change. the world bank, for example, estimates that more than 143 million people will be displaced by climate by 2050. first of all, i would like to thank the alternative rapporteurs who have taken part and improved the text - frances fitzgerald, catherine chabaud, beata kempa and miguel urbán - and also the rapporteur for the libe committee, saskia bricmont, and those from the envi and femm committees, since i understand that this report is not as ambitious as we would have liked, but it is the best that can be done to provide a minimum framework for the protection of people who do not have it today. i would like to thank the commission for the coordinated work and active listening of dg intpa, of mrs urpilainen's team, and especially you, commissioner lenarčič, and your echo team, for your willingness to make progress on protective mechanisms for people with concrete measures. we have been debating in this parliament for some time about how we are making progress in protecting the environment and how we are becoming more resilient to climate change. we have a great green deal with important laws like climate, but it is urgent to put the most vulnerable people in developing countries on the agenda. we are the most important actor in humanitarian aid and international cooperation and therefore have an added responsibility. other parliaments around the world have already expressed their views, such as the african union with the kampala declaration and latin america with the cartagena declaration. we must address climate change as a cause of migration and as a phenomenon that directly or indirectly threatens human rights, including the right to housing, water, sanitation or food. we are saying in this report that there is a direct link between the effects of climate change and migration, that there are longer and more widespread crises because of climate change. we must therefore develop this external dimension of the green deal, support the partner countries and curb its impacts. droughts, floods, hurricanes, etc., are behind many of the conflicts that cause these crises. so we are talking about climate justice. the countries that have contributed the least to global warming are the ones that are most exposed to its suffering, the ones that are least prepared to mitigate its impact. and the most vulnerable populations, such as, for example, the original peoples, the indigenous peoples, are among the most affected. this report proposes a comprehensive strategy and we ask the commission to make a concrete communication which includes, on the one hand, a climate policy to increase international funding, compensation for damage; in short, to strengthen the warsaw mechanism, as demanded by the developing countries at the last cop 25 in madrid; to increase financial support for disaster prevention and preparedness, in accordance with the sendai framework agreements, particularly in the small island states on the verge of disappearing, such as kiribati. second, a development and humanitarian aid policy to address geographic vulnerabilities, such as housing location in risk areas, or livelihood bases, such as crop loss from drought or sea rise, by promoting local sustainable agriculture and food security initiatives. addressing personal vulnerabilities, for example through gender-sensitive climate actions to design and implement adaptation programmes. women must be at the centre of these policies, both because of their vulnerability and because they are agents of change. we call for a 'nexus' approach to be implemented that bridges emergency responses and long-term objectives to address the impact on people and implement sustainable solutions. thirdly, and very importantly, immigration policy. we call for the protection of existing legal mechanisms to be extended to ensure the rights of people who are forced to move internally or across borders, building on the nansen initiative for the protection of displaced persons; for the risk to life threatened by climate change to be explicitly included among the eligibility criteria for humanitarian protection, following the resolution of the un human rights committee in the case of teitiota, as stated by unhcr itself. the star proposal is a climate visa, a humanitarian visa as a temporary protection measure to ensure legal and safe migration routes for people in need of protection because they are victims of disasters. we cannot forget the awareness raising actions that serve to explain why and where so much immigration comes from. recognising the contribution of young people to global awareness-raising, as well as the work of ngos and local organisations, local and regional governments; enhancing intercultural dialogue between migrants and refugees to raise awareness and prevent racism. all these measures need funding. the european union, its member states and the european investment bank are the main contributors, but they are not enough and we need to involve the private sector. we've made commitments in the ndici, in the new neighbourhood, development and international cooperation instrument, like allocating 40 percent of the funds to climate action, but now we have to plan, we have to land with concrete measures through programming and continue to count on middle-income countries. in addition, the humanitarian aid instrument will contribute to preventing, preparing for and responding to natural disasters. if there is a will, there will be funds available. in future, ladies and gentlemen, judicial decisions on climate and non-deportation will not be an anecdotal fact. it is a matter of time and jurisprudence to define progressively which specific natural events are to be considered and their link with the risk to life. i therefore urge you to vote in favour of this report and to avoid amendments which deny the link between climate and migration. this is why this own-initiative report is more timely than ever and we are convinced that the european institutions can and must do this. i hope that the work on this report will continue in the commission itself, through dg echo and dg intpa, and also from the libe commission, for example through the regulations of the new pact on migration.

in writing. european industry accounts for more than 20% of the economy, employs 35 million people and is one of the highest carbon emitting sectors. therefore, the review of the industrial strategy published in march 2020 in light of the situation created by the pandemic is essential to draw lessons from the crisis, accelerate the recovery of our economies and societies while building a greener, digital, innovative and strategically autonomous industry. the s&ds welcome the references to the green and digital transition, the commission's taking into account of the consequences of the crisis for workers and businesses, the strengthening of the role of smes, the regulation on the control of foreign direct investment, the opening up of support measures in derogation from state aid, the sectoral analyses in response to the s&ds' request, and the emphasis on how to use the actual programmes of the multiannual financial framework to revive the economy. however, as regards competences, the strategy remains unclear, and we therefore call for the social implications and dimensions to be strengthened to ensure a sustainable recovery with social justice.

madam president, mr minister, madam commissioner, welcome to the house of european democracy, mr minister, for the first time in five months in this capacity. many will speak today, and with propriety, of the dead in the mediterranean which in 2021 alone already exceeds 700 and already now those in the atlantic and the desperate situation in which they find themselves in the canary islands and ceuta. but this unspeakable tragedy must not make us forget the tragedy of migrants who are not at sea or in refugee camps, but who are exploited and enslaved on land, on the european continent and also in my country. for two weeks now we have known that tens of thousands of immigrants, almost all of them asians, live in subhuman conditions of total economic exploitation, almost on the verge of captivity or slavery. dozens of them live in one room, pay exorbitant rents, lose part of their salary, sometimes their passport, and work day and night in agriculture. the portuguese government, like others in europe, was aware of this intolerable exploitation. these migrants too must be rescued and our governments also have obligations, not just third countries. we must take care of all migrants, those who risk their lives at sea and those who lose their dignity on land. there are no first-class immigrants, no second-class immigrants. as john xxiii taught, everyone is a person.
madam president, madam commissioner, mr president-in-office of the council, deaths in the mediterranean, search and rescue at sea, again! once again, deaths in the mediterranean, in the absence of sufficient rescue and salvage, remind us that every human life counts: the 130 who perished trying to reach lampedusa on 21 april, the one who was lost yesterday trying to swim to ceuta among five thousand others - the european union's external border, the european union's only land border with the african continent - and, allegedly, those 60 who left mauritania, whose three survivors, including aicha, as you recalled, commissioner johansson, lived a real hell that evokes that nightmare that happened in 1816 and that immortalized the romantic oil painting by gultéricault, the raft of the medusa. this cannot be solved by cooperating with the libyan coastguard in a non-country where there are massive human rights violations of those trying to reach the shores of the european union, nor can it be solved by externalizing the borders, nor by forgetting that life and its integrity must prevail over the protection of the borders of the european union. we need, we say again in this european parliament, a european rescue and salvage mechanism, which does not rely solely on that heroic spanish air force which rescued three survivors from sixty who left mauritania; we also need legal and safe routes, humanitarian visas, as this european parliament has repeatedly demanded, and safe landings in european ports, and, of course, aid at the source and in the countries of transit, but also a relentless criminal prosecution of human trafficking so that we do not have to be permanently, or recurrently, turning these debates on deaths in the mediterranean into a duel, not only in the mediterranean, but in the european parliament, which would represent the citizenry with genuine consternation and shock.

the commission has already made a number of proposals. if my predecessors have rightly pointed out that this is a debate on sea rescue, then we can only say clearly and emphatically: of course, every person whose life is in danger must be rescued here. the political question is whether it makes sense to rescue someone 20 kilometres off the libyan coast and then bring them 500, 600 kilometres to europe, or whether those people who need to be rescued - no question - should be sent back to where they came from - in the case of libya. we have also had absurd situations, such as the spanish enclave of ceuta, where last night and yesterday up to 6,000 people simply waded or swam from morocco to spain. they create an effect that many more want to come than have already come. the debate has actually been going on since 2015, and i've been in this house since 2014, and every year we have the same debate. the european union is not - i conclude - in a position to solve this problem effectively, and that can only mean that europe must finally close its borders.

sustainable solutions. we can’t continue with ad hoc solutions. so, for example, right now we are relying on voluntary relocations. that will not be enough. that’s why i proposed in the pact on acting president of the council. madam president, first of all, i thank the european parliament for this debate. it is very important that this issue remains on our agenda and that the european political groups contribute to consistent progress in our approach to this problem. it is therefore a credit to the european parliament. we need to continue to save lives and save more and more lives, each other to find solutions for the tracing and integration of the rescued people, and therefore it is also an honour for the member states which have worked towards this on a voluntary basis. we need to combat trafficking, we need to combat the smuggling networks of people who are criminals; they are highly organized criminals and they are, for all practical purposes, killers. but we must tackle and respond to the root causes of migration and refugee flows, and to do so we must work on several fronts: strengthening the protection and management of the european union's external borders, balancing the responsibility of frontline states with the solidarity of all other states towards them. we need to work on the pursuit of legal, safe and orderly migration routes to europe. europe needs migrants and it needs legal, safe, regular and orderly pathways of migration and we need to work on the external dimension of migration. we need to work more and more with the countries of origin and transit, particularly with the neighbouring countries in africa, but also in the middle east. and it's possible to move forward in all of this. we have a very important proposal from the european commission, the proposal for the new asylum and migration pact, and the portuguese presidency of the council has made it a priority to work on the basis of this proposal to try to build consensus on the proposal or on the central elements of this proposal. the proposal put forward by the european commission clearly meets all the challenges i have outlined, it is a good basis for work and the presidency of the council will fight, until the last minute of its mandate, to make progress in putting this proposal into practice and in obtaining the necessary consensus to make it possible. the approval, the agreement we reached yesterday on the blue card, which has nothing to do directly with the proposal for the new pact, is nevertheless a sign that we can understand each other, that we can reach agreements and, on the basis of the agreements we have reached, we can even move forward on the legal and safe channels of migration that europe so badly needs. but we also need to work more on the external dimension of migration. on the initiative of the portuguese presidency and the european commission and the high representative, a jumbo information meeting was held in march, bringing together the council's foreign and home affairs ministers. the council has not met for six years and the consensus reached by all was clear. it is possible to work on the basis of this consensus. a few days ago, a ministerial meeting was held in lisbon, also attended by the commissioner, bringing together representatives of the member states of the european union and representatives of states from north african countries, and it was also possible to identify ways forward together. and finally, we have today very important instruments for our cooperation, in particular with africa, the agreement reached at the end of the post-cotonou negotiations, the framework for cooperation with the countries of sub-saharan africa beyond the pacific and the caribbean and the fact that we have today the neighbourhood, development and international cooperation instrument, global europe, which has a very important set of funds that allow us to bring to the centre of our work the development of comprehensive agreements with different countries, within which development issues, partnership issues, investment issues can be addressed, thereby addressing the root causes of migration. it is very important to save lives, as it is equally important to address the root causes that have caused so much pain and so many lives lost in the mediterranean.

member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members of the european parliament, migration is a key policy area for the eu. this debate today is a timely opportunity to discuss the human rights aspects of our external migration policy and i would like to thank ms strik for her report. as the report highlights, migrants and refugees are among the most vulnerable groups in the world and i am deeply saddened that loss of lives continues to occur on the perilous journeys to europe. this is a constant reminder of the dangers migrants face. we will continue to do everything to prevent this from happening. over the past years, the eu has developed a comprehensive migration policy framework. our aim is to ensure that migration takes place in a safe and regular manner avoiding loss of life and providing international protection to those who are eligible. there is a strong agreement at eu level that migration has to be an integral part of overall relations with partners. eu foreign ministers and ministers for the interior agreed in march this year at the joint foreign affairs and home affairs council that the eu must ensure a comprehensive approach and that we need to work in close partnership with third countries. we aim to address migration in all its aspects. this also includes improving cooperation on return and readmission and the conclusion of formal readmission agreements or legally non—binding arrangements. but most of all, it means that the protection of all migrants, their dignity and their human rights must be at the heart of eu migration policy. this is reflected in the eu action plan on human rights and democracy, which calls for specific protection of migrants, refugees and internally displaced persons. the report calls for engagement with third countries on the rights of migrants. this is exactly what we are doing in our relations with partner countries. we are at all levels regularly advocating for the protection of human rights in the context of migration. our eu special representative for human rights, eamon gilmore, frequently addresses these issues in country visits or human rights dialogues he chairs. the report underlines the importance of the relevant international frameworks. i am strongly committed to multilateral solutions and approaches. the promotion and protection of human rights are inherent in our cooperation with international partners, such as the international organization for migration or the unhcr. high commissioner grandi and the high representative met very recently and discussed the situation in ethiopia, lebanon, colombia and the western balkans. our partnership to protect refugees and migrants in libya, as part of the african union, european union and united nations taskforce provides another example of specific cooperation. the new neighbourhood, development and international cooperation instrument – ndici, ‘global europe’ – will improve our ability to address migration—related challenges. the promotion and protection of human rights is enshrined in the instrument. the level of democratic scrutiny by the european parliament is enhanced by bringing the european development fund – which represented a third of the external action funding – under the union’s budget. the commission services and the eeas are committed to geopolitical dialogue with the european parliament, where general orientations on the implementation of the ndici will be discussed, the first one taking place on 15 june, where both the high representative, myself and commissioner urpilainen will be present.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. madam president, we were told that the pandemic would change everything, but the immigration policy remains the same or worse. these days we are witnessing in ceuta the practical translation of the externalization of european borders to dictatorships: six thousand people have swum across the southern border in the umpteenth blackmail exercise by the moroccan government to continue buying complicit silence in the face of the illegal occupation of the sahara. this is not just a spanish problem, but also a european migration policy problem, and it shows that the externalization of borders and the conditionality of development aid in migration control is not only criminal - with more than two thousand deaths this year - it is not only a violation of human rights - which are precisely the ones this report is talking about - it is not only not working - as we are clearly seeing - but it is also giving unscrupulous dictatorships a weapon of blackmail. if we want to put an end to this blackmail and protect the human rights of migrants, there is only one way: to dismantle the policies of fortress europe. the rest is buying into the far-right agenda by sending the army to the borders.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, dear minister, it is not an easy task to be the rapporteur for this report on turkey. at one point i have allowed myself the irony of saying that my in an environment which has not been easy and, moreover, by saying the same thing here in this gallery as we say in turkey. this report is probably the most critical of the historical series, because it reflects a critical situation in this parliament, in which we have spoken a lot about turkey in the last two years, and because it reflects probably the two worst years of our relationship with that country. i am not going to try to summarize the 30 pages you already know, but to clarify some of the messages contained in the report. a message to the turkish government: to restore confidence, first of all, we must change the anti-european rhetoric, which has been used so frequently in a nationalist atmosphere in turkey, but not only that. what really needs to change is the authoritarian tendency in the way the country is governed, an authoritarian interpretation of the presidential system that leads to an absolute inability to accept even the slightest political criticism - whether students, doctors, human rights activists, opposition parties - in a system centralized in the government, in which the parliament, and even the government itself, no longer have much to say. so what we are asking turkey for are facts, not words. do not send us any more programmes, any more action plans, if that political intention is not backed up by facts, for example, when it comes to implementing the judgments of the european court of human rights or returning to the istanbul convention, as everyone is asking that society to do. i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the future of the community. a sincerity that wouldn't need incentives. sometimes in turkey they say, "we have no incentives". excuse me, incentives to be a democracy? does a society really need incentives to want to be a mature democracy? i therefore believe that the turkish government must change a great deal of what has happened in recent years in order to put the country back on the path of convergence with europe. a message to turkish society, a society which miraculously still shows a huge commitment to european values and policies and which still considers itself, by and large, to be still largely pro-european: this parliament will not abandon pro-european and pro-democratic turkish civil society. turkey is much more than its government. sometimes in europe, only the turkish president is talked about as if there is no country behind him. a big country, a huge country, a very vital country; a country with a great civil society, which sometimes we don't see from here. this parliament will therefore continue to support turkish civil society, whatever the attitude of its government. and a message, mr minister, to the council and the member states: we need serious reflection. it is not possible that we should not have a unified policy with turkey; it is not possible that the question of values should be left on the agenda of parliament and that the democratic situation in turkey should be avoided whenever the council makes an offer to turkey. this creates an element of confusion for our turkish partners which is used against the european union. turkey is a candidate country; we must not forget that. the council cannot deal with turkey as if it were a third country, and parliament cannot deal with turkey as if it were only a candidate country, but we must unify our policies if they are to be useful for turkey and its society. so no positive agenda can be offered if strong democratic conditionality is not demanded. they want to talk to turkey about the customs union. in the end, mr minister, the customs union is going to come into this chamber and this chamber is saying that it will not support any reform of the customs union unless there is democratic conditionality. the sooner the council accepts that this is going to be necessary, the better for everyone. so this is a very critical report. i hope it is the most critical because in the future things will get better and we will have to change our approach to turkey. the report also has positive messages: it acknowledges turkey's efforts in the field of migration and it recognizes, behind its rulers, a country that is sometimes not seen from europe and that i think we all have to discover, despite the prejudices that sometimes assail us. the door to europe is therefore still open; at least, from the point of view of this parliament, with all the criticism contained in this report, the door to europe is still wide open.

cooperation between tax authorities in europe. the challenges are well known. in the context of the pandemic, the package adopted in july 2020 seeks to boost tax fairness by intensifying the fight against tax abuse, curbing unfair tax competition and increasing tax transparency. yesterday, in this very plenary, we had the opportunity to discuss the new communication on business taxation for the 21st century. however, even the best rules will not unleash their full potential if they are not enabled through fast and constructive cooperation between tax authorities, and here comes the importance of the fiscalis programme. tax authorities still have insufficient capacity and cooperation, both within the eu and with third countries, to carry out their missions effectively and efficiently. there is a need to provide quick and joint responses to problems such as tax fraud, tax evasion and tax avoidance, as well as to encompass the challenges related to digitisation and new business models, while reducing unnecessary administrative burden for citizens and businesses in cross—border transactions. the fiscalis programme offers member states a framework within which to develop cooperation activities to increase tax transparency and enhance cooperation. more than 70% of the fiscalis programme budget is used for financing it systems linking national tax administration. the continued operation of these it systems is essential for the exchange of tax information to fight tax fraud, evasion and avoidance. the programme also pursues a less visible but nevertheless very important objective to facilitate and modernise the work of the tax administration, which ultimately should result in a better service and less administrative burden for taxpayers. in writing. in the context of the negotiations on the 2021-2027 multiannual financial framework (mff), a roadmap for the introduction of new union own resources was agreed. for the first time the system was reformed. the three institutions, parliament, the commission and the council, also recognised that the introduction of a basket of new own resources would support the adequate financing of union expenditure and the costs of the next generation eu recovery plan. in this regard, the interinstitutional agreement reached at the end of 2020 established the own resources roadmap including which new own resources are introduced and their timetable: an own resource based on non-recycled plastic packaging waste which entered into force on 1 january this year, a carbon border adjustment mechanism, a digital tax and a european emissions trading system which are expected to be presented by the commission this month and should be introduced by 1 january 2023. the purpose of the plenary debate at this part-session was to keep up the pressure on the commission to implement the agreed own resources roadmap.

spanish. and from time to time it is good for me to speak spanish. nadie puede dudar de que los derechos humanos son un elemento central de nuestro acuerdo de diálogo político y de cooperación con cuba, y quiero aprovechar este momento para defender este acuerdo y su aplicación. son parte central de este acuerdo y continúan siendo una parte esencial de nuestra política con respecto a cuba, que podríamos describir como una política de compromiso crítico con este país. no hace falta decirles por qué. porque los europeos creemos que las libertades individuales y una sociedad civil dinámica, elementos en los que se basa nuestro sistema político, son fundamentales para el desarrollo social y económico de cualquier país. en ese sentido, hay casos concretos que sé que preocupan a algunos de los diputados que están en el origen de esta petición de debate y que también nos preocupan a nosotros, los responsables de las instituciones europeas, como el caso del artista y líder del movimiento san isidro luis manuel otero alcántara, caso que hemos tratado con las autoridades cubanas en repetidas ocasiones, tanto en bruselas como en la habana. conocemos este caso. nos hemos preocupado por él. sé que preocupa a sus señorías. y, por eso, celebro que el señor otero haya sido liberado el pasado 31 de mayo; nuestros servicios han estado en contacto con él desde su liberación. nos ha comunicado que continuará con su activismo político y ha expresado su agradecimiento por el apoyo que le ha prestado la unión europea. no tengan ninguna duda de que continuaremos haciendo un seguimiento de su situación personal y de las peticiones de libertad de expresión artística que ha formulado el movimiento san isidro. también, ciertamente, sé que les preocupa y nos preocupa al mismo nivel que a ustedes y por las mismas razones la situación de personas que protestaron pacíficamente en la calle obispo, la famosa y hermosa calle obispo de la habana vieja, para apoyarlo. cinco de ellas siguen todavía detenidas. lo mismo ocurre con otros miembros del movimiento san isidro. puedo citarlos: denis solís, o luis robles, detenido tras pedir la liberación del señor solís. hemos tratado estos y otros casos con cuba, con las autoridades cubanas. porque, como les digo, el diálogo sobre derechos humanos está en el centro de nuestra relación. es una de las razones de este acuerdo de diálogo político y de cooperación. y tratamos de desarrollar este acuerdo de una forma abierta y franca, tanto en cuestiones de derechos humanos como en otras muchas cuestiones de la relación que tenemos con cuba y con su gobierno. y seguiremos reforzando nuestro diálogo, porque esta agenda de compromiso crítico con cuba es precisamente lo que nos permite acompañar al país en la reforma política, económica y social siendo, como somos, conscientes de que la situación económica en cuba se ha agravado por la pandemia de covid—19 y también por otras importantes razones exógenas, como la vuelta, por parte de las autoridades de los estados unidos, a medidas restrictivas en el sentido económico y del intercambio material y de personas. en este contexto, el anuncio por parte de cuba de reformas económicas que incluyen la introducción de mecanismos más orientados al mercado y un mejor marco regulatorio para el sector privado es un paso importante. pero que la administración trump suprimiera la posibilidad, para muchos ciudadanos estadounidenses, de poder acudir como turistas a cuba fue un paso atrás para el mantenimiento de la actividad económica y, en consecuencia, también del bienestar de los ciudadanos cubanos. nosotros estamos dispuestos, por supuesto, a apoyar las reformas emprendidas, que todavía tienen que desarrollarse más. esto forma parte de nuestro compromiso con cuba en el marco del acuerdo al que antes me he referido. señoras y señores diputados, este acuerdo nos ha proporcionado un marco estable para un diálogo político regular que antes no existía y para una mayor cooperación en estos y en otros temas, y nos permite apoyar el proceso de modernización y reformas en cuba. tratamos cuestiones de derechos humanos, pero también trabajamos juntos para fomentar un desarrollo inclusivo y sostenible a través de una cooperación que es muy amplia. por ejemplo, en este momento estamos estudiando las posibilidades de aumentar la producción de vacunas contra la covid—19 sobre la base de algunos avances científicos realizados en la propia cuba. seguimos siendo el primer socio de cuba en cooperación, en comercio, en inversiones. seguimos apoyando las reformas, la inversión, como una forma de fortalecer las capacidades que son necesarias para una mayor integración de cuba en el comercio internacional. este acuerdo tiene solo tres años de vida y en esos tres años ha creado nuevos espacios para la participación de la sociedad civil. desde que se empezó a aplicar, el diálogo político ha ido regularmente precedido de encuentros con la sociedad civil, que reúnen a organizaciones europeas y cubanas. hasta ahora —es cierto—, estas reuniones formales han incluido solo a organizaciones cubanas registradas ante las autoridades, pero la unión europea está ahora recabando la opinión de todas las partes de la sociedad civil cubana en otros escenarios y a través de otros contactos. en conclusión, creo que puedo asegurarles que, como es costumbre en las relaciones diplomáticas de la unión europea, sea con cuba o con otros países, con otros muchos países con los que no compartimos el mismo sistema político, pero sí compartimos importantes objetivos de desarrollo humano, continuamos expresando nuestras preocupaciones y trabajando para que en cuba la ciudadanía pueda también disfrutar de los derechos que entendemos que forman parte del bienestar social de acuerdo con nuestro modelo político, que es el que creemos que debería ser aplicado en otros países. y para ello tenemos el acuerdo de diálogo político y de cooperación, que creo que es un instrumento para conseguirlo. no se me ocurre otro mejor y, por eso, aunque sé que algunas de sus señorías tienen serias reservas y reticencias sobre lo bien fundado de este acuerdo y de su aplicación, quisiera aprovechar esta ocasión para defenderlo.

author. madam president, madam secretary of state zacharias, commissioner schmit, i really thought that mr šefčovič was coming, but, well, you are also important to us. you're worth something to us, too. you have a number of responsibilities and i certainly greatly admire your work as employment commissioner and your commitment to the social pillar and its incorporation into the treaty, as well as the commitment of the portuguese presidency to the social summit. as regards the subject we are dealing with today - the right of inquiry of the european parliament - as we all know, the current framework is one which we might consider to be relatively outdated. it is an interinstitutional agreement of 1995, therefore, well before the treaty of lisbon, and it is certainly the treaty on the functioning of the european union, in article 226, which establishes a legal basis for the european parliament's committees of inquiry and gives parliament the initiative. the last paragraph states that the european parliament will determine the detailed rules for exercising the right of inquiry by means of regulations adopted on its own initiative, after approval by the council and the commission. after approval by the council and the commission. in 2014, the european parliament adopted a proposal for a regulation, known as the martin report, on the exercise of the european parliament's right of inquiry, which is a right that we consider very important in the context of a strengthened european democracy, as well as a right of legislative initiative also strengthened by the european parliament. the commission is also proposing that the european parliament should have greater co-decision powers in taxation and debt issuance matters, possibly also in the light of the eu recovery plan. but this report set out what seems to be somewhat normal if we look at comparative law, how committees of inquiry work in most national parliaments: it set out the ability to make it compulsory for those called to appear to do so, the ability to make visits to the member states in the context of the investigation being conducted, the right also to access the relevant documentation, and also a framework of sanctions in the event that any of these obligations, namely that of natural persons to appear, were breached. unfortunately, since 2014 - many years have passed, seven years - we find that the council still refuses to open formal negotiations with the european parliament, because many of these elements, if not all of them, up to six or seven, are considered red lines by the council that must be lifted and removed from the report before opening a negotiation process. obviously, from our point of view, it does not seem to us that the principle of loyal and good faith cooperation with parliament is being followed in this case. it hurts to say it, but that's how we understand it. and in any case, i think we should also bear in mind that the european parliament cannot go backwards either, that is to say, maintain the framework of a general and indiscriminate 'suppression', 'amputation' and, moreover, outside the framework of negotiation of the report, which would lead to a situation where we would be the same as in 1995. i think it is important for the council to understand this. i think that too much time has passed and that we must find a way of bringing positions together, of at least opening a more substantive dialogue on the substance and seeing which of these objections can find some kind of articulation.
madam president, today, 8 june, world oceans day, we must remember the role of the oceans in the fight against climate change, as a buffer against global warming, and fisheries as a sustainable element that also helps to maintain the oceans. it is true that climate change has made fishermen victims of global warming, and it is also true that much of the pollution that our oceans suffer is produced on land, more than 80%. so we must pursue the sustainability of fisheries, as we do in europe, with that maximum sustainable yield and by applying tacs and quotas, the landing obligation, with the most regulated fisheries in the world, but taking into account that our fishermen also provide us with food. healthy food and also respectful of the planet if done in a sustainable way. fishing that is harmful to the planet and the oceans is illegal fishing; sustainable fishing respects our oceans.

madam president, commissioner hahn, secretary of state zacarias, the european budget must be implemented in accordance with the principle of sound financial management, but this requires respect for the principles on which the union is founded, in particular the rule of law. the situation in some member states, where the rule of law is deteriorating very seriously, is alarming. if there are no guarantees that the authorities of a member state are acting in accordance with the law, that fraud and corruption are prosecuted and punished by an independent judiciary, or that free and pluralistic media can inform the public, they cannot receive european funds. commissioner, this parliament does not insist on the application of the conditionality mechanism on a whim. it is an unquestionable necessity and every day that passes makes it more urgent to act. we cannot put europe's recovery at risk because of mismanagement of funds. we have said it many times: the conditionality regulation is in force and directly applicable from 1 january. the commission has sought to adopt guidelines for its implementation in contravention of the co-legislators. but six months later, we're still waiting for them. we can understand caution and, of course, we all want things to be done right. but it has been a long time since we heard from the commission, which we consider to be inaction. i hope that you will respond to this call for attention and that we will see these guidelines very soon, but above all that which really matters: that serious violations of the rule of law affecting the union's budget are investigated and brought to an end. that's our goal. there's no time to lose. every attack on the rule of law is an attack on the freedoms and rights of european citizens.

madam president, commissioner schmit, secretary of state, after a decade of austerity policies, the european union has a great opportunity ahead of it. the covid-19 crisis has challenged the strength of our welfare and social protection systems yes, but at the same time it has reaffirmed the importance of the state and public action, has underlined the importance of having quality public services and has highlighted the effects of insufficient funding. the social summit in porto therefore represents a turning point, a great opportunity, the starting point for a more social, more inclusive and more sustainable recovery, putting people before gdp and using the european semester to implement reforms to build a strong social network. because economic growth is worthless if it does not improve people's daily lives, if it does not create more and better jobs that guarantee good working conditions for all. and that "everyone" as i always say, includes younger people, who are called upon to play a key role in the green and digital transitions, in the economic recovery and in the very defense of democracy. i would like to end by thanking commissioner schmit for his commitment to young people and making his words in porto my own: do not doubt that we will look after you and work hard to build a social europe that will allow you to grow and prosper.
in writing. the debate focused on the recent porto summit and its importance for the implementation of the principles of the social pillar. the socialists have been the main precursors of the holding of this summit, which is undoubtedly a new starting point for europe: putting the well-being of people at the forefront by meeting social objectives by 2030, including social indicators for the first time within the european semester, and giving social objectives the same importance as green and digital ones for a just and socially sustainable transition. after years of austerity, the pandemic has revealed a latent reality: only by pushing for strong social policies can we help to tackle this crisis. we therefore need a strong and robust social network, through initiatives (many of them legislative in nature) that will promote the reduction of poverty, the creation of quality employment, the reduction of inequalities and the gender gap. europe cannot afford to repeat past mistakes, and our group will continue to work to ensure strong welfare systems in the eu.
