the chairman of the council. mr president of the european parliament, madam president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen! almost exactly thirty years ago, the slovenes created their own state. a year earlier, we had our first multiparty elections. during that period, as many as 90 percent of voters in a referendum supported the dream of an independent state. only once in history has so many of our citizens supported a particular decision. and that was the decision on slovenia's accession to the european union. for us slovenes, being part of the european union has never been just an economic opportunity. it meant returning to a family bound by the values of respect for human rights and fundamental political freedoms and democracy. everything that was taken from us or violated in communist yugoslavia. this return to europe coincided with the fundamental historical mission of the european union, which was dictated by the fall of the totalitarian communist regimes in europe. the creation of a europe that is whole and free, at peace with itself and with its neighbours. the european union today is quite different from what it was when we joined and also during the first presidency of the council of the european union and then also of the european council. it can be said that the presidency of the first half of 2008 was the last presidency not to be marked by one or other of the severe crises. and then there was the financial crisis, the migration crisis, the occupation of crimea and the creation of frozen conflicts in our eastern neighborhood, and then brexit, and since the beginning of last year, the coronavirus pandemic. and in times of crisis, the european union was primarily compelled to respond to them and also to try to mitigate them as quickly as possible. we strongly hope that this semester marks the time when the european union can and must begin to act more strategically, more long-term, towards the goal set by the founding fathers of the european union. europe, free, at peace with itself, whole and at peace with its neighbours. slovenia is taking over the presidency of the council of the european union for the second time since it became a member of the european union. it will round off the work of the trio, in which we have been involved with germany and portugal, and with initiatives, some initiatives and activities, we have been involved in the work of the trio from the very beginning. at this point, we would like to thank germany and portugal for a job well done in the very difficult circumstances of the pandemic. for the second half of this year, our semester, we have some challenges and priorities that arise from the situation in which the european union finds itself today, but which we believe also contribute to the existence and development of the union. the first priority is, of course, resilience and recovery after the pandemic and the establishment of a strategically autonomous union. this appropriation is intended to cover the financing of the purchase, hire, maintenance and repair of equipment and installations, and the purchase of equipment and installations for the construction, maintenance, repair and overhaul of buildings, including the purchase of equipment and installations for the construction of buildings, and the purchase of equipment and installations for the construction, maintenance, repair and repair of buildings. we are pleased that the recovery is set in a way that is also reform-oriented and that we will recover simultaneously as we implement the green and digital transition. the next priority is a union of the european way of life, the rule of law and equal standards for all, for all member states and for all citizens in the member states of the european union. this is also a union of balanced rights and responsibilities, with a high level of protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, including the right to freedom of expression. the priority is then to have a credible and secure european union, a union capable of ensuring security and stability not only on its own territory but also in its neighbourhood. this is also a question of good cooperation with and within the north atlantic alliance, since most of the member states of the european union are also members of this alliance. then it is about projecting our values and stability into our neighbourhood and it is about a union of protected external borders and clear demarcation between legal and illegal migration. and then we have, or we have already started well, this conference on the future of europe, or, to be more precise, first a conference and a discussion on the future of the european union and, of course, also talks on the future of europe as a continent. here we want to organise as many debates as possible over the next six months, open to all who wish to contribute their suggestions to shaping a common european future. since this is a question of the common european future, we are all called to this debate, without anyone feeling that he or she is chosen and called to teach others about the future of europe. here, it is necessary to ensure a level playing field so that everyone, regardless of their differences, can contribute their views on how they envisage this common european future. we have the basis for this debate in the existing treaties, and within that framework, all views are welcome, even if they are contradictory, because only an open debate can bring us forward. let me just highlight a few key points, not all of which are possible at this time, and start with the challenge that we still have ahead of us, which is the covid-19 pandemic. the effects of this crisis are visible every day, and we feel them here today because we wear masks. we're wondering what's going to happen in the coming weeks and months, when the number of delta cases will inevitably increase, and what kind of fall is in store. now, of course, with a lot of caution, despite the much less pressure of the pandemic and the opening up of public life, we are doing everything we can to be prepared for this possible fourth wave and that it does not present the same obstacles and the same trials that we saw last fall. we are optimistic above all because we see that the european vaccination strategy is working, that it is delivering results. of course, the more optimistic expectations for the future are primarily about accelerated vaccination and the actual willingness of the vast majority of our fellow citizens to actually get vaccinated, not to wait for others to do it for them, and to reach a certain level of vaccination that is sufficient to keep them out. this is the key question now, how to convince our fellow citizens that everyone who gets vaccinated is the one who contributes to our future normal life, and that's anywhere in europe, because as we see, the virus knows no borders and this is our common challenge. one of the things that allows us to live much more normally, or expect to live much more normally, through the summer and the fall, despite the virus, is the european digital covid certificate. congratulations on reaching an agreement between the institutions in such a short time, so that this certificate can actually be used and that this certificate also allows the member states, in matters falling within their national competence, to live and organise much more freely than without it. in short, if our first short-term priority is to do everything we can to avoid a fourth wave that would shut down public life and threaten development in the european union again, then our best hope is that we will nonetheless return to a cautious pre-covid normalcy in these six months, even though some precautions will obviously have to be maintained for some time. the resilience and recovery of the european union and a strategically autonomous union is something that is a priority at this time, regardless of who is leading the council of the european union. in addition to the vigilant, vigilant and as coordinated and coordinated as possible further response to the pandemic, we therefore have the responsible task of recovery and also of ensuring a more resilient future for the european union, a greater resilience, a greater readiness to deal with a crisis such as the epidemic. a lot has been done in europe since the beginning of the covid crisis, when we were not prepared to do our best. in fact, no country in the world, with a few exceptions, was quick to respond, but outside the european continent, because no country was prepared for it and we didn't have the best start, but today the picture is quite different. a timely agreement on a recovery plan was reached, which is a huge success. those of us who were present at the four-day european council in july know this firsthand. i would like to thank the commission for having, from the outset, removed some of the restrictions on the instruments needed to respond to the financial crisis. this has prevented the drastic declines in standards and crises that occurred during the financial and economic crisis, in particular in 2009, and has facilitated the recovery. the european union is also among the leaders in research, production and also export of vaccines. the european vaccination strategy is working. what remains to be done at this moment and what lies ahead of us is no longer up to the european commission, the european parliament, the governments of the national states, it is now up to each individual. we have the tool, we have the vaccine, and now it's up to you, my fellow citizens, my fellow europeans, to use it and actually stop this epidemic. we're also at a point where we can help others. the european union is by far the largest solidarity donor, the one that donates vaccines, and so far, it's over 100 million doses to the less developed countries, and we can and should do a lot more of that in the future. during the covid crisis, we learned some very important lessons. the european commission's lessons learned document lists them in more detail, and i will mention just a few. it is clear that we need a common european plan to deal with crises such as covid, a plan for cases where such a crisis is, where such a threat is symmetrical, where it affects everyone, as well as plans for situations where the threat is asymmetrical, where it affects only some member states and where we can help others. it is very important here to know what we can do together and when we need to do something together. as we saw last year, national measures, which are obviously necessary in the absence of a common plan, can have major crossborder effects on other member states, the internal market of the european union and the four freedoms are very vulnerable in a crisis, all of which we experienced last year. just think of the truck trains that were all over europe a year ago, and we'll all know what needs to be done. now, of course, we also have our vulnerability and our dependence on third countries for certain strategic assets that were critical in this crisis, such as personal protective equipment, critical medical equipment, medicines or ingredients for medicines, and, ultimately, the ingredients needed for vaccines. our aim must be to replace these ad hoc solutions, which we used during the crisis and learned a lot from, with permanent structural measures, plans that will be made in advance, and here we want to complete the work on the establishment of a european health union. a lot of work has already been done here. and i think that at least there is a high level of agreement among all the member states and the european institutions on what steps need to be taken to build this health union. as recent events in the united states and ireland have shown, we can very quickly find ourselves in a situation where a large-scale cyber attack can have consequences as devastating as the spread of a virus, and even worse, if our energy grid is attacked, for example. the development of joint cyber defence plans and the building of joint capabilities, which is already underway, are our primary tasks. the european union also exists to deal successfully with such a symmetrical or asymmetrical threat. no member state, not even the largest, is strong enough to deal with such a threat, given that we share energy networks and so on. and here only a common plan and also common capabilities make effective defence possible, because there are at least two sources of serious threat, which no single country in the european union can, according to the information known so far, stand alone against. all countries have committed to a significant share of digital and green investments in their national recovery plans. and here, when we talk about digitisation and the digital transition, the european union faces considerable challenges. in many places around here, we're lagging behind the other major players in the world. to give you a few examples: in the european union, we have companies that produce the best photolithography equipment, which is the key technology for making semiconductors, but we assemble and manufacture less than one percent of the world's production in europe. moreover, although europe has the most prestigious universities and the most technologically advanced laboratories, we only design or ultimately manufacture one per cent of the world's semiconductors, and without semiconductors there is no sign of digitisation and digital transition. we have the knowledge, we have the capabilities, but we need to use them and we need to decide where the boundary between trade cooperation is and where european autonomy begins when it comes to critical infrastructure and when it comes to critical products. and here is the fact that the european union must become as autonomous as possible. on the other hand, of course, when it comes to digitisation, we want to act in line with our european values. among them, of course, are the right to privacy, the protection of personal data. these are values that some of our competitors, when it comes to digitization, are not really at the forefront of. the regulation of digital services, the regulation of artificial intelligence and the related area of data management are therefore more challenging for us than for anyone outside the european union, and these are all topics where we will continue to seek a balance between competitiveness on the one hand and respect for european values on the other during our semester. and if we can find the right balance in our internal debate, then i believe that the european union can also take a leading role in shaping digital standards on a global level, which is the next very big challenge. last december, we set a very ambitious target of reducing emissions by 55 percent by 2030. to this end, we would like to encourage other countries around the world to follow our example. but it's not just a question of ambition, it's also a question of how to convince others of the standards that are needed to achieve those goals. outside europe, i think, more than 90 percent of co2 is emitted, and here success can only be achieved globally. europe can be a leader, but it cannot achieve this goal alone, and here, but in this, we must also ensure that the individual parts of europe do not pay too high a price for this transition, that we do not destroy european industries and, of course, what our fellow citizens are most concerned about, that the prices of electricity and fuel do not rise disproportionately and have a significant impact on the decline in the quality of life. the european commission will propose a major legislative package on climate and energy next week. we expect a proposal to be presented that is balanced and fair to all, and in this way we can hope to reach agreement on how to translate our ambitious climate goals into binding law in the shortest possible time. it has also provided a good basis for the union's action in the international arena, notably at the climate negotiations in glasgow this november. a union of the european way of life, the rule of law and equal standards for all. europeans, hand to heart, we don't often think about what the european way of life means, because we live it, we are in the middle of it. it seems obvious to us, but of course it's not. the social market economy is a european invention. in other parts of the world, economic and social relations are regulated somewhat or quite differently from ours. there are many who envy our solutions. so when we talk about european legislation on minimum wages or the cross-border transfer of social security rights, let us keep this in mind. we have, for example, the european model of sport. it's not based on elitism, it's not based on elitism or exclusion in principle, but on equal opportunities, starting points, opportunities for all, on connecting local communities, on belonging. and of course at the very heart of the european way of life are some of our common european values. this is the equal dignity of every human being, the inherent inalienable rights of man and the fundamental political freedoms. respect for the rule of law on the basis of equal criteria is essential for citizens' trust in public institutions. it is also a key condition for mutual trust between member states in the european union and, when it comes to rule of law issues, we must be clear that in the end, when it comes to the rule of law, what is right and what is wrong is always decided by an independent judicial body and not by a political body. the quality of the functioning of the justice system is also important here. it must be based on an independent, impartial and non-selective judiciary which, in each member state, strives for justice and ensures legal protection without delay and without unreasonably long time limits. what mankind speaks of as right, the rule is that right is delayed, right is denied. the commission will also continue to monitor the implementation of the eu's new rules on the protection of personal data. this is particularly necessary in environments with media monopolies, which unfortunately also exist in the european union. in this context, the slovenian presidency recalls the resolution of the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe no 1096 and the european parliament resolution on european consciousness and totalitarianism. the guidance and warnings they provide are of lasting importance for the development of resilient, vital democracies, and in particular for the realisation of the historic goal of a europe that is whole, free and at peace with itself. some of the guidelines and warnings of both resolutions have not yet been implemented in some of the younger european democracies. this is where we see some of the deeper reasons for the mutual misunderstandings on the rule of law in the individual member states of the european union. many are unwilling and unable to see cases where the standards and guarantees of the rule of law do not in fact protect the european values enshrined in article 2 of the treaty on european union, but on the contrary, the institutions of the rule of law, which have only formally assumed new roles with the transition to democracy, and have not undermined them, serve primarily to defend undue privileges and to maintain a culture of action built up over decades of undemocratic regimes and practices that diminish the space of freedom and perpetuate entrenched inequalities and even injustice. these issues will also be discussed at the international conference to be held in slovenia on the occasion of the european day of remembrance for the victims of all totalitarian regimes on 23 august this year. it is also our common responsibility and our permanent task to keep alive the memory of the fact that the awareness of the necessity of european integration processes was formed precisely in the difficult and undemocratic historical trials of the twentieth century, which have befallen and marked the peoples of the present-day member states of the european union, although each in its own way and for different periods of time. a credible and secure european union, capable of ensuring security and stability also in its neighbourhood. we believe it is time for the european union to become more strategic in its thinking and actions in its engagement with the world. and that's especially true for our immediate neighborhood. slovenia, as the presidency of the council of the european union, will therefore give priority to the european union's cooperation with the western balkans region as well as with its eastern neighbourhood this semester. when we talk about the western balkans, it is a region of strategic importance for the union, and that is why we will co-host the european union summit on the western balkans with the president of the european council in slovenia in october. we believe that the enlargement of the european union is the logical response to the strategic challenges we face, both in the eastern neighbourhood and in the western balkans. slovenia is well aware, from its own experience, of the importance of the european perspective for the implementation of reforms in the accession negotiations process. but that perspective must be tangible, such that it can be believed to be realized within the lifetime of the current generation, or it is no longer an incentive. and this sensitivity must inspire and be the source of the political energy needed to implement the necessary reforms at the political level, it must be the source of the energy and the focus of the political awareness of citizens to be able to offer bottom-up support to these reforms. our aim is to reaffirm, reawaken and revive the european perspective of the western balkan countries, as set out at the thessaloniki summit in 2003. and i think that if we do that, then we will prove that we are a strategic player here, and if we are not able to do that, if we do not take steps forward in the western balkans, someone else will take those steps and they have different interests and different values. the issue of migration is also closely linked to the western balkans region. this is one of the two main migration routes into the european union, i mean illegal migration, and when it comes to migration, there is a demanding dossier on the table here too. i think we can agree on the importance of cooperation with countries of origin and transit. we know what we need to do here, theoretically. there is also no difference between us on the importance of reinforcing control of the external border, there is a high level of agreement. there is, of course, less agreement on some parts of the migration pact, such as the issue of relocation and solidarity and responsibility. and here we are looking for solutions that are acceptable to all countries, because only in this way can we ensure that the new system will eventually be put into practice. illegal migration has also put a heavy burden on the functioning of the schengen area over the past years. schengen is one of the most important achievements of our integration process. we believe that it is particularly important here, at a time when we are hopefully returning to normalcy, to ask about the extension of this area, so that it can be put on the agenda. we consider that any member state that fulfils the conditions should be allowed to join the schengen area. in our view, bulgaria, romania and croatia are being unnecessarily kept in a waiting room, and this is not in their interests or in the interests of the european union. and let me conclude by saying a few words about the conference on the future of europe. i am glad that the discussion on the organisational aspects of the conference is over, that it is now time for a substantive debate, time for the voice of europeans to be heard. the debate will allow very concrete conclusions to be drawn in the spring of next year. i think we are facing a great opportunity for this frank debate, that somehow this is the time with the conference on the future of europe, that it coincides with many issues that are open or that are re-opened. in slovenia, we will be organising debates on the future of the european union as part of this year's bled strategic forum, to which we will be inviting a number of guests from the european union institutions, national leaders, former leaders who participated in the debates on the constitution for europe, the lisbon treaty, european think tanks, citizens and, of course, representatives of all the political groups in this parliament. there are a number of open questions here, such as the poor demographic trends in most member states and the different views on how to tackle the demographic issue. then, in much of the european union, we face, for example, low voter turnout in elections to the european parliament. other fundamental questions of european democracy remain open, the question of the gap between the average european and the european institutions, the attempts by unwilling actors to take over the role of those elected by the voters. we have more and more time to spend on political bickering within the european union and less time to have serious discussions about strategic and development dilemmas. we are at the crossroads of many paths, but we also need some answers, or at least a debate on which way to go to find answers to some strategic foreign and security policy dilemmas. for example, how to strengthen the role of the european union so that it can have a stronger influence on the trends of globalisation. when we adopted the lisbon treaty, i was one of the signatories, in lisbon, we said that this treaty would enable the european union to steer globalisation. today we must ask ourselves where we are actually capable of doing this and where we still have a great deal to do to do it. then, there is a need to reach a consensus on whether and how rapid enlargement of the european union in the western balkans and the eastern neighbourhood is a strategic response to strategic challenges. the question then arises whether there is any good alternative to a stronger security and military engagement by the european union in sub-saharan africa, in the sahel region, where terrorism is preventing the most basic humanitarian, educational and development projects from being carried out, and this danger is growing almost month by month. then how to define the long-term relationship between the european union and the russian federation, between the european union and turkey, which is becoming the most influential factor in the mediterranean. then, as already mentioned, where is the boundary between the economic and trade relations between the european union and china and the necessary strategic autonomy of the european union. then how to strengthen relations with india, the largest democracy on the planet, in a comprehensive and rapid manner. i think we also need to have a frank conversation in this debate about, say, our responsibility for the victims and the suffering that has been and will be because we are pulling out of afghanistan and leaving the people there at the mercy of the taliban. we must agree that in the future we will not engage in activities that merely destroy something, not allowing for the building of something new, better, more lasting. we also need to wake up and realise that the european union's great, good and indispensable soft power, unprecedented in the global world, is nowhere good enough, because we are not able to guarantee people basic security and basic human rights. that the european union, if it is to become a leading regional and then equally global power, simply needs a combination of soft and hard power. ladies and gentlemen, for our near-term future, the most important thing right now is to stop the pandemic and recover as quickly as possible from it, and to include the digital and green transitions in that recovery. for the good of the future in general, for the good of our own future and that of future generations of europeans, it is most important that we openly discuss the open strategic dilemmas and find common solutions that will pave the way forward.

mr president just two years after prime minister abiy was awarded the nobel peace prize, the ethiopian government launched an armed operation in tigray that has, as we have already mentioned, claimed 2,500 civilian lives so far. every day new reports come to light of the atrocities committed by ethiopian and eritrean soldiers. the hardships of the population were compounded by the fact that humanitarian organizations were unable to reach tigray for months. we must say that the military action of the addis ababa government has caused a humanitarian catastrophe. but the biggest threat now is food shortages. two million people are hungry, it's been mentioned here, five million people, 90 percent of the population, are in need of humanitarian assistance. the armed conflict and the unilateral decisions taken by ethiopia in the context of the renaissance ghetto, without reaching an agreement with sudan and egypt, threaten the stability of the whole region. the ceasefire announced by the ethiopian government is a very limited but very important opportunity to respond. all obstacles to the delivery of aid must be removed. it is in europe's fundamental interest to act swiftly and effectively. the conflict must be prevented from escalating further and all bilateral contacts, including those at the un, must be used to bring the opposing sides to the negotiating table. do you see any concrete opportunities for european action, joint action, to help the peace process?
mr president, with great concern and sadness, we follow the ongoing tragic events in tigray and elsewhere in ethiopia. the situation in tigray has seriously escalated, but the crimes against human rights are happening in other regions and towards different ethnicities. our first and foremost priority is to help civilians who have no access to medical assistance, are dying of famine and are often victims of sexual violence. furthermore, the exclusion of tigray from general elections and communication disruptions makes this horrible situation even worse. we need to do everything to support a ceasefire that all would respect. that way, they can ensure that the humanitarian aid is delivered on the ground to the ones in need urgently. we also need concrete eu measures, including an arms embargo and targeted sanctions against all perpetrators. tigray is without doubt one of the urgent, if not the most pressing, humanitarian situations we should work on to the full extent of our capabilities and powers.
mr president, since the beginning of the conflict in the tigray region of ethiopia eight months ago, more than 400 000 people have now been plunged into famine and more than one and a half million people are at risk of famine. it is one of the worst humanitarian crises in the region in the last decade. you both said it, both in the council and in the commission: the first priority is of course respect for the ceasefire, access to humanitarian aid for all those at risk and the protection of civilians. but in the medium term, the european union, the african union and the entire international community will have to support all efforts for an inclusive dialogue between all communities in this country and also ensure that external military forces leave this country. the solution, as we know, cannot be military, but the perpetrators of serious human rights violations must be prosecuted if we want to have reconciliation, because there is no reconciliation in impunity.
mr president, i am also very worried about the ongoing situation in ethiopia. the fresh start we expected with the election has turned into a nightmare. a few days ago, i spoke with the representatives of various tigrayan communities and i received extremely worrying information concerning human rights. the ethiopian government is extensively cracking down on civilians throughout the country. this is the reason why i would not focus only on tigray, but i would rather highlight the situation regarding the whole of ethiopia, where several human rights violations have been reported, including arbitrary arrests and detentions, torture, executions and forced displacements. ethiopia needs to see an inclusive national dialogue with all communities, political parties and wider civil society. the commitment and the fundamental role of the european union lies in humanitarian aid and in promoting inter—regional dialogue and the restoration of security. let’s act right away!
mr president, finally, after eight months of hostilities, the tigray people’s liberation front is willing to accept a ceasefire proposed by the ethiopian authorities. i encourage this move towards a peaceful future and call on both sides to find an agreement on the conditions of the ceasefire via diplomatic means. the violent actions need to stop as soon as possible for the good of the ethiopian people. the atrocities have deteriorated the humanitarian situation in tigray. more than 400 000 people are estimated to live in famine and another 1.8 million are on the brink of it. that’s a shame. a shame for civilisation. a shame for us today, because we all remember ethiopia in the eighties and the great famine, and history is repeating itself with us helpless and watching it. coordinating actions of humanitarian support is of crucial importance at this moment. i welcome the clear commitment of the european commission to support ethiopian citizens and to prevent further humanitarian catastrophes. however, aid workers still face difficulties in reaching out to the people in need. the parties in the conflict should facilitate the access of aid to all parts of tigray and provide assistance according to the principles of international law. and we have instruments: we just voted ndici. we voted this huge amount of money, that’s the only weapon that we can use nowadays. stop cooperating with people who don’t want to cooperate with us and save further loss of life.
mr president, commissioner, minister, the tigray conflict is a painful and sad moment in contemporary history in which hunger is being used as a weapon of war and the lives of thousands of people are being put at risk. the situation on the ground is very unstable, access to food, energy or the internet is extremely limited and the armed conflict has generated numerous human rights violations, massacres, violations, thousands of wounded, dead, displaced or refugees. the international community must act urgently and stop treating this matter as an internal matter of the ethiopian state. this is a serious regional conflict, with eritrean troops participating alongside government troops, with severe implications for civil society. the electoral process of 21 june, which was important in the construction of the democratic process, did not pave the way for the pacification of the present situation, nor did it open the way for the urgent humanitarian response. it is therefore urgent to forge international diplomatic bridges capable of bringing the two sides to the table and finding a peaceful solution to this conflict. the ethiopian prime minister, who won the nobel peace prize for his contribution to the solution of the conflict with eritrea, now has a golden opportunity to be considered, once again, in his own home, the peacemaker and not the warlord.
mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to stop this. the conflict in the tigray region has taken a brutal toll on the civilian population. according to reports by international human rights organizations, there have been mass killings of civilians, human rights violations, acts of violence against the civilian population, including rape. in addition, the conflict has led to the mass displacement of up to 1.7 million people in the tigray region, a region completely cut off from communications, the internet, and a huge humanitarian crisis. according to the un, as many as 5.5 million people are in need of food, and as many as 10 percent of children are severely malnourished. at the same time, the delivery of aid to the region is hampered not only by the lack of electricity, telecommunications and access to fuel, but also by road closures and transportation. we must strongly urge the ethiopian authorities to enable and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid to the tigray region and other areas in need of support. it is also very important to investigate all killings and human rights violations, including cases of excessive use of force against civilians.
president, if the european union is to be a global actor and to have credibility in its own policies, it must urgently take stronger action in tigray, in front of the local population and against those responsible for the war crimes and crimes against humanity that have been and are still being committed there. the unilaterally declared ceasefire seems to me to be more of a military, tactical calculation than a step towards lasting peace or a solution to the humanitarian crisis. the international community can no longer remain aloof from what is happening in tigray. first of all, i am looking at the united nations and the european union, which, because of its belief in the multilateral approach to regional conflicts and humanitarian crises, can play a leading role within the un. i therefore urge the council to show more decisiveness and to take real decisions. the humanitarian crisis must be addressed immediately, but the international community must also invest in ending the conflict, in restoring stability and rebuilding the destroyed society, and in an international investigation and a proper prosecution of the crimes committed against the population.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like sincerely to thank honourable members for this debate. i took note with great interest of the comments that were made during the discussion. as we have heard, the humanitarian situation in tigray continues to deteriorate at an alarming pace. in spite of the recent unilateral ceasefire by the ethiopian authorities, access issues and protection risks remain, and they remain widespread throughout the tigray province. for us, the absolute priority right now is to ensure the protection of civilians and to provide significant humanitarian aid to reach all those who need it. in these famine conditions, the last thing we can afford is the situation of siege that we are witnessing. we are witnessing a situation where humanitarian supplies and humanitarian personnel face parties to the conflict who are blocking roads and destroying bridges, vital bridges. so we must continue to call on all parties to respect international humanitarian law, to facilitate access for humanitarian aid, and to commit to an immediate, indefinite and negotiated ceasefire arrangement, which will be necessary to end all violence for good and to restore stability in the tigray region and beyond. and yes, the european union is ready to contribute even more in both directions, on the humanitarian front as well as to contribute to the efforts to find a political solution. as far as the humanitarian front is concerned, we are ready to activate our european union humanitarian air bridge service to reach the tigray region, but for that we will need the agreement of the ethiopian government. on the political front, we have been working all along, since the beginning of this crisis, with like—minded countries such as the united states and the gulf countries, and in particular with the african union, and we’re trying to push for political solutions. we have also been working through our eu special representative for the horn of africa, and the new one is to visit the region in the coming days. finally, as you know, the high representative has appointed a special envoy, who has visited ethiopia and the region several times, and is working incessantly to find a way towards a political solution to this conflict. once again, let me thank you for this debate. we have learnt very useful views that will help us chart the way forward.
the chairman of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union will do its utmost to contribute to ending the conflict and human suffering and to creating a lasting solution. the situation is very sensitive, unstable and uncertain. at this stage, it is difficult to establish reliable channels of communication with the main actors on the ground in terms of consolidating the ceasefire, assuming responsibility in the field of human rights and establishing dialogue between the parties to the conflict. ethiopia is our strategic partner in fighting for regional peace and for international discussions such as climate change. recently, on 10 june, we met in political dialogue at the level of deputy foreign minister, which shows that we can work together despite our differences. we are determined to take action against the many abuses and violations of human rights and to find out who is responsible for them. whoever did this must be punished. as i mentioned in the opening debate, we have tabled a resolution on this in the human rights council. we are in contact with the office of the high commissioner for human rights and advocate for support and unhindered access for a joint fact-finding mission to find the perpetrators and hold them accountable. as i have already said, we will discuss this situation with the foreign ministers and the high representative at the council next week, to which i will also convey the content of today's debate. thank you again for the discussion today.

the next item is the council and commission statements on the 70th anniversary of the geneva convention (2021/2779 ((rsp)). i would like to inform you that there will be one round of speeches by the political groups in this debate.
president-in-office of the council. – madam president, honourable members, commissioner, 2021 marks the 70th anniversary of the refugee convention, a global instrument that has assisted millions of displaced persons over many decades. in the context of continuing wars, conflict, human rights violations, persecution and record levels of displacement, the geneva convention continues to protect the rights and lives of refugees, and it is as relevant today as it was in 1951. at the end of 2020, the number of displaced persons worldwide reached a record of 82.3 million, including 26.4 million refugees and 48 million internally displaced persons, in addition to an estimated 4.2 million stateless persons. multilateral and multi-stakeholder action is thus more essential than ever to ensure protection for the displaced and to realise a sustainable solution. the standards set forth in the 1951 convention with all later versions were profoundly tested by the covid-19 crisis that also affected international protection and solidarity. the pandemic spared no country or region and disproportionately affected populations which were already vulnerable. refugees and displaced persons are among those most adversely affected by the crisis. the only way to help them and to effectively address global challenges is through a global response and international solidarity. a renewed commitment to the principles enshrined in the 1951 convention is crucial. the eu remains the leading donor in humanitarian and development assistance. moreover, the eu supports and will continue to support capacity-building in partner countries, strengthening asylum and reception capacities and providing protection to those in need. while doing so, we must not forget that only a truly collaborative approach can make a difference and help us establish clear and workable methods, while ensuring necessary solidarity. thank you very much for your attention.
member of the commission. – madam president, we celebrate today the signing 70 years ago – 70 years ago this very month – of the refugee convention, a legally binding commitment made by the countries of the world to help millions of european refugees – victims of nazi and communist tyranny; survivors of persecution, mass murder and genocide; their homes destroyed, their possessions stolen; uprooted and adrift in a continent shattered by six years of brutal war. the parties to the convention, members of the united nations, promised to support european refugees with practical aid and treat refugees like their own citizens, without discrimination. they voted to uphold the right to housing, the right to education, the right to work, to freedom of religion and other fundamental rights. above all, the principle of non-refoulement, the cornerstone of the convention, the commandment not to put refugees back in harm’s way, not to turn people fleeing terror, oppression, persecution straight back into the hands of their persecutors as happened so often with such tragic deadly consequence in the years before world war two. ever since 1951, the convention has been a beacon to guide refugees towards safe haven, from hungary in 1956, czechoslovakia in 1968, vietnam in the 1970s, the balkan wars in the 1990s, from syria, somalia, afghanistan today. in all those years the convention’s scope has increased, as has the power to inspire. at the same time, the right to asylum is under pressure. the convention remains as important as ever. today, i would like to think about my friend kati piri, who was until recently a member of this house and now represents her voters in the dutch parliament. her father fled hungary in 1956. he could raise his daughter in freedom, and i just say: thank goodness for the convention. thank goodness that no one pushed him back across the border and that no one at that time said, ‘let’s process his application on another continent’. there is another treaty we remember this year. seventy years ago six european countries signed the treaty of paris creating the european pact on coal and steel, laying the foundations for our union, resolving to replace a bloody conflict on the battlefield by negotiations at the conference table. we now have 76 years of peace in europe. because we have peace, refugees are no longer leaving europe. because we have peace, democracy and freedom refugees are now coming to europe. worldwide, 80 million people have fled their homes and developing countries host more than 86% of all refugees. the convention was once a global answer to a european catastrophe. today, we must give a european answer to a global emergency. we can and must do more. i want us to commemorate the convention by taking action through our funds. the eu is the leading humanitarian aid donor. we support people in more than 80 countries. last year the eu used almost its entire eur 900 million humanitarian aid budget to help refugees, displaced persons and host communities. the commission supports turkey as one of the largest refugee-hosting countries in the world, with nearly 3.7 million refugees. i want to commemorate the convention by action, by making progress on the new pact on migration and asylum. that’s the only way to make sure refugees can fully enjoy their rights under the convention. step by step, we are advancing on the pact, as we did last month with a political agreement on the blue card and as we did last week with a political agreement on the eu asylum agency. and i call on you all today to commemorate by action and make progress on the union resettlement framework. we must move from ad hoc support to a stable system of resettlement. this will be another important step to deliver the pact. i want us to commemorate the convention by stepping up on resettlement. since 2015, member states have granted 2.5 million people protection who came to europe on their own initiative, often after dangerous journeys. and at the same time, europe gave more than 80 000 people a new home through resettlement. last year, just over 10 000 refugees came to europe in this safe and orderly way, impressive in covid conditions but a 60% drop all the same. i want more people to be able to come to europe safely so fewer people feel the need to risk their lives on dangerous journeys. i want us to get back to pre-pandemic levels and beyond. the global need is high. this friday i will host a high-level forum on resettlement. i will call on member states to increase their pledges. i’m very grateful for the support and participation of this house in the forum and the participation of ministers from italy and finland, two countries that are very active on resettlement and community sponsorship. we can only make a difference if we join forces worldwide. that is why, for the very first time, i’ve brought together key international partners on resettlement. at this first unprecedented forum un high commissioner for refugees filippo grandi, canadian minister of immigration marco mendicino, and us secretary for homeland security alejandro mayorkas. at the joint eu-us justice and home affairs meeting last month, secretary mayorkas told us the us is back. the time is right to show democratic leadership and to give many more refugees a safe route to a welcome home. the convention is at the heart of our union. it’s part of our history. it’s part of the treaty and the charter of fundamental rights. it’s part of who we are. i call on you in this house: let’s celebrate the convention in words today, and by action tomorrow.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, the 21st century will be historic because of its great challenges and threats. on the one hand, the covid-19 pandemic has caused great havoc, but on the other, climate change, totalitarian regimes, conflicts, economic and social inequality, insecurity, poverty and corruption of multiple governments are all provoking huge migratory flows. migration can be understood as a challenge, but also as an opportunity, both for the receiving societies and for those who emigrate. and so has history. according to the iom, some 281 million people live in a country other than their own. according to the unhcr, there are nearly 83 million forcibly displaced persons because of conflict and human rights violations. today we mark the 70th anniversary of the geneva convention relating to the status of refugees, a treaty that sets the parameters of international protection for those who have been forced to leave their country because their lives were in danger. for them, being a refugee was not a choice, it was an imperative. i speak with propriety when i say that i have seen the bitterest face of forced migration, that of more than five million venezuelans who, like many other peoples, have been forced to take desperate paths outside their borders due to inhuman dictatorships. the member states of the union have an international responsibility towards refugees, but the european union also has a moral responsibility towards the countries of origin to bring them closer to democracy and to accompany them in that process, and also to punish those who commit crimes against their populations. crimes against our humanity.
madam president, allow me to begin by congratulating my colleague, tanja fajon, on the successful outcome of the negotiations on these reports, which are indispensable in supporting people in need of international protection. but the situation in the mediterranean, commissioner, is getting worse. the deaths this year have tripled and we still have no plan to deal with the increase in arrivals, which we know happens every year. in the meantime, the epp group in this house seems to be held hostage to the far-right discourse. gentlemen of the far right, i'm looking at you. they have just published a declaration on the future of europe, which they say is based on christian values. well, let's see what the pope has to say about christian values, shall we? some authority i say you will have in the matter. he says that migration is not a threat to christianity, that to reject an immigrant in distress, of whatever religious confession, is a grotesque falsification of christianity. i conclude with a quote from the gospel. jesus said: "i was a stranger and you welcomed me".
madam president, commissioner, rapporteur, since the summer of 2015, when europe experienced an unprecedented humanitarian and political crisis, we have witnessed a systemic lack of solidarity towards forced migrants. we have suffered the absence of a narrative that fights exclusionary discourses. in this context, strengthening integration policies is essential. in many cases it is the regional authorities who are responsible for implementing these policies and, while we welcome the increase in the budget for the amif, we regret that the regulation only provides for a minimum allocation of 20% for the fund's solidarity objective and an allocation of 5% for local and regional authorities. it is clearer than ever that europe's challenges can only be tackled from a multi-level perspective, in which all actors, including local and regional authorities and civil society, contribute to building a stronger and more united europe.
mr president, every european knows that a homosexual is more comfortable walking the streets of budapest or warsaw than those of molenbeek, gaza or tehran. but you'd rather submit to the lobby's agenda and spend all day ranting about hungary or poland. how dare they lecture hungary or poland on democracy? how dare they lecture on the rule of law and human rights to those who have fought and defeated the most brutal and well-known totalitarian movement in europe, which is communism? it is precisely you, the people behind the cordon sanitaire, who threaten to cut off european funds to anyone who does not submit to your ideological straitjacket. how can a maltese socialist sentenced to two years in prison for distributing homosexual pornography of his ex-partner speak about gay rights in hungary? with you it's always the world upside down. but they don't scare us. the wave of patriotism and common sense sweeping europe is here to stay. the founders of the union are turning in their graves to see what they are doing with their project, with the ideological dictatorship which uses the community institutions not to serve the member states, as the treaties require, but to threaten them, harass them and give them orders. they look desperate. we're sticking with common sense.
mr president, commissioner, minister, last saturday a young man from galicia, samuel, was beaten to death. that same night in my town, san cugat, another young man was beaten unconscious. both attacks were carried out to the cry of "gay!" the escalation of violence against the lgbtq community is an emergency that we must fight without palliatives. and that means fighting all those movements, organizations and governments across europe that normalize persecution and stigmatize people for their way of wanting or thinking. the law passed in the hungarian parliament is an example of the institutionalization of this reactionary drift, as is the fact that political parties in this house, such as vox, point to the workplace of the editor of the satirical magazine el jueves, thus inciting violence against him. they point to others to act. the far right always works against freedom to the cry of "go for them!" or "gay!" but we assure you, again, that they will not pass.
in writing. article 7 teu aims to ensure that all eu countries respect the common values of the union, as set out in article 2 teu, including the rule of law. the european parliament has always been very active in addressing the challenges related to the rule of law in the eu, in particular by adopting resolutions initiating the abovementioned article 7 (1) teu procedure with regard to both countries. since then, and particularly in the wake of the deterioration of the situation with regard to respect for fundamental rights and the rule of law in both countries, parliament has continued to call on the council to act under the abovementioned article 7 (1) teu procedure; it is a crucial matter to ensure respect for the values of the european union and, above all, respect for the rule of law.

in writing. hungary's new law goes against all the fundamental values of europe, including for example the protection of sexual minorities. no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation. all lgbtiq people should be able to be who they are in the eu, without fear of being marginalised or even personally attacked, anywhere in the eu. the european commission cannot only do more, it must do more. citizens must be able to count on europe to protect their rights. that's why the eu just came into being. i call on the european commission to take hungary to court and to guarantee the rights of lgbtiq people in hungary. but let's be honest at the same time. unfortunately, in practice, hungary has too often failed to apply the rule of law. it is time for the european commission to get its balls in the game. hit hungary where it undoubtedly hurts the most, in the wallet, and freeze hungary's share of the european recovery fund worth €7.2 billion.
in writing. – the overwhelming majority of the council members were outraged by the anti-lgbtiq law orbán introduced in hungary. rightfully so. orbán has crossed redlines before but that was a new low. i welcome the response by most heads of state and government but it should not stop here. the council needs to trigger article 7 against this hungarian government. all legal means should be applied in order to show orbán that he has gone too far. we are a union of values whether orbán likes it or not. he does not want to listen to reason, he therefore must face the consequences. the hungarian anti-lgbtiq law goes against everything the european union stands for. when you are a member of the eu, you sign up to our values. it is not an ‘a la carte’ menu. we need to stand up against the deteriorating situation of lgbtiq-rights in hungary. we have to take action and hold the hungarian government accountable. this is about protecting what is most precious, the freedom of our people.
in writing. the situation of sexual and gender minorities needs to be significantly improved throughout europe. changing the situation requires changes both in legislation and in attitudes. the first-ever strategy on lgbt equality published by the eu commission in november 2020 is a good step in the right direction, but the situation in hungary shows how far we still have to go to achieve tolerance and equality. in hungary, a law passed in june is effectively teaching children about discrimination and preventing organisations representing sexual and gender minorities from carrying out educational activities and communication in the country. such a restriction of minority rights and the trampling of human rights is in flagrant contradiction with the fundamental values of the european union. it is clear that the eu cannot finance activities that are contrary to its values, which include the essential values of equality, freedom of expression and the promotion of minority rights. the commission is now much more vigilant as it begins to implement the rule of law mechanism which allows eu funding to be withheld from a member state which is in breach of the union's fundamental values. the commission notes that the hungarian authorities have not provided any evidence that the aid is compatible with the internal market. we must also find ways of ensuring that human rights and fundamental values are better respected in all the member states in the conference on the future of europe, which is now under way.
in writing. the resolution, which concerns a law for the protection of minors that was democratically passed in hungary, has surreal aspects. the hungarian legislation is a matter of national competence and its main objective is the protection of minors and the possibility for parents to express an opinion on the sexual education of their children. however, brussels has once again decided to give an instrumental reading to the matter, meddling in purely national affairs and threatening to use every possible countermeasure, such as the freezing of european funds, to get hungary to turn around. this method of action, based on coercion and blackmail, is contrary to the basic democratic principles so often invoked by the institutions. i think it is a serious matter that a member state is continually subjected to controls on matters of national importance simply because it does not align itself with the prevailing opinion in brussels. the attitude of the european institutions is in complete contradiction with the principle of cooperation on which the eu was founded. in the light of what has been said so far, i consider it unacceptable that the only parliament in europe which systematically denies institutional representation to the opposition and attacks those who do not conform to the dogmas imposed by the current majority should try to dictate the line to some member states on democracy.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, thank you very much, honourable members of the european parliament and all of those who are on the speaker list. we know each other very well from our in writing. on 1 july, the european union digital covid certificate regulation came into force with the aim of helping to restore freedom of movement within the eu, a right severely restricted after the declaration of the pandemic. from that date, member states should be prepared to issue and verify the physical or electronic document certifying that persons have been vaccinated, tested or have recovered from the disease. the regulation provides, however, for a period of six weeks in which member states may prepare to issue the certificates referred to in the regulation. twenty-one of them, as well as norway, iceland and liechtenstein, had already started issuing certificates before 1 july, and five more started doing so as from that date. however, according to the european commission's data of 1 july, six member states are still not prepared for its implementation (hungary, ireland, malta, the netherlands, romania and sweden), which will require redoubling efforts in this respect.

the rapporteur. madam president, allow me to begin by addressing my words to the european medicines agency and the commission, to mrs kyriakides for her cooperation and, of course, to the alternative rapporteurs, to whom i would like to express my sincere thanks for the work they have done, for the always constructive tone and the willingness to reach agreement. we have not reached unanimity, but we have come close. our obligation to the citizens after what we have experienced in this pandemic is to achieve broad agreements to move towards a true european health policy, reinforcing fundamental structures such as the european medicines agency. while we celebrate the success of the vaccination campaign today, we must not forget the improvisation, the lack of coordination and the confusion experienced at the beginning of the pandemic. if there is one thing we cannot repeat again, it is the closure of borders, the banning of exports of medicines and medical supplies or the deafening of the call for help. i think we have corrected this with the important subsequent reaction, but we should not forget it, because it goes against the foundations of the european project and against the most basic principles of health crisis management, which normally go beyond borders. after years of so-called austerity, europe entered this crisis weakened by budget cuts and staff cuts in its health systems, and without the humility to admit that what was happening on the other side of the world would eventually strike this one with all its virulence. the truth is that we did not have a recognizable european health policy and we have seen how necessary it is to understand each other in the face of challenges of this calibre. the three health union regulations are clearly intended to be amended. a common and coordinated health crisis management system and strengthened mandates for both the ecdc and the european medicines agency. because we also need more europe in health. what does this reinforcement mean for the european medicines agency? an institutional framework defined by the medicines steering group, the health products steering group and the emergency working group, delimiting who does what at any given time. a framework for monitoring and controlling the supply chain of medicines. provide scientific advice on medicines that may have the potential to treat, prevent or diagnose the diseases causing these crises and define lists of critical medicines. coordinate follow-up studies on the efficacy and safety of vaccines. coordinate the clinical trials. and for the first time, a common definition of the shortage of medicines, so necessary and so demanded by this parliament. i have supported the commission's proposal and with the other alternative rapporteurs we have focused on reinforcing some aspects not adequately addressed in the commission's proposal, which has resulted in the agreement we are going to vote on. an agreement whose main principles are the reinforcement of the preventive nature of this regulation, providing that both the steering groups and the working group meet not only when there is an emergency but also in preparation for possible emergencies; the reinforcement of synergy between the steering groups and the working group; the introduction of the one health approach to address future challenges; greater transparency with the publication of agendas, minutes, internal operating rules and recommendations of these groups; a stronger role of healthcare professionals and patients consultation decisions; a sanction regime for marketing authorisation holders and manufacturers of healthcare products that do not comply with the obligations laid down in this regulation; public information on clinical trials and marketing authorisation decisions; and a crucial element, which i believe, of the european medicines supply database that we have introduced. if we are to deal with emergencies like the one we are facing, we need reliable, harmonized, coherent and timely information. the agency can never again receive the information it needs to process data in excel sheets. this is not acceptable. we need tools from this century, not repositories from the past. we need an interoperable and digital database at union level, but also based on data communicated through national electronic platforms, capable of monitoring the supply chain and determining the volume at any given time, as well as the actual level of demand, and providing data capable of detecting, predicting and preventing shortages of medicines. a database like cismed is already functioning in some countries with european funding. i believe it has also been funded by horizon europe. similar systems are already in place. we can and must put in place a system of this kind to tackle the problem of shortages. i hope that this parliament will not have to keep on asking us to find solutions to this problem. the european health union is not about who has the health competence or taking it away from anyone. it will strengthen europe's health response, because we know, we have seen: public health has a decisive influence on the health of the economy, of our society as well. let's not let the relief of a light at the end of the tunnel, of a possible way out of this pandemic, make us forget the lessons learned.

madam president, commissioner, i have to ask you to stop. ladies and gentlemen! the prices of building materials have been showing a continuous upward trend for some time. in the case of poland, the prices of wood, in particular osb, styrene, aluminium and drywall, have increased particularly sharply. with regard to the price of wood, we are talking about a 40 percent increase, and the price of some materials has even doubled. this situation is the result of the impact of a number of factors, such as the imbalance of supply and demand on the market and the resulting shortages of building materials, as well as higher energy transport and labour costs. this situation has a very negative impact on both the manufacturers of construction companies and developers and consumers. for the undertakings, this causes enormous difficulties in planning production, delays and loss of predictability of production and costs, as well as the need for increases and a threat to the competitiveness of the undertakings. consumers, on the other hand, have to deal with significantly longer delivery times or lack of availability of selected materials and significantly higher costs for repairs, purchase of a house or apartment. because we have to remember that the cost of building materials is over 50% of the cost of any residential property. in addition, price increases and significant delays will have a very negative impact on investments under the cohesion policy or the reconstruction fund. i therefore believe that action is needed to counter this situation, including an in-depth analysis by the european commission of the causes of such price increases and possible recommendations on this matter.

author. – madam president, it has been more than four years since the arrest and imprisonment of dr djalali, a dual swedish national, in violation of numerous human rights conventions. after having spent over 100 days in solitary confinement, his health has dramatically worsened, as well as his psychological condition, after having been subject to different forms of torture. the case of dr djalali is not an isolated one. there are at least a dozen other eu nationals who are arbitrarily detained in iran. in this resolution, we urge the iranian authorities to end the practice of arbitrarily detaining individuals as leverage over foreign countries, to stop his execution and abolish the death penalty. his case reminds us of the need to further strengthen our human rights dialogue with iran at all levels, while we increase the protection and support for human rights defenders, particularly women. we also need to use all our diplomatic channels to improve relations with iran and particularly with its civil society. the ongoing joint comprehensive plan of action (jcpoa) talks in vienna on the revival of the 2015 nuclear deal presents us with an opportunity to deepen this dialogue and build the foundations of a new multidimensional relationship based on the respect of international law and human rights. these talks should also serve to adopt a wider regional perspective that allow us to play a more strategic role in responding to security crises in the region. the jcpoa is a cornerstone for a durable mutual trust between the eu, iran and the us, but also the best instrument to ensure stability and security in the middle east. this parliament should irrevocably support a return to the nuclear deal and particularly to have a strong voice in defence of human rights in the country. and that is why i want to join my voice also today to say: ‘free djalali’.
