on behalf of the renew group. mr president, commissioner vălean, if there is one sector that has been strongly affected by the coronavirus crisis, it is, without any doubt, the aviation sector. the drop in traffic due to the coronavirus will have dramatic consequences in the coming years and, above all, threatens the economic viability of companies, the jobs generated by and linked to air transport and, of course, working conditions. that is why, mrs vălean, in march 2020, my parliamentary group, the renew group, presented you with a very concrete proposal: a specific support plan for the transport sector. an ambitious plan with a whole series of specific batteries aimed specifically at the aviation sector. and that is why we are very pleased that some of these measures have been very well received and successfully implemented by your department. but still, 15 months later, we are faced with a similar scenario. the pace of recovery in the air transport sector is totally uncertain and, above all, it requires strong support from the european union to safeguard businesses and, consequently, jobs. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the safety of the air transport sector. firstly, public/private financial support; incorporating public/private partnerships, also in this sense, to meet the challenges of the future. secondly, legal and operational security for the entire value chain of the industry, of course ending all abusive labour practices that are found, whenever that occurs. and finally, thirdly, and very importantly, fundamentally: institutional support, political commitment. we must therefore stop criminalizing a sector which is fundamental to territorial cohesion in europe and which also directly contributes to one of the three basic pillars of the european project: the free movement of people. only then can we safeguard jobs and, above all, the competitiveness of european aviation.
mr president, commissioner, aeronautics is a strategic sector of the union, with over 600 000 direct jobs. aircraft manufacturers have been affected by the cancellation of deliveries and, in the basque country alone, 600 workers have lost their jobs. 20% of the sector has disappeared as a result of the redundancies at aernnova, itp, alestis, aciturri and lauak, and this places the european commission before the need to take action in this regard. the sector's employment and its future must be strongly defended, because the dismissals linked to the pandemic are unacceptable. we are talking about an absolutely circumstantial situation. and we must protect the sector from relocations, the result of the large-scale buying and selling operations taking place in the context of the loss of value of some companies. the union cannot facilitate the creation of an opportunistic concentration in response to the pandemic. and finally, the great challenge of the aeronautics sector is also, in this case, the ecological transition. as is being done, more or less successfully, in the automobile sector, the aeronautics sector needs a public plan to link it to the objectives of the green deal and thus protect the employment of thousands of workers as a matter of priority.
mr president, commissioner, covid-19 has dealt an unprecedented blow to the aviation sector. we are all aware of this, and it is urgent to work on his recovery. in addition, we have been calling for a social agenda for aviation for years and the revision of regulation (ec) no 1008/2008, which is open and on standby since 2015, something incomprehensible. if working conditions in the sector were already precarious, with atypical forms of employment, social dumping and unfair competition, after the pandemic they are even more so. we have to act now. the commission itself acknowledged in 2019 the existence of abusive practices that circumvent national and european social legislation. and, as you said, commissioner, in the sustainable and intelligent mobility strategy, you promised a revised proposal by the end of this year. we need aviation to recover to ensure connectivity and cohesion across europe, but it must be done in a sustainable and socially responsible way. decent working conditions must be ensured for all staff. and i would ask the commission to be a real ally in this process and to act accordingly. responsibility and competitiveness do not have to be at odds.
mr president, commissioner, a couple of months ago a servant was arguing in this house that labour mobility in the european union should move towards a freer, fairer and safer model. however, the practices we have seen in the airline industry in recent years are far from being a breakthrough for all workers in the sector, and are contrary to european law: wages below the inter-branch minimum; zero-hour contracts; pay-for-flight schemes; illegal transfer of workers; workers being replaced by fake self-employed; lack of legal protection; obstacles to union and collective bargaining; and so on. this is the reality of what is happening in the european union today. a race to the bottom has been created, to the bottom of the precariousness of a sector such as aviation, which is vital for spain and, above all, for europe. the lack of adequacy of regulation (ec) no 1008/2008 gives rise to companies that base their business model on precariousness to circumvent compliance with the law. do you not think it is time we revised this regulation immediately? do you not think it is time to develop legal measures to ensure a level playing field and legal certainty for crews? the single market is not a jungle. let us take action to prevent it being used as a pretext to undermine fundamental rights and perpetuate precarious working conditions.
mr president, commissioner, we have to learn the lessons of the covid-19 crisis, and one of them is that we must prepare ourselves for future health crises in a much more effective, optimized and coordinated way. first of all, i would like to highlight the joint purchase of vaccines that has been coordinated by the european union, which has enabled all the member states to have access to vaccination and to have the vaccination rates that are being achieved today. but i want to focus on three important elements: the first of these is that i believe that the joint purchasing procedure by the member states needs to be improved. we must also improve the transparency requirements in joint procurement procedures and, finally, strengthen the monitoring role of this european parliament. from an internal market perspective, it is important that we support the creation of a minimum stock of strategic products reserves so that, in future crises such as the one we have experienced, the european union and all the member states have a minimum stock of health products, products related to medicines, ppe, vaccination, etc., so that in a future crisis the european union is much better prepared.
mr president, the two regulations we are discussing today - the ecdc and crossborder threats - are being combined with the ema regulation, for which i am the rapporteur, to make this the first step towards a european health union, a genuine european health policy. we have seen how at the beginning of the pandemic we demanded data, information, etc. from the ecdc and it was not able to give them because there was no real european coordination and it did not have the resources or the sufficient robustness. among other things, staff was lacking. we must staff it, and this regulation is moving in that direction. there is also room for european health policies in crossborder threats. the rapporteur, véronique trillet-lenoir, and sara cerdas have said that we need to make progress in european health policies. there is room for this without assuming the competence of the member states. we must move forward in creating these state health plans, coordinating them and, why not, moving towards joint positions to treat pandemics and include noncommunicable diseases. 'more europe' is about being better prepared for health. that's the way. let's keep moving along there.
madam president, commissioner, we hear talk of flexibility and optimisation, of resources, of technological development and new forms of employment, but reality is spraying the advertising engineering of the platform economy, a model built for fiscal dumping and social dumping, that is, on the basis of the denial of labour rights and tax evasion. the first thing to do is to recognize the presumption of the employability of our workers in line with european jurisprudence: that at this stage of the struggle our struggle is not to extend our rights but to recognize ourselves as workers is already telling us something. the enormous profits of these companies are due to the precariousness and the temporary nature of their contracts, that is to say, to the exploitation of their workers. secondly, the management of algorithms has to be transparent, because these algorithms today monitor, discriminate and violate individual and collective rights, but no one is held accountable for them. and thirdly, with the platform economy, our tax and contribution revenues are being reduced. either that is corrected or there will be no financial balance or social protection for anyone.
madam president, commissioner, digitalisation and the application of artificial intelligence in the workplace are creating new models that involve clear precariousness, hyperconnection, control and surveillance or algorithmic decisions without human supervision. the implications for the mental health and emotional well-being of workers are already clear, and we need new legislation now: a directive to prevent psychosocial risks in the workplace and a directive to regulate the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace. to do this, the commission must listen and meet with all the parties, companies and trade unions, because workers do not need psychologists, but decent working conditions, safe and quality work. the digitisation of the workplace cannot be a purely technological process; it must be a socio-technical process, where technology and humanism go hand in hand.
madam president, commissioner, at the beginning of september we saw a shocking picture: while hurricane ida was causing severe flooding and dozens of deaths in the united states, a door-to-door food delivery worker was still working, pedaling with difficulty with water up to his waist. it's a shocking, but also outrageous image, and it helps us to confront new emerging inequalities, such as that of workers without rights. while it is true that new types of employment and platform work can help or have the potential to help reconcile work and family life, that does not change the fact that many are precarious jobs and below labour standards, and this is not tolerable. europe must be characterised by respect for workers' rights and fundamental freedoms, including in the digital field. and so, from parliament, we call for human control behind the algorithms, for companies to have an obligation to report on the algorithms used and to ensure transparency in relation to the personal data used. we therefore take a clear stand against surveillance capitalism in the workplace as well.
mr president, every new ipcc report is telling: climate change is alarming. behind the climate act we have an ambitious legislative package on the road to 2030. i thank the commission and vice-president timmermans for presenting it. but let's focus on the basics: 75 percent of emissions are related to the energy sector, which is largely fossil and imported. we need to move forward on renewables in a sustainable way and with a respectful deployment, and be efficient. the best energy spent is the energy we don't consume. but let's not forget that there will be costs and that this effort needs to be transformed into a cleaner, more autonomous economy. what we cannot allow is for those costs to increase the gap of inequality. the alarming evolution of wholesale prices is a reminder that calls us to concentrate efforts to engage citizens, accompany them so as not to give way to populism and decarbonise our economy. now, we who are here must legislate. i call for a focus on people and the health of the planet. it's a great challenge.
in writing. the european commission's target 55 package is essential for the eu to achieve its target of reducing net eu emissions by at least 55% by 2030 compared to 1990 and becoming the first climate neutral continent by 2050, binding targets following the adoption of the european climate law. spanish socialists support the need for a green transition, but it is essential that it be fair, leaving no one behind. the process of decarbonising europe must take account of the social impact it may have on the most vulnerable people, which is why we call for the establishment of adequate compensation mechanisms. the socialist group also believes that the border adjustment mechanism must play a key role in the green transition, with rapid implementation. on the other hand, we spanish socialists stress the need to make progress in the deployment of renewable energies in a sustainable and efficient way.

in writing. the scientific community is alert that extreme weather events linked to climate change will become more frequent and more severe, affecting all regions of the planet and becoming increasingly difficult to predict. the hundreds of deaths from floods and fires in advanced countries demonstrate how ill-prepared society is to deal with global warming, the resulting natural disasters, and the numerous personal and material damages they bring. the european union must step up its mechanisms to repair damage and losses in affected regions, while developing more effective climate change adaptation strategies. in this regard, in addition to opening the door to potential new instruments, the european solidarity fund and the civil protection mechanism should be strengthened. this summer's disasters highlight the need for a specialised disaster preparedness and response body in europe, working on prediction, prevention, preparedness and planning, as well as on the quickest and most effective response to natural disasters, with sufficient technical, human and economic resources.

rapporteur. – madam president, let me first thank my colleagues for their good cooperation on the report. we stand here as a united parliament. united in our belief that we must put our naivety aside when dealing with china. a united parliament that is very clear in its rejection of the investment agreement, as long as our colleagues are sanctioned and human rights violations are ongoing in china. in our report, we recognise that the rise of china will have an enormous impact on our way of life and europe’s role in the world. we also warn that europe is not prepared for this change because, until now, we have defined our relationship with china in terms of trade. don’t get me wrong, china is indeed a very interesting trading partner, and it’s great for european business that many chinese are now able to afford german cars, french wines and italian fashion. but economic gains should not make us blind to the challenges that the chinese communist party is posing to the liberal world order. the eu must be determined to defend our key values, and this requires a new and more assertive strategy. first, we must realise that china is too big to ignore. we cannot deal with climate change, terrorism and global security without working together with china. if you want to save our planet, china must be our partner in this field. that is why i fully disagree with those who plead for a complete decoupling between the west and china. but let’s not be naive. china’s cherry-picking of the rules of the united nations and the world trade organization must end. and china has to show that it means business on climate change; otherwise, the eu must introduce a border tax to offset the higher carbon emissions of chinese products. second, the eu must step up its defence of human rights and the rule of law. the communist regime tries to wipe out uyghur heritage from chinese soil. hong kong has been subject to one of the most brutal crackdowns we have seen in recent history. this repression is not limited to china. chinese ‘belt and road’ money is pouring into africa, the western balkans and latin america. it is financing regimes and companies that trample on human rights. reports of labour exploitation, land-grabbing, pollution and health issues are frequent. i call on our leaders to finally come up with a credible european alternative to the belt and road initiative. we must support sustainable investments which do not exploit workers, which respect the environment and enhance good governance. and let us increase the pressure on china to stop its crackdown on hong kong. and, as i have already said a lot of times, and i will repeat it again, we need to stop importing cotton from the xinjiang area because products from slave labour have no place in the european union. third, the eu will clearly never be a match for china or the other world powers unless we get our act together. the disaster in afghanistan has shown that we need a european army, a real foreign policy without national vetoes. it is also very clear to me that we need a european fbi and cia to counter foreign threats. china’s rise has only just begun. some say europe’s decline started a long time ago. let’s prove them wrong and step up our ambitions. let’s show that the time for naivety is over. let’s make europe fit for the future with a new strategy to deal with the rising dragon, combined with a strategy to make a fist on the world stage.
member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, today’s debate is a timely opportunity to discuss our common approach to china. as reflected in your report, a lot has changed in the past months when it comes to this important relationship and not necessarily for the better. relations have become increasingly challenging. until the end of 2020 we saw positive steps in developing eu-china relations, rebalancing our economic relations and developing our international toolbox to address challenges brought along by china. this increased leverage and credibility allowed us to conclude the negotiations of the comprehensive agreement on investment in december, but also to agree on human rights sanctions over chinese individuals under the eu global human rights sanctions regime. since then, the situation has changed. the chinese decision to impose counter measures, including on members of this parliament simply for having expressed their opinions, has led to a worsening of relations. china will remain an increasingly assertive global power that does not shy away from applying economic pressure on countries and actors whose policies it disagrees with. our values gap is growing, so is the need for eu solidarity and for signalling that certain actions are unacceptable. this plenary debate and the report on a new eu-china strategy testify to this. i believe that our overall approach towards eu china relations, our multifaceted approach that treats china as a partner, competitor and rival, remains valid. we need to engage with china as a key economic partner and political player without whom we cannot address global challenges effectively. at the same time, the eu must continue to speak its mind, stand its ground and push back in areas where fundamental disagreement with china exists, first and foremost on human rights. our current framework to handle relations with china fits closely with the recommendations of this report. our overall approach encompasses key foreign policy aims that are not actor-specific, such as strategic autonomy. we aim at international cooperation which preserves our values and a rule-based multilateral system. we foster partnerships with the like-minded, as you will see in the indo-pacific strategy. all of this, taken together, reflects the recommendations put forward in the report. i thank ms vautmans and the shadow rapporteurs for the recommendations and the general support for our policies in this report. our unity remains our strength. i am looking forward to continuing our exchange.

madam president, commissioner, cyber surveillance tools are fundamental to the work of the state security forces and bodies. as a career judge and magistrate and as a minister, i have been able to witness firsthand how the fight against terrorism, against organized crime, against drug trafficking and many other threats to our security depends on these cyber surveillance tools. but we must be aware of its enormous power and its risks. a software like pegasus has come to be categorized as a weapon by the israeli government itself, and like any weapon, pegasus can be used for good or evil. the problem is not the weapon itself, but who wields it and for what. unfortunately, if the recent revelations are confirmed, it would show that this software has ended up in the wrong hands and has been used for spurious purposes. it is unacceptable that governments use these tools to spy on journalists instead of terrorists, and to pursue political opponents instead of drug traffickers. however, since it is impossible to control the use of this software, once it is acquired, democratic countries must establish stricter controls for its sale. the european union, together with countries such as israel, must ensure that only those countries with sufficient democratic credentials and respect for the rule of law, such as spain, have access to this technology.
madam president, commissioner, several countries around the world have used the pegasus spy programme to illegitimately monitor journalists, political dissidents and activists. in this europe which stands for values such as democracy, the rule of law and respect for fundamental rights, we find that its member states are using this technology. the spanish state uses pegasus to investigate political rivals, including the president of the parliament of catalonia, mr torrent, or a former colleague of yours, ernest maragall. we demand that in countries where any cases of illegal surveillance have occurred, independent investigations be carried out and accountability demanded. finally, the use of surveillance technology must be suspended until the european union has a regulatory framework in place to ensure full respect for fundamental rights.

on behalf of the left group. mr president, gender-based violence is insufficiently and unequally recognised and prosecuted in the european union. many countries have not ratified the istanbul convention or are threatening to withdraw; most do not differentiate between domestic violence and gender-based violence, or do not even consider domestic violence a crime; and the few that do consider gender-based violence do not define it in the same way. spain is currently the most advanced country in this respect, but if we look around us, the legislative disparity is such that: we lack sufficient and comparable data; we do not have the legal tools to protect, support and compensate victims adequately; we do not have sufficient resources, funding or professionals; and, as there is no cooperation between states, the aggressors can camp at large in one country of the union, while justice pursues them in another. it is incomprehensible that crimes against women are considered less serious than crimes such as corruption or computer crime, which are prosecuted in a more homogeneous, coordinated and resource-rich manner. for all these reasons, gender-based violence must be a 'european crime', because of its extreme gravity, its cross-border dimension and because it can only be stopped if we have common criteria. we know that the road is long and that some parties, governments and denialist lobbies will try to avoid it at all costs, but this thursday's vote is the first step towards achieving it.

the next item is the debate on the request for an oral answer to the commission on transparency in the eu as regards the development, purchase and distribution of covid-19 vaccines by dolors montserrat on behalf of the committee on petitions (o-000046/2021 b9-0033/21) [2021/2678 (rsp) ].
author. mr president, as chair of the committee on petitions, i would like to put the committee's oral question on the full transparency of the european union's covid vaccine strategy. from the outset, parliament has closely followed the process of vaccine research and development. he has repeatedly stressed the need for citizens to have confidence in vaccines and the importance of fighting misinformation. meanwhile, the committee on petitions has received several petitions on the strategy, one of them pointing to the lack of transparency in the agreements on covid19 vaccines that the european commission signed with pharmaceutical companies. lack of transparency has fueled uncertainty and misinformation about covid-19 vaccines. the public has a right to know the details of contracts and the results of clinical research. transparency in vaccine development, procurement and distribution is necessary to address the covid pandemic and is a prerequisite to stimulate and maintain public confidence in vaccines, end vaccine nationalism and ensure the legitimacy of the european union's joint health procurement. the commission and the member states have legally restricted the publication of details of vaccine contracts with pharmaceutical companies. this has happened despite the fact that the european union and the member states have publicly funded much of the research into vaccination, covering the initial costs of vaccine manufacturers, and granted emergency authorisations. in this context, public health must be given greater priority. in addition, parliament can hardly exercise its budgetary control duty without full access to vaccine purchase contracts. in this context, the committee on petitions asks the european commission the following questions: when will the commission publish all details of the vaccine contracts, in particular as regards the sharing of costs between the public and private investors of the vaccines, the number of doses allocated to each country and what have been the deliveries per quarter and also to future quarters, the prices per dose of vaccines, the number and location of available production facilities, agreements on intellectual property rights, technology transfer and liability and compensation schemes for any damage that may be caused by vaccines? what will the commission do to ensure that the results of clinical trials and protocols of potential vaccines against covid19 are published in a timely and clear manner in order to reduce vaccine doubts and counter misinformation? will the commission carry out and publish an evaluation of the european union covid-19 vaccine strategy, reviewing all elements in detail and making recommendations on the framework for future eu joint procurement, especially in relation to transparency?
in the name of the s&d group, i would like to say that europe is beginning to put the hardest months of this pandemic behind it, and this is happening, without any doubt, thanks to the spread of vaccination and the responsibility shown by the vast majority of european citizens, who have invested all their hopes in a vaccination process that is making history and has succeeded in immunising more than 70% of the population of the european union, as the commissioner said. i think it is important to start by praising this excellent level of immunization and congratulating the health and, in line with this, we are debating today the mistakes made - whether intentional or not - such as the lack of transparency and opacity in access to information on the process of vaccine large investments of public money advanced by the european union to companies that have barely taken risks. europeans therefore have a right to know how their money has been spent. how is it that at also ridden on previous crises, by offering policy solutions that leave no one behind, no matter where they live. it is our historic duty to improve the welfare of all citizens. we must continue to work on the new road map, in which social rights and equity prevail, if we are to build a europe with a future. and we can only do that by insisting on the need to design our economic policies with social conditionality in mind. this was necessary before covid-19 and it is even more so now, because we are talking about people and we know that economic policies have a differential impact on social groups and, also, on people, because we do not all have the same preferences, interests or desires, not all people have the same access to resources or decision-making space, nor have we been socialized or prepared in the same way or to have the same role in society, as we very well know women. when we go out into the streets, we see that there are still families who do not make ends meet, fathers and mothers who cannot give their sons and daughters the education they would like. the consequences of the pandemic have in some cases opened up and in other cases widened deep gaps that already existed within the union. we are risking our future, our well-being and the consolidation of the european project. if inequality continues to increase, it will make us weaker, and if we don't stand up for the well-being of our society, or a gender-sensitive economy, or opportunities for the most vulnerable, we will be burdening the opportunities of everyone. it is urgent that our economy includes macroeconomic indicators which, from their design, incorporate or mitigate the unequal consequences of economic policy between different social groups, individuals, economic sectors or territories, reflect the reality of our society and take into account all citizens. it is the people who are building europe and we, their representatives, must live up to that. i will highlight a dozen key points in this report. first, the european semester must be aligned with the objectives and strategies of the sustainable development goals, the european pillar of social rights and the green deal, and support member states' recovery plans. secondly, the semester should be based on an approach that integrates economic, social and environmental policies and promotes structural change so that social progress, sustainable development and well-being take into account the root causes of long-term economic and social imbalances. only then can we ensure that europe continues to enjoy the most advanced welfare systems in the world and also becomes the first climate-neutral continent. third, we must therefore work with indicators that cover the social risks that arise from the effects of the pandemic and from previous imbalances in the economy, employment, health, as well as the transformations that green and digital transitions can bring about. fourthly, our current social indicators do not provide clear targets for measuring the impact of european union action and we call on the member states to set ambitious national targets. fifthly, along these lines, we believe that sustainable welfare should be integrated into the annual strategy for sustainable growth and into the country-specific recommendations. the national reforms must therefore be clearly oriented towards solidarity, integration and social justice, with the aim of creating quality employment, fixing it to the territory and moving towards a new social organization of care so that it does not fall unrecognisedly on women. sixthly, inequalities, as well as the labour, social and health situation in the member states concerned, must be taken into account before the decision to deactivate the general safeguard clause is taken. seventhly, we must work to establish a european fiscal capacity that provides stability to the economies of the euro area. well-designed tax systems are essential to ensure a high level of protection for workers against risks throughout their lives, and also for their pensions. eighthly, we must protect individuals and also small and mediumsized enterprises so that they do not become over-indebted and because we know that they need support in the case of non-performing loans. ninthly, we must tackle the need for coherence between the objectives of sustainable welfare and monetary policy. we need to better integrate social objectives, social progress, welfare and sustainability into all european union policies, especially in budget planning to make public investment in social and environmental objectives efficient. and tenth, and last, the architecture of the new governance of the european union must be based on solidarity, social justice and integration, with equitable distribution of wealth, gender equality, high quality public services - including a high quality and universal public education system - decent employment and sustainable growth. that is why we consider investment in sustainable welfare to be vital. the landscape has changed and with the digital and ecological transitions looming it will change even more. we need new recipes because we know the old ones didn't work.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, from tomorrow, leaders will meet in brussels for the october european council, where they will discuss the key issues facing the eu and its citizens today and in the future. the meeting will, of course, start with the usual exchange with the european parliament. leaders will discuss the current state of play on covid—19. the vaccination rollout in the eu has been largely successful, but more needs to be done, especially regarding vaccination hesitancy and disinformation. further coordination is also needed with regard to free movement and travel to the eu. given the global nature of the pandemic and the emergence of new variants, international solidarity remains important. the rapid removal of obstacles hampering the global rollout of vaccines is crucial to allow member states to speed up delivery of vaccines to countries most in need. covid—19 has taught us that we need to be better prepared for the pandemics of the future. in this context, leaders are expected to call for the conclusion of the negotiation on the health union legislative package. member states continue to support the strong and central role of the who in global health governance, as well as the creation of an international treaty on pandemics. the hike in energy prices is, without a doubt, one of the most pressing issues for our citizens and industry today. following their informal dinner in brdo in slovenia, leaders will discuss recent developments in energy prices and possible measures at eu and national level, taking into account the recent commission communication. the commission has identified various measures that are at their disposal at national level to mitigate the effect of soaring energy prices. in addition to that, we also expect the leaders to take a closer look at what could be of help at european level, both in the short term and in the medium and long term, to reduce our dependency on fossil fuel. at a more strategic level, leaders are expected to have an open discussion on trade. when it comes to the eu’s global influence, trade remains the most effective instrument in our toolbox. leaders will discuss how to make the best use of this instrument in light of recent experiences. leaders will also assess the implementation of the june european council conclusions on the external dimension of migration. eight action plans for countries of origin and transit have been presented. now these plans need to be made operational and implemented without delay. leaders are expected to call on the commission to present proposals for financing action on all migratory routes and to report regularly to the council in this regard. europe’s digital transformation is also on the agenda, as it is an important driver of economic growth, job creation and competitiveness. leaders will take stock of progress on the digital agenda, including cybersecurity and connectivity, and give a political push to work on existing and future proposals and initiatives. inclusive and sustainable digital policies and digital connectivity remain important. with regard to external relations, leaders will discuss the preparation for the upcoming asia-europe meeting (asem) summit in november and the eastern partnership summit in december. the prime objective of the eastern partnership summit is to demonstrate the importance of the relationship with eastern partners. a united eu position is essential if we want to engage these partners successfully. the leitmotif of resilience, recovery and reform should guide the way. in view of the upcoming cop26 summit, leaders are expected to call for an ambitious global response to climate change, urging major economies that have not yet done so to set ambitious, nationally-determined contributions in time for cop26, to present a long—term strategy for reaching net zero emissions by 2050, and to meet their commitments on climate finance. we will come back to cop26 in our next debate. leaders will also call for an ambitious post-2020 global biodiversity framework ahead of next year’s cop15 meeting on biodiversity in kunming. i very much look forward to hearing your opinions on these important matters.

exporting vaccine doses throughout all the difficult months we have just overcome. so we really managed to keep our promise to export every second dose that is produced in europe, and to date we’ve exported to 150 countries around the world. of course, we will also be discussing different topics, like cyber or digital. the polish debate we had yesterday, so i will not focus on that. today, i want to focus on the topic of electricity prices, which is very important for us. let me begin with three simple facts. the first fact is that gas prices are, and have always been, cyclical, and they are set by global markets. so it’s not a regional or local phenomenon; it’s a global phenomenon. but, of course, we see that because of the price rise in gas, it is now difficult for many families to make ends meet and we see businesses, for example, at risk of closing. the second fact is that renewables are on a winning path. if you look at solar energy today, it’s 10 times cheaper than it was 10 years ago. if you look at wind power – which, by definition, is more volatile – it is 50% cheaper today than it was a decade ago. the third topic is the question of imports. here, if we look at gas, we see that 90% of the gas we use is imported, while 97% of oil is imported. renewables are home-grown. so these three facts show us that the transition to clean energy is not only vital for our planet, but is also crucial for our economy and for resilience to energy price shocks. what are the causes of the current spikes? first of all, the global economy is recovering from the pandemic and, with that, energy demand is rising. second, we had an unusually long and cold winter, which meant lots of heating, followed by an unusually hot summer, meaning lots of cooling and use of energy, and this affected the entire northern hemisphere. third, the whole world is affected, so this means that irrespective of a country’s energy or climate policies or energy mix, they are affected by the rise in energy and electricity prices. in fact, we see that the prices in asia are even higher than they are here in europe. yet there is something specific to the european situation. if we look at gas and our suppliers, while gazprom has honoured its long-term contracts with us, it did not respond to higher demand as it did in previous years. so europe is today too reliant on gas, too dependent on gas imports. as i said, we import 90% of the gas we use, and this makes us vulnerable. the answer is to diversify suppliers, but also to keep the role of natural gas as a transitional fuel – and we have to debate this in depth – and, crucially, to speed up the transition to clean energy. so the european green deal is, in the mid to long term, a crucial pillar of european energy sovereignty in the 21st century. i was speaking about the mid to long term, but citizens rightly expect us to act now. they want quick responses. therefore, let me turn to the measures we are deploying to address the situation in the short term. our priority is to give relief to vulnerable families and businesses. some measures can be taken very swiftly under the current eu rules. this includes relief for businesses and families – and when i say ‘businesses’, of course i’m talking about smes – through state aid, targeted support to consumers, and cuts to levies and taxes. because, let us remind ourselves that if we look at the price itself, on average one third of the wholesale energy price is set by the market, one third depends on infrastructure and one third, on average, depends on taxes and levies. there are some member states where 50% of the electricity price is taxes and levies. so this is where member states can act very quickly, and 20 of our member states are already doing that. à moyen et long terme, la commission agira dans cinq domaines cruciaux. premièrement, nous devons mettre fin à la spéculation sur les marchés de l’énergie. c’est pourquoi nous renforçons notre surveillance des marchés du gaz et du carbone et nous avons demandé à l’autorité européenne des marchés financiers d’examiner les comportements en matière de négociation de quotas d’émission. deuxièmement, nous évaluerons le fonctionnement du marché de l’électricité. l’organisation de notre marché de l’électricité a donné de bons résultats. toutefois, à l’heure actuelle, les prix du gaz tirent les prix de l’électricité à la hausse. nous avons donc demandé à l’agence de l’union européenne pour la coopération des régulateurs de l’énergie (acer) de réaliser une première évaluation du système à la lumière de l’expérience actuelle d’ici mi-novembre. elle formulera ensuite des recommandations sur la manière de mieux lutter contre l’extrême volatilité des prix. troisièmement, nous établissons activement des contacts avec les fournisseurs étrangers de gaz. equinor norvège, par exemple, a déjà annoncé une augmentation de ses livraisons. et début 2022, nous présenterons une stratégie de dialogue international sur l’énergie, également pour aider les états membres dans leurs contacts internationaux. viertens werden wir uns mit der frage der gasspeicherung befassen. es gibt derzeit keinen europäischen rahmen für strategische gasreserven, wie wir ihn beim öl zum beispiel haben. wir könnten uns besser vorbereiten, etwa durch regelmäßige stresstests unserer speicher- und reaktionskapazitäten, und wir werden neben der strategischen gasreserve auch erkunden, welches potenzial zum beispiel die gemeinsame beschaffung von gas am globalen markt hat – gegebenenfalls auf freiwilliger basis der mitgliedstaaten. wir könnten da nämlich einen großen vorteil am markt nutzen – die skalierungseffekte –, wenn wir unsere kräfte auf europäischer ebene bündeln. auch hier kann ein gemeinsamer europäischer ansatz eine positive, starke hebelwirkung entfalten. schließlich zeigt diese krise, dass wir bei den investitionen in erneuerbare energien mehr tempo brauchen. jedes kilowatt strom aus erneuerbaren energiequellen ist nicht nur eine versicherung gegen steigende energiepreise; es trägt eben auch dazu bei, unsere abhängigkeit von importen zu verringern, und es macht unsere gesellschaft und unsere wirtschaft krisenfester. wir müssen daher mehr tun bei den investitionen in erneuerbare energien und in ein energiesystem mit angemessenen lagerungskapazitäten, ein energiesystem mit grenzüberschreitenden netzverbünden, gesicherter grundlast und flexibler stromerzeugung. und genau das – nämlich diese investitionen – das tun wir jetzt zum beispiel mit nextgenerationeu, unserem aufbauprogramm. in den bisher vorgelegten nationalen plänen – und das sind 22 mitgliedstaaten, in denen die pläne jetzt bestätigt sind – sind 36 milliarden euro gezielt für saubere energie vorgesehen. das beginnt bei grünem wasserstoff bis hin zur offshore-windenergie. schließlich und endlich – und dieser punkt ist mir wichtig, auch wenn er sich vielleicht banal anhört: was auf dem weg in eine energiezukunft – wenn ich es so nennen darf – entscheidend ist, ist echte europäische teamarbeit. denn eine wesentliche hürde sind hierbei die genehmigungen. das hört sich sehr banal an, ist aber ein riesenthema. es dauert im durchschnitt sechs bis sieben jahre, bis eine windkraftanlage genehmigt ist. damit ist sie noch lange nicht installiert, geschweige denn up and running. das muss sich ändern. hier will ich ganz klar sagen: hier sind wir alle mit im boot, das heißt, die lokale ebene, die nationale ebene und die europäische ebene. da ist keiner, der sagen kann: bei mir ist alles in ordnung. wir alle müssen da besser werden. die kommission wird im nächsten jahr deshalb im rahmen der erneuerbare-energien-richtlinie leitlinien zu dem thema genehmigungen in writing. the 26th united nations climate conference (cop26), taking place in glasgow from 1 to 13 november this year, cannot be another summit marked by grand proclamations, big headlines in the press and focused only on setting ambitious goals, which, while important, are also clearly insufficient for effective and sustainable decarbonisation to happen. a more fine-tuned analysis is needed that leads to actions that ensure a just transition, where the poorest and most disadvantaged do not bear the costs of change, engaging individuals, families and communities in a challenge that structurally improves their lives, not only in terms of air quality and protection from natural disasters, but also in reducing economic and social inequalities and preserving biodiversity. the increase in energy prices that has marked the global post-pandemic economic recovery demonstrates that urgent action is needed, including better regulation of markets and measures to discourage the use of fossil fuels and to encourage clean energy production and energy efficient practices, including investment in better interconnections and storage.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, the eu is built on diversity and tolerance. however, extremisms are still present in different forms. the covid-19 pandemic has put our societies under additional pressure and exacerbated risks for extremist behaviour. there is evidence from different sources such as the eu agency for fundamental rights and the council of europe, or the european union serious and organised crime threat assessment (‘eu socta 2021’) by europol, that confirms an alarming increase in intolerance, hatred and extremism in europe. i would like to emphasise that our union was conceived and developed as a project of solidarity, cooperation and tolerance. these values are quintessential to our project and need to be defended in a decisive manner. last december, the european council underlined the importance of combating incitement to hatred and violence, as well as intolerance. at that meeting, the european council stated that it was essential to prevent radicalisation and address the ideologies behind terrorism and violent extremism, including online. it is particularly important to respond to the risk of extremism in a timely manner. we need to react to it at an earlier stage of its emergence. early identification of radicalisation that can lead to violent extremism and even terrorism, and the identification of drivers of radicalisation are of crucial importance. prevention of fertile grounds for radicalisation is also important. extremism and racism are spread, notably over the internet, through disinformation campaigns, conspiracy theories, terrorist content, illegal hate speech, challenging the functioning of our democracy and other possible occasions. as you know, the commission has adopted a number of important initiatives to respond to those challenges, the most recent being the first eu strategy on combating anti-semitism and fostering jewish life. the presidency attaches great importance to combating illegal content online. we aim to reach a general approach on the digital services act by the end of november. on 28 october 2021, the slovenian presidency is organising jointly with the commission a virtual conference to discuss how to effectively combat hate crime and hate speech, with a particular focus on combating hate speech online and on the protection of victims of hate crime. there is no better way to fight extremism and racism than education and open public debate. we have a lot of experience and best practice to share among ourselves to improve democratic resilience, media literacy, critical thinking and conflict resolution skills. i would like to conclude by stressing how important it is to prevent our societies from becoming dominated by hatred. we are therefore obliged to take all incidents of that kind seriously and never ignore them. we shall be respectful to each other.
member of the commission. – madam president, the terrorist attacks in christchurch, hull and hanau are strong and very worrying signals of how violent right-wing extremism is posing an increasing threat globally. recently, violent right-wing extremist groups have also used covid-related conspiracy theories and disinformation to incite violence. in rome, on 9 october, a neo-fascist group used a demonstration against covid-related measures to unleash chaos on the city and attack the headquarters of a trade union confederation. these facts also show that hatred, violence and intolerance are not only hiding in the dark corners of the web or in the inner circles of clandestine organisations. they have become more and more mainstream and risk erupting into public violence and undermining the stability of our democracies. article 2 of the treaty of the european union refers to a union founded on respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights, including the rights of persons belonging to minorities, of course. i firmly believe that if we are to uphold our fundamental eu values and to apply the fundamental rights enshrined in the charter, we need a prompt and comprehensive response to the rise of violent extremism, as well as racism and xenophobia. no compromise is possible. this commission decided to tackle these issues openly and on all fronts. from a legislative perspective, the regulation addressing the dissemination of terrorist content online will oblige internet service providers to remove all forms of terrorist content within one hour of receiving a removal order by an eu member state, while making sure fundamental rights are respected. at the same time, under the eu internet forum, guidance to internet platforms on proscribed violent, right-wing extremist groups, symbols and manifestos, is under preparation to support them in their content moderation efforts. the commission is also working with member states to agree on a common, non-legally binding, working definition of violent right-wing extremism, to facilitate their identification and information-sharing about the phenomenon. in september 2020, we adopted an eu anti-racism action plan establishing the main policy actions for the next five years. racism needs to be addressed at all levels of governance and through different measures. that is why the eu anti-racism action plan includes not only legislative measures, but also measures addressing social attitudes, stereotypes and economic concerns. the action plan also refers to ongoing commission initiatives to address extremist propaganda and to support the safety and security of public spaces, like places of worship or other establishments that could be targeted by extremists. the commission has appointed a new coordinator on anti-racism because we would like to have a more direct dialogue with communities and civil society. in addition, two weeks ago, the commission adopted the first-ever eu strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering jewish life. antisemitism is incompatible with eu values. yet, nine out of ten jews in europe consider that antisemitism has increased in their country. with this strategy, the commission is determined to significantly step up the fight against antisemitism. it is europe’s long-term commitment to a safe, inclusive future for our jewish communities and jewish life in all its diversity in the eu. at the same time, we see increasing evidence of anti-muslim hatred throughout the eu. attacks, such as the one in hanau, were also fuelled by anti-migrant and anti-muslim sentiments. the european commission will continue to work with the european muslim community in a long-term commitment to a safe, inclusive future for our muslim communities and muslim life in all its diversity in the eu. furthermore, we often observe a continuum between the spread of hate speech or hateful conspiracies circulating online and episodes of violence or hate crime inspired by right-wing extremist ideologies. racist and xenophobic hate speech is illegal under eu law. the commission is seeing to the proper transposition and implementation of this legislation through dialogue with member states and, where needed, infringement procedures. in the last 12 months, the commission has launched 10 infringement proceedings against member states. with a view to enhancing the criminal law response to hate crime and hate speech, the commission is working on an initiative which aims to extend the current list of eu crimes in the treaties to include hate speech and hate crime. to respond to the online dimension of illegal hate speech, the commission has also developed a voluntary code of conduct with major social media platforms. the code has achieved fast progress on removing online hate speech. we have seen removal rates go up from 28% in our first monitoring in 2016 to a removal rate of up to 71% in 2020. the most recent evaluation, published on 7 october, shows a slight decrease in the average removal rate, while a large majority of the notices were reviewed within the 24-hours prescribed by the code. the proposal for a digital services act tackles all forms of illegal online content across member states. all these initiatives have contributed to progress. we constantly speak to member state authorities, civil society organisations, as well as it companies to address right-wing violent extremism and its manifestation of intolerance and racism. there is no single solution or a single actor that can win in isolation. we have to work together and join forces to protect our democracies and protect our common values.

in writing. the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing is vital for financial stability and security in europe. legislative gaps in one member state have an impact on the eu as a whole. for this reason, eu rules must be implemented and supervised in an efficient and consistent way to fight crime and protect our financial system. the recent pandora scandal has also revealed the extent to which the international financial ecosystem, and particularly the european one, is generating tax evasion and contributing to money laundering, which makes the adoption by the commission of the legislative package against money laundering, which meets one of the demands we have long been advocating in the s&d group, all the more important. in view of developments in capital markets and technological innovation, and in the run-up to the start of the negotiations on the anti-money laundering (aml) legislative package, this debate has been very timely. ensuring the efficiency and consistency of the eu aml framework is of paramount importance.

in writing. let us not be so used to such scandals that we overlook the seriousness of the facts. the nearly 12 million documents publicly exposed in the pandora papers show that those who should be the gatekeepers against money laundering and tax evasion are, in many cases, the ones who make headlines. we, the public representatives of the european union, must act and condemn this in force, both in brussels and in the capitals of the 27 member states. when exploring measures, one of the priorities should be the creation of a european agency, with a solid foundation and sufficient human resources, to monitor such practices. beyond the resolution adopted by this parliament, there is a blacklist of tax havens which is updated regularly. despite repeated requests from this house, the eu's ministers for economic affairs and finance decided to exclude several countries from the list for diplomatic reasons. in this way they sent a signal which, in my view, is totally wrong. it is now time for the eu to set out requirements and criteria that will put an end to tax evasion.
madam president, commissioner, the humanitarian situation in haiti is devastating, as have been the successive natural disasters that have hit the country in recent years. disasters and the fragility of institutions have induced an endemic cycle of poverty and social chaos. it is essential to link humanitarian aid to building the resilience of haitian society, including by supporting the state's capacity to provide basic services to the population. the humanitarian situation in haiti has been discussed in this parliament on several occasions. we have always called for, and it makes sense to call again today, a strong mobilization of the international community. we have always advocated the involvement of the european union in a broader sense. however, without political stability and more institutional capacity, the country's sustainable development cannot be built on. emergency humanitarian aid will be more effective if it is combined with a stability and development dimension to which the haitian authorities must also be committed.
member of the commission. – madam president, the eu stands in solidarity with the people of haiti. the situation there is very dire and the country bears a resemblance to the most fragile countries in africa. haiti is the largest beneficiary of the european union’s humanitarian aid in latin america and the caribbean, with eur 434 000 000 provided since 1994. a very significant part of this funding has been mobilised in response to the different disasters hitting the country during this period. the intention behind the visit of commissioner lenarčič was to put the spotlight on this protracted crisis affected by donor fatigue and resulting in underfunding. at the moment, only 17% of the 2021 un humanitarian appeal is funded. eu humanitarian aid for haiti will continue. this year it amounted to eur 17 000 000, including eur 3 000 000 allocated in the aftermath of the disaster. our commitment will continue next year. the eu’s co-funded post-disaster needs assessment is ongoing, with results expected in early november. a reconstruction conference is expected at the end of the year. once again, i would like to thank you for this debate.

rapporteur. – mr president, dear colleagues, i address the chamber today as rapporteur for the legislative package on europol to ask you to confirm the decision adopted by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe) to enter into interinstitutional negotiations on the two draft legislative acts, namely the revision of the europol regulation and the consequential amendment of the regulation on the schengen information system. the reform of europol’s mandate is a long-standing request by this parliament, and i was mainly motivated by the need to equip the agency with new tools and capabilities to face the digital transformation. criminals have adapted their modus operandi to the new digital reality, and consequently it is necessary to enable europol to better support member states in the fight against these evolving security threats. the two legislative reports, which were adopted by a large majority of 75% of the votes cast in libe last week, build on the main elements of the legislative proposals of the european commission, while introducing additional safeguards to ensure the fundamental rights, in particular, the right to the protection of personal data, are respected. the report, furthermore, includes provisions to enhance parliamentary oversight and the accountability of europol, marking a substantial progress and striking the right balance between new capabilities and closer democratic scrutiny and oversight. consequently, i kindly request for your support for both decisions, which gather a broad support in the libe committee, so allowing us to enter into negotiations so we can start the discussion with the council and the commission soon with a view to deliver new legislation that will allow europol to better support the member states to counter serious crimes and terrorism in full respect of fundamental rights.

the rapporteur. madam president, voltaire said that the best, the perfect, is the enemy of the good. we have a very good agreement here, but it is not optimal, it is not perfect; nor do we intend to be. it's hard to pretend to something like that when you're sitting at a negotiating table. but we do bring something that significantly improves the situation we had before. we have had five years of deadlock on the table since this parliament first pushed for the negotiation of this public report country by country. five years that have allowed us to go through a few milestones on the way from the panama papers to the pandora papers and each and every one of those situations has been equally infamous. i want to thank the people who have made it possible for us to have progressed. first of all, of course, to the alternative rapporteurs, in an exercise of pragmatism, but also an enormous exercise of solidarity, regardless of other issues such as the political cost. and i would also like to thank the portuguese presidency. without your help, it would have been practically impossible to even move forward. this is an agreement that sets up situations and sets up conditions so positive and so changeable that, as i say, it has been blocked for many years and has caused even some of the member countries to still hesitate to take it to court. but we're not going to take a step back. it cannot be that companies - and this is a 2015 estimate - that multinational companies - the ones we were talking about, which bill more than 750 billion euros a year - are estimated to avoid between 50 and 70 billion euros every year. this is an estimate for the year 2015 and i want to, above all, focus on that, that it's an estimate. and it's an estimate because we have no method of actually knowing that kind of information that is essential in proposing a fair tax policy and a sufficient tax policy. from now on, this will no longer be the case with regard to the taxation of these large companies and their activities within the european union, but also with regard to the list of tax havens: the black list and the grey list - a list which, by the way, may be extended if necessary. we also have a clause that will allow us to be able to renegotiate, to reimplement, to increase the scope of a standard that may be, as i say, perfect or more perfect, but which is already essentially good. i think with this agreement that we are reaching and that we are going to support we are sincerely making history. and history in democracies is not made by conquering that hill or watering the countryside with blood, it is made by a vote in a democratic parliament - as we are going to do here - and by publication in an official gazette. that's the epic in democracy. that's the way we have to make history: by building one more building, by building a floor in that one more building that's called civilization. so i ask for all the support for this text, i think a great job has been done and i want to thank again all the people who have made it possible.
the rapporteur. madam president, thank you very much, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you very much, madam commissioner, for your words. it is true that this support seems massive and it is. i would just like to clarify a few points. first of all, i don't think this is a small step. i think it's a colossal step. i think it's a unique step, a pioneer in the world. and i hope that, from this step that we are taking, others will also take the same step, because that will mean that we are also building not only a better europe, but a better world. and for those who are concerned about whether the basis is fiscal, well no, it is a basis which is based on transparency and will serve, yes, so that citizens can do their accounts, they can know how much money these multinationals are actually earning in the european union, how many jobs they are generating, how many are, in fact, the profits they have and not only in the main company, but also in the branches. and from there they can do their calculations and they can also ask their own governments for decisions and their own members of parliament for decisions. and perhaps, if necessary, to change the treaties; and perhaps, if necessary, to include the tax base in the treaties so that we can act collectively. this is what we are approving today, because you cannot sustain a society in which big multinationals that are making tons, giants, huge amounts of money, are taxing some of them less than 2% - which is what is happening in real life. let us first put our house in order: it would certainly be better to have an agreement which entails an analysis, a global examination. but first we must put our house in order: the european union. and that's the end of it. for those who said that the european union was not a state: no, it is not, unfortunately it is not, but it will be, it will be. and it will also be a federal, social and legal state.

on behalf of the left group. mr president, commissioner, behind the unattractive title of this debate, we have one of the most important issues of the moment. at the end of the day, to debate the extraction of critical raw materials is to talk about the limits of the planet, about the effort we are willing to make to make a just transition, about the audacity to change the ways of production. we're debating about what resources we're leaving for future generations. and that is that, to build a wind turbine, a tablet or a robot in a production line, you need a huge amount of raw materials. many of these are critical because they are scarce, difficult to extract or because their deposits are concentrated in certain regions of the world. only in this device do we have tungsten, coltan, tin, lithium or rare earths. many are known as blood minerals because their extraction, in addition to destroying ecosystems and people, is done at the expense of armed conflicts such as that of the democratic republic of the congo, for the control of coltan, coups d'état such as that of bolivia, for the control of lithium, or the illegal occupation of morocco over western sahara, to exploit the reserves of phosphates or tantalum. that is why we think this report is not very ambitious. given the opportunity to abandon extractivism and think about where we are going and how to orient our production model in a fair way to the challenges of climate change, we continue to bet on models that will deepen the ecosocial crisis. perhaps starting with a strategy that reduces the use of materials and recovers those that are in circulation is the wisest thing to do today.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin by thanking all the groups and the alternative rapporteurs for the great work they have done together over these months: europe is leading the fight against climate change, and after the pandemic we must lead europe's pharmaceutical and healthcare innovation. the fight against covid-19 has made us build in one year what previously probably took a generation. in record time, we have been able to lay the foundations for the future european health union: the covid-19 vaccination strategy; the reinforcement of the european centre for disease prevention and control; the reinforcement of the european medicines agency; the creation of the european health emergency preparedness and response authority - hera - and its incubator; and the new euprohealth programme, with a tenfold increase in its budget, as well as the european plan to fight cancer, which, together with the new pharmaceutical strategy, inaugurate the european decade for health, innovation and research, giving europe a greater social dimension. we have been hit by severe crises, but we have learned that science and technology are two huge social shields, along with a more competitive pharmaceutical industry and public-private collaboration. we therefore bet on innovation made in europe after decades of offshoring and also of having been too dependent on third countries, perhaps losing autonomy in a sector which is strategic. it is 20 years since the last strategy and the world has changed, so we must update the laws and the incentive system: the new strategy is the ideal framework for updating and strengthening a whole new generation of pharmaceutical regulations for this decade. the new strategy proposes a paradigm shift through six objectives. for starters, we put the patient at the centre of all health policies; we reduce time to market for medicines by aligning the ema's approval times with national agencies; and we also support a new framework for the design of innovative clinical trials by giving patients' associations a leading role in prioritising their therapeutic needs. as regards the second objective, we are ensuring that all patients have access to the most advanced treatments in the shortest possible time: we cannot tolerate a gap in access in europe of between nine and a thousand days for some treatments, or that in the last twenty years the shortage of medicines has increased twentyfold. that is why we are promoting more research into and availability of generics and biosimilars on the market, encouraging the use of gene and cell therapies, personalised medicine, nanomedicines and mrna derivatives, and standardising the implementation of the priority medicines scheme across the eu to speed up the availability of essential medicines. the third objective is to respond to untreated medical diseases, such as the more than 8 000 minority diseases of which only 5% are currently treatable, with 30 million people in europe without a response, as well as paediatric cancers, neurodegenerative diseases and antibiotic resistance, which i would dare to say is one of the silent pandemics of our continent. we therefore call for a european fund to acquire orphan medicines through joint purchases, and we also call for the harmonization of a european framework to be applied in the national plans against minority diseases. the fourth objective is that we are committed to a competitive pharmaceutical industry with supply chains that are not dependent on third countries, encouraging the production of medicines of high therapeutic value which, of course, respect quality standards and the european green deal. we therefore support a secure, predictable and less bureaucratic regulatory system and we advocate a strong framework for the protection of intellectual property rights. the fifth objective: we ensure the sustainability of our national health systems in the 27 member states, which are one of our great strengths and distinguish us from other third countries. we therefore encourage public-private partnerships to tender for funding research, the production of innovative medicines and the reuse of medicines, and we invite member states to promote the use of biosimilars. as regards objective 6, we strengthen the european union as a world leader in health to make it better prepared for future health crises by creating hera and its incubator, and by promoting trade agreements with third countries that reward innovation-based competitiveness to achieve greater access for each and every patient, not only in europe but also in the rest of the world, and by requiring third country companies accessing our market to meet european quality standards. we also promote a structured dialogue with all actors in the pharmaceutical sector to have diversified supply chains and a plan to mitigate the risk of shortages of medicines. the new pharmaceutical strategy strengthens collaboration with who and international bodies, as well as the link with the european union's industrial strategy, the sme strategy and, above all, the future european health data space. so to achieve the european health union, we must work together with patients, the scientific community, health professionals, industry and member states, together with the european institutions. this strategy balances promoting innovation, patient access and the sustainability of our national health systems in europe, putting patients at the heart of all policies. the health of europeans depends more than ever on the health of the european union and i am convinced that the european health union is one of the great pillars of this european union.
i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on his excellent report. i welcome the report, but it is true that there are many measures to support the pharmaceutical industry which somehow ignore a social component, which i think would have been good to reflect. on the one hand, a new system of research incentives is proposed, but the report does not mention the misuse of some of these incentives. for example, in the framework of the orphan medicinal products regulation, which will soon be revised. the report talks about transparency and price fixing, but we should have harmonised criteria for price fixing in the european union, with a new legislative proposal on price transparency and also reimbursement of medicines. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i think that centralized purchasing should be a general rule. finally, i also miss some mention of plasma, because we are totally dependent on third countries and the report does not mention this. that said, i congratulate you on the report, because it contributes to a fairer, more inclusive and more social health policy in the european union.

mr president, congratulations to all those involved in the process of adopting the common agricultural policy. we are at the end of some complicated debates, but at the same time at the beginning of a long road of policy implementation that will affect the lives of farmers in the coming years. the cap will enable european farmers to develop and modernise their farms, provide them with a better livelihood and a safer future for their children and families, and provide real support in their efforts to keep the countryside alive. whether it's rain, sleet, frost or blizzard, farmers have been and will continue to be the frontline soldiers in the battle to ensure food security, combat climate change and be the deciding factor in preserving biodiversity. although they are often affected by unfair competition, because of policies that are not well anchored in the realities on the ground, they have provided us all with quality food at affordable prices, and we must ensure that we maintain this capacity in the future. the money provided through the cap is nothing more than an advance paid to farmers for the food that more than 500 million european citizens enjoy every day. it is therefore the responsibility of the member states to draw up national strategic plans that put farmers at the centre, reduce red tape and ensure the sustainability of farms, and the european commission must monitor the implementation of this policy in every corner of the european union, as it is the guarantee of a better life for each of you.

in writing. the european union needs the vision of young people to shape a more democratic and stable future. their ideas, enthusiasm, involvement and dedication can make a defining contribution to the political and social architecture of europe of tomorrow. moreover, it is imperative that young people participate in electoral processes and political life. only in this way can we have a functioning democracy, where human rights and the rule of law are respected and no one is left behind. the covid pandemic has left a deep mark on the lives of young people, and 2022 must be the culmination of their efforts to overcome the disadvantages they have faced during this difficult period. youth unemployment has become an even more worrying issue because of the pandemic. this appropriation is intended to cover the financing of the european schools in the member states and the european schools in the union. the european year of youth has once again demonstrated that the young generation is a priority for the eu, so that they become active and engaged citizens, inspired by a sense of european belonging, offering the possibility to emerge collectively stronger from the pandemic and opening up opportunities and perspectives.
in writing. the crisis caused by the covid-19 pandemic has disproportionately affected young people. whether it's access to education, integration into the labour market or mental health, it's young people who have suffered the most in this period. the european youth year is thus a great opportunity to focus on solving some of the problems that young people are constantly facing. the mental health of young people is a particular concern. the pandemic has made a situation that was already dire worse. the european union therefore needs a plan for managing mental health problems, especially among young people. civic participation of young people should be particularly encouraged. civics offers significant benefits, both to society and to the individual, in particular by reducing the risk of suffering from mental health deficiencies. the european year of youth should also encourage us to reflect on the situation of young people in rural areas. the increased support for young farmers in the new cap is welcome, but young people need support beyond the agricultural sector, through actions that give them access to social and community services.
